p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Alabama — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate (the executor or administrator appointed by the probate court) may file a wrongful-death claim. Ala. Code § 6-5-410(a). (Exception: a parent may file for the death of a minor child under 19 within six months of the death. Ala. Code § 6-5-391.) — Alabama Wrongful Death Act Ala. Code § 6-5-410 — deadline in Alabama: 2 years from the date of death. Ala. Code § 6-5-410(d). Alabama courts treat this as a statute of creation, not an ordinary limitations period, so it is generally not tolled — the claim expires after two years. — what can be recovered: Alabama is unique: only punitive damages may be recovered — money meant to punish the wrongdoer and deter similar conduct, based on the seriousness of the conduct. No compensatory damages are allowed, so families cannot recover funeral costs, medical bills, lost wages, or loss of companionship as separate items. There is no cap on punitive damages in wrongful-death cases. Any recovery goes to the heirs under Alabama's distribution rules and is not subject to the deceased person's debts. — Alabama is the only state where wrongful-death recovery is punitive damages only — there is no compensation for the family's financial losses or grief, and the award is measured by how bad the defendant's conduct was. — Legal Services Alabama

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Alaska — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file the wrongful-death action, for the benefit of the surviving spouse, children, or other dependents. Alaska Stat. § 09.55.580(a). — Alaska Wrongful Death Act Alaska Stat. § 09.55.580 — deadline in Alaska: 2 years from the date of death. Alaska Stat. § 09.55.580(a). (A separate 120-day written notice applies for claims against a government entity. Alaska Stat. § 09.65.070.) — what can be recovered: The court or jury awards an amount that is fair and just, considering lost expected financial benefits, lost support, lost services and assistance, loss of consortium, and lost training and education, plus funeral and medical expenses. If the deceased left no spouse, children, or other dependents, recovery is limited to pecuniary (financial) loss and goes to the estate. Noneconomic damages are capped at the greater of $400,000 or the deceased person's life expectancy in years times $8,000 (Alaska Stat. § 09.17.010); the cap does not apply to reckless or intentional conduct. Punitive damages are allowed for outrageous, malicious, or recklessly indifferent conduct, capped at the greater of $500,000 or three times compensatory damages (Alaska Stat. § 09.17.020), with half of any punitive award going to the State. — Who benefits depends on whether the deceased left a spouse, children, or other dependents: with dependents, the recovery goes to them; without any, it is treated as estate property and limited to financial loss only. — Alaska Legal Services Corporation

p: Arizona Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Arizona — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — The surviving spouse, a surviving child, a surviving parent or guardian, or the personal representative of the deceased person (acting for the surviving spouse, children, or parents, or for the estate if none of them survive) may bring the action. Either parent may sue for the death of a child. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-612. — Arizona Wrongful Death Act Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 12-611–12-613 — deadline in Arizona: 2 years from the date of death. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-542. The discovery rule can delay the start of the clock in rare cases where the wrongful cause of death could not reasonably have been discovered. A claim against a government entity requires a notice of claim within 180 days of the death. — what can be recovered: The jury awards damages it deems fair and just for the injury resulting from the death, including funeral and burial expenses, medical bills, lost wages and benefits the deceased would have earned, loss of love, affection, companionship, consortium, and guidance, and the survivors' grief. Arizona has no cap on compensatory damages in wrongful-death cases. Punitive damages may be awarded for aggravating circumstances under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-613 (the statute's 'aggravating circumstances' language has been read by Arizona courts as allowing punitive damages), but not against the State. A separate survival action (Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 14-3110) can recover the deceased person's pre-death medical expenses and pain and suffering for the estate. — Arizona sets a priority order for who files — spouse first, then children, then parents, then the personal representative — but only one lawsuit is filed and all beneficiaries' claims are combined into it; a family member who caused the death (for example, by homicide or child abuse) is disqualified from recovering. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-612(D). — Community Legal Services

p: Arkansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Arkansas — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — The personal representative of the deceased person's estate must file the action. If there is no personal representative, the heirs at law may file — the surviving spouse, children, parents, siblings, a person who stood in loco parentis to the deceased, or a person to whom the deceased stood in loco parentis. Ark. Code Ann. § 16-62-102(b), (d). — Arkansas Wrongful Death Act Ark. Code Ann. § 16-62-102 — deadline in Arkansas: 3 years from the date of death. Ark. Code Ann. § 16-62-102(c)(1). If a nonsuit is suffered, the action must be brought within 1 year of the nonsuit. The 3-year period does not change the deadline for medical-malpractice wrongful-death claims, which is 2 years. — what can be recovered: Families may recover both compensatory and punitive damages. The estate's claim covers losses between the injury and death (medical expenses, conscious pain and suffering, and loss of life as an independent element), while the family's claim covers grief, loss of companionship, emotional suffering, and loss of financial support. Punitive damages may be awarded for willful, malicious, or reckless conduct. Arkansas has no cap on wrongful-death damages. — Arkansas has one of the broadest beneficiary lists in the country — siblings and people who stood in the place of a parent (in either direction) can share in the recovery — and its statute expressly covers the death of an unborn child, with exceptions for legal abortion, the pregnant woman's fault, and assisted reproduction. — Legal Aid of Arkansas

p: California Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in California — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — The surviving spouse, registered domestic partner, children, and issue of deceased children may file; if there is no surviving issue, the persons who would inherit by intestate succession (including the spouse or domestic partner) may file. A dependent putative spouse, the putative spouse's children, dependent stepchildren, dependent parents, and legal guardians (if the parents are deceased) may also file, as may a minor who lived in the deceased's household for the previous 180 days and depended on the deceased for at least half of their support. The decedent's personal representative may bring the action on their behalf. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 377.60. — California Wrongful Death Act Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 377.60 — deadline in California: 2 years from the date of death. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 335.1. The clock may be delayed under the discovery rule if the wrongful cause of death was not reasonably discoverable, and it is tolled (paused) for a minor plaintiff until age 18 under Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 352. A claim against a government entity requires a written government claim within 6 months of the death (Gov. Code § 911.2), and medical-malpractice wrongful-death claims follow the separate deadline in Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 340.5. — what can be recovered: Survivors may recover economic damages (lost financial support, funeral and burial expenses, the value of household services) and noneconomic damages (loss of love, companionship, comfort, care, assistance, protection, affection, society, and moral support). There is no cap on wrongful-death damages. Punitive damages are generally not available in the wrongful-death action itself, but may be available in a related survival action brought by the estate (Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 377.30). — California is unusually broad about who can sue: registered domestic partners have the same standing as spouses, and financially dependent stepchildren, a putative spouse, and even a dependent minor who lived with the deceased can qualify. Only one wrongful-death lawsuit may be filed per death, and all heirs must join it. — LawHelpCA (Legal Aid Association of California)

p: Colorado Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Colorado — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Who may file depends on timing. In the first year after the death, only the surviving spouse may file (or the spouse together with the heirs, or the heirs alone if the spouse elects in writing); if there is no spouse, the heirs or a designated beneficiary may file. In the second year, the spouse, the heirs, or a designated beneficiary together with the heirs may file. If the deceased was unmarried with no descendants and no designated beneficiary, the parents may file; since Jan. 1, 2025, siblings (or their heirs) may file if there is no spouse, no heirs, no designated beneficiary, and no surviving parent. Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-21-201. — Colorado Wrongful Death Act Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 13-21-201–13-21-204 — deadline in Colorado: 2 years from the date of death. Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 13-80-102, 13-80-108(2). A 4-year period applies when the death involved vehicular homicide combined with leaving the scene of a fatal crash. — what can be recovered: Survivors may recover economic damages (funeral and burial expenses, medical bills before death, lost income and support) with no cap, and noneconomic damages for grief, loss of companionship, and emotional distress. Noneconomic damages in wrongful death are capped at $2,125,000 for claims accruing on or after Jan. 1, 2025 (Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-21-203, as raised by HB 24-1472, with inflation adjustments starting Jan. 1, 2028); the cap does not apply if the death resulted from a felonious killing. A separate survival action (Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-20-101) covers the deceased person's own pre-death losses for the estate. — Colorado's tiered, time-based filing rule is unusual: children generally cannot file in the first year unless the surviving spouse agrees in writing, but gain the right in the second year — and only one wrongful-death action may be brought per death. Siblings were added as eligible filers only in 2025. — Colorado Legal Services

p: Connecticut Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Connecticut — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Only the executor or administrator of the deceased person's estate may file a wrongful-death claim, on behalf of the estate. Family members cannot file in their own names. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-555. — Connecticut Wrongful Death Act Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-555 — deadline in Connecticut: 2 years from the date of death, and never more than 5 years from the act or omission that caused the death. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-555(a). There is no time limit when the person responsible was convicted of (or found not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect of) murder, felony murder, arson murder, or first-degree manslaughter. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-555(b). — what can be recovered: The estate recovers 'just damages' plus the reasonable cost of medical care and funeral expenses, including lost lifetime earning capacity, the deceased person's conscious pain and suffering before death, and the loss of the capacity to carry on and enjoy life's activities — Connecticut measures damages by the value of the life lost, not only by the family's financial loss. Any recovery is paid to the estate and distributed under the will or intestacy law, after debts and expenses. A surviving spouse may separately claim loss of consortium (loss of companionship, care, and support), which must be joined with the wrongful-death action. Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 52-555a–52-555d. — Connecticut's claim belongs to the estate, not the family — so the money is distributed like any other estate asset and can be used to pay the deceased person's debts — and its damages focus on what the deceased person lost, including the enjoyment of life itself. Only a spouse (not children) can claim loss of consortium. — Statewide Legal Services of Connecticut

p: Delaware Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet

In practice the personal representative of the estate files the suit on behalf of those beneficiaries. Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, § 3724. — Delaware Wrongful Death Act Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, §§ 3721–3725 — deadline in Delaware: 2 years from the date the cause of action accrues (the date of death). Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, § 8107. Delaware also tolls the limitations period for minors and people under a mental disability until the disability is removed, plus 3 years after. Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, § 8116. — what can be recovered: Damages are set at a sum that fairly compensates for the injury from the death, considering lost expected financial benefits, lost contributions for support, loss of parental, marital, and household services (including the reasonable cost of caring for minor children), reasonable funeral expenses up to $7,000, and the mental anguish of the surviving spouse and next of kin. Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, § 3724(d). Punitive damages may be available for malicious, reckless, willful, or wanton conduct. Delaware has no cap on compensatory damages in wrongful-death cases. — Delaware is unusual in two ways: siblings are named beneficiaries alongside spouses, parents, and children, and the statute expressly allows recovery for the family's mental anguish — but funeral expenses are capped at $7,000. — Community Legal Aid Society, Inc. p: Florida Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Florida — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file the wrongful-death lawsuit, in one action on behalf of the estate and all eligible survivors. Individual family members cannot file their own claims. Fla. Stat. § 768.20. Eligible 'survivors' are the surviving spouse, children (including adopted children), parents, and blood relatives or adopted siblings who were partly or wholly dependent on the deceased for support or services. Fla. Stat. § 768.18. — Florida Wrongful Death Act Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16–768.26 — deadline in Florida: 2 years from the date of death for deaths on or after March 24, 2023. Fla. Stat. § 95.11(4)(d) (as shortened by HB 837 in 2023; the prior period was 4 years). Medical-malpractice wrongful death has a 2-year period with a 4-year statute of repose. Fla. Stat. § 95.11(4)(b). Claims against a government entity require pre-suit notice under Fla. Stat. § 768.28. — what can be recovered: Damages depend on the survivor category under Fla. Stat. § 768.21: all survivors may recover lost support and services; a surviving spouse may recover for loss of companionship and protection and for mental pain and suffering; minor children (defined as under 25) may recover for lost parental companionship, instruction, and guidance and for mental pain and suffering; adult children may recover those noneconomic damages only if there is no surviving spouse; parents of a deceased minor child (and, since 2025, parents of a deceased adult child in medical-negligence cases) may recover for mental pain and suffering. The estate separately recovers lost earnings from injury to death, lost prospective net accumulations, and medical and funeral expenses. There is no cap on compensatory damages. Punitive damages are generally not available under the Wrongful Death Act itself. A separate survival action (Fla. Stat. § 46.021) can recover the deceased person's pre-death pain, suffering, and expenses for the estate. — Florida defines 'minor children' as under 25 — much broader than the usual 18 — and in 2025 it repealed the so-called 'free kill' loophole, so adult children of decedents 25 and older, and parents of adult children 25 and older, can now recover noneconomic damages in medical-negligence wrongful-death cases (Ch. 2025-107, Laws of Fla.). Grandparents, unadopted stepchildren, and unmarried partners are not survivors under the Act. — Florida Legal Services

p: Georgia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: wrongful-death wrongful death death caused by negligence — Wrongful death in Georgia — who can file personal representative surviving spouse children parents — statute of limitations deadline from date of death — damages economic losses loss of companionship funeral medical bills punitive — what to do preserve evidence no recorded statement do not sign — what not to do wait out deadline social media first settlement criminal case — Georgia sets a strict priority order: the surviving spouse files first (and represents any minor children); if there is no surviving spouse, the surviving children file; if there are no spouse or children, the parents file; and if none of those survive, the administrator or executor of the estate files for the benefit of the next of kin. O.C.G.A. §§ 51-4-2, 51-4-4, 51-4-5. — Georgia Wrongful Death Act O.C.G.A. §§ 51-4-1–51-4-6 — deadline in Georgia: 2 years from the date of death. O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. The clock is suspended while a criminal case over the same events is pending, up to 6 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-99), and tolled for up to 5 years if the deceased person's estate has not been probated (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-92). — what can be recovered: The family recovers the 'full value of the life of the deceased' — both the economic value (lost wages, benefits, and earning capacity) and the intangible value (loss of companionship, care, guidance, and the deceased person's own enjoyment of life) — calculated without deducting for the personal expenses the deceased would have had if they had lived. O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1(1). There is no cap on compensatory damages. The estate has a separate claim for medical bills, funeral costs, and the deceased person's pre-death pain and suffering, which can be reached by creditors. The surviving spouse is guaranteed at least one-third of the family's recovery. O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2(d). — Georgia creates two separate claims from one death: the family's wrongful-death claim for the 'full value of the life' (which belongs to the family, not the estate, and cannot be taken by creditors) and the estate's claim for bills and pre-death suffering. Only one person in the priority order may file, and an estranged surviving spouse still outranks adult children. — Georgia Legal Services Program

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Alaska — vote comes back after the sentence is complete Only a felony involving moral turpitude takes away the right to vote, from the date of conviction until unconditional discharge. A felony not involving moral turpitude, and any misdemeanor, never takes the vote away, even while incarcerated. Unconditional discharge means release from all Department of Corrections custody and supervision, including prison, halfway house, electronic monitoring, probation, and parole. — restoration automatic The right returns by law upon unconditional discharge. The person must then get proof of unconditional discharge from the Department of Corrections or supervising entity, submit it to the Division of Elections, and re-register to vote. No discretionary application or pardon is required. — fines fees restitution block not applicable The statute does not list payment of fines, fees, or restitution as a voting condition; restoration turns on unconditional discharge. Unpaid financial obligations can in some cases delay discharge from supervision, so a person should confirm discharge status with the Department of Corrections or the Division of Elections. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Alaska Stat. § 15.05.030 Alaska Stat. § 15.05.030 — Alaska is unusual in that only felonies involving moral turpitude disenfranchise at all, so many incarcerated Alaskans, including people held pretrial and people serving misdemeanor sentences, remain eligible to vote by absentee ballot. — Alaska Legal Services Corporation

t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Arizona — vote comes back after the sentence is complete and fines/fees are paid A felony conviction suspends the right to vote until civil rights are restored. Restoration requires completing the full sentence, including prison, probation or community supervision, and paying court-ordered victim restitution and fines/fees. A single in-state felony is restored automatically on completion; two or more felonies, or a felony from another state or federal court, require a court application. — restoration it depends Single Arizona felony: automatic on completion of probation or absolute discharge from imprisonment and payment of restitution; re-register to vote. Two or more felonies, or an out-of-state or federal felony: apply to the Superior Court (in the county of conviction, or the county of residence for federal/out-of-state convictions); for a prison sentence, the application generally cannot be filed until two years after completion of imprisonment and supervision, and a judge decides whether to grant it. — fines fees restitution block yes Automatic restoration for a first offender requires payment of any victim restitution imposed, and the Secretary of State's guide also requires payment of other court-ordered fines and fees before restoration; unpaid restitution blocks automatic restoration. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Ariz. t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Florida — vote comes back permanent for some offenses For most felonies, the right to vote returns once the person has completed all terms of the sentence, including prison, parole, probation, and payment of all fines, fees, costs, and restitution ordered as part of the sentence. But a Florida conviction for murder or a felony sexual offense is excluded: the right is lost permanently unless restored by the State Clemency Board (the Governor and Cabinet). — restoration it depends Most felonies: automatic once all sentence terms are complete, including payment; then register to vote, and the person may request an advisory opinion from the Division of Elections if unsure about fines or fees. t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Georgia — vote comes back after the sentence is complete A felony conviction takes away the right to vote until the sentence is fully complete, including prison, parole, and probation. The right then returns automatically. People on misdemeanor probation, and people serving an unrevoked First Offender or Conditional Discharge sentence for a felony, can vote while serving that sentence. — restoration automatic No application, pardon, or expungement is needed. Once the sentence is complete, simply re-register to vote. If unsure whether the sentence is complete, request a Certificate of Sentence Completion from the Department of Community Supervision. — fines fees restitution block no According to the Georgia Secretary of State and the Georgia Justice Project (July 2024), a felony sentence is considered complete even with outstanding monetary obligations other than fines, such as unpaid restitution, fees, costs, or surcharges, and fines imposed as a condition of probation are automatically cancelled on completion of probation. However, if probation was extended because fines were not paid, the person is still on probation and not yet eligible. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Ga. Excluded cases: submit an Application for Restoration of Civil Rights to the Department of Corrections for the governor's consideration of a partial pardon. — fines fees restitution block no For the automatic-restoration path, the state's FAQ states expressly that rights are restored even if restitution, fines, or other court-ordered money has not been paid. Exception: the individual-application path for excluded offenses requires verification that restitution has been paid in full. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Kentucky Constitution, Section 145 (as implemented by Governor's Executive Order 2019-003, Dec. 12, 2019) Ky. t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in West Virginia — vote comes back after the sentence is complete A felony, treason or election-bribery conviction takes the vote away while the person is serving the sentence, including imprisonment, probation and parole. The right is restored automatically on completion of the full sentence. — restoration automatic No application or pardon is needed once the sentence, including probation and parole, is complete; re-register to vote. p: Wisconsin Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Wisconsin — vote comes back after the sentence is complete A felony, treason or bribery conviction takes the vote away until the person is off paper: the whole sentence must be complete, including imprisonment, parole, probation and extended supervision. The right is then restored automatically. — restoration automatic No application, court order or pardon is needed once off paper; the Department of Corrections or the county jailer must notify the person in writing that the right is restored, and the person must re-register to vote, as the old registration does not carry over. — fines fees restitution block no The restoration statute turns on completion of imprisonment, probation, parole or extended supervision and does not require payment of fines, fees or restitution. Some secondary guides describe being off paper as including payment, but that is not in the statute; payment can delay completion only if it is a condition of supervision that has not been satisfied, so confirm off-paper status with the probation or parole agent if money is owed. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Wis. p: Wyoming Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: felon voting rights disenfranchisement restoration — Felon voting rights in Wyoming — vote comes back permanent for some offenses A felony conviction takes the vote away. People convicted of a first-time nonviolent felony, or nonviolent felonies from the same occurrence, get voting rights back after completing the full sentence, including probation and parole. People convicted of a violent felony, a repeat felony, or a felony that is not first-time nonviolent can get the vote back only by a governor-issued certificate of restoration, and federal convictions are not eligible for restoration through the Wyoming Department of Corrections. — restoration it depends For a first-time nonviolent Wyoming conviction completed on or after January 1, 2010, the Department of Corrections issues a certificate of restoration of voting rights automatically after sentence completion; people who completed before that date, or were convicted outside Wyoming, must submit a written request on the department's form. Anyone else must apply to the Governor for a certificate of restoration. Once restored, re-register to vote. — fines fees restitution block no The statute does not list fines, fees or restitution as part of the sentence for voting restoration, and a sentence does not include fines or restitution imposed separately by court order. Payment can still matter indirectly if it is a condition of probation or parole that must be satisfied before the sentence is complete. — probation parole jail pretrial misdemeanor absentee ballot re-register — voting while ineligible crime check registration election office — Wyo. Stat. §§ 6-10-106, 7-13-105 Wyo. Stat. §§ 6-10-106, 7-13-105 — A 2023 law (SF 120, effective July 1, 2023) made voting restoration automatic on sentence completion for first-time nonviolent felonies, removing the old five-year wait for the vote; the five-year wait still applies to the other rights lost under the statute, such as jury service and holding office. h: Zoning, variances & land use in Alabama
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Alabama — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance is granted only where special conditions make literal enforcement of the ordinance an 'unnecessary hardship' and the spirit of the ordinance is still observed. Alabama courts grant variances sparingly, only in peculiar and exceptional circumstances. — how to apply Apply to your city or town's board of adjustment (five members) for a variance from the zoning ordinance. The board holds a hearing and can grant the variance only if you show special conditions unique to your property that make strict enforcement an unnecessary hardship, and that the variance will not harm the public interest. You cannot get a variance to allow a use the ordinance forbids. — appeal An aggrieved party may appeal a board of adjustment decision to the circuit court under Ala. Code § 11-52-81. deadline 15 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful use that predates a zoning change may continue as a grandfathered use until it is lost through abandonment. Expansion and abandonment details are set by local ordinance. — Zoning Enabling Act Ala. p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Alaska
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Alaska — variance test unnecessary hardship The statute frames the test as whether literal enforcement would deprive the owner of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in the district. A variance is barred if the hardship is self-caused, if it would permit a prohibited use, or if it is sought only to relieve money hardship. The wording is unusual and does not track the classic 'unnecessary hardship' formula, so it is flagged as ambiguous below. — how to apply Apply to your borough or city planning commission or board of adjustment (or hearing officer), which holds a hearing on the variance. You must show special conditions affecting your property, that the hardship is not of your own making, and that the variance would not allow a prohibited use or simply save you money. Home-rule boroughs are not bound by the state statute and set their own procedures. — appeal An aggrieved person appeals a variance decision to the superior court under AS 29.40.060, heard solely on the record as an administrative appeal. Alaska Appellate Rule 602(a)(2) generally requires filing the notice of appeal within 30 days after the decision is mailed or distributed, once the decision states it is final. deadline not stated in the statute — nonconforming use varies — it depends on local law No state statute protects nonconforming uses; whether a grandfathered use may continue, expand, or is lost by abandonment is set entirely by local ordinance (for example, Anchorage Municipal Code chapter 21.13). — Planning, Platting, and Land Use Regulation Alaska Stat. § 29.40.010 et seq. — Alaska Department of Commerce, Community & Economic Development, Division of Community and Regional Affairs — Much of Alaska has no zoning at all, and home-rule boroughs are exempt from the state framework law, so a homeowner's first step is to find out whether their borough or city even has zoning. t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Arizona — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance is granted only if special circumstances (size, shape, topography, location, or surroundings) mean strict enforcement deprives the property of privileges enjoyed by other property in the same district. The hardship must not be self-imposed, and a variance can never allow a prohibited use. — how to apply Apply to your city or town board of adjustment (or, in unincorporated areas, the county board of adjustment) for a variance, with a public hearing. You must show the special circumstances of your lot, that the problem is not of your own making, and that the variance keeps with the spirit of the ordinance. t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in South Carolina — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance requires unnecessary hardship proved by four written findings: extraordinary and exceptional conditions peculiar to the property, conditions that do not generally apply to other property nearby, application of the ordinance would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict use of the property, and the variance will not substantially harm adjacent property or the character of the district. — how to apply Apply to the local board of zoning appeals, which holds a public hearing and may grant a variance only if it makes and explains in writing all four findings in Section 6-29-800. The board may not use a variance to allow a use not otherwise permitted in the district, extend a nonconforming use, or change zoning district boundaries. — appeal Appeal a board of zoning appeals decision to the Circuit Court under Section 6-29-820 by filing a petition stating plainly how the decision is contrary to law; the property owner may also request pre-litigation mediation. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use limited — protection has conditions State law lets the local governing body provide for the continuance, restoration, reconstruction, extension or substitution of nonconformities, but it also lets the locality terminate a nonconformity by setting a period in which it must cease or be brought into conformance, or by an amortization formula allowing recovery of the investment. — South Carolina Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act of 1994 S.C. Code Ann. Sections 6-29-310 to 6-29-860 (zoning: Sections 6-29-710 to 6-29-850; nonconformities: Section 6-29-730; variance: Section 6-29-800; appeal: Section 6-29-820) — Municipal Association of South Carolina — South Carolina is distinctive in expressly barring use variances: a variance can never authorize a use the district does not already allow, so a homeowner who wants a different use must seek a rezoning or a special exception instead. — South Carolina Legal Services

p: South Dakota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in South Dakota
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in South Dakota — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance requires unnecessary hardship: because of special conditions on the property, literal enforcement of the ordinance would cause unnecessary hardship, and the variance must not harm the public interest. Financial loss alone is not enough. — how to apply Apply to the local board of adjustment (in many towns the city council or planning commission sits as the board). The board holds a public hearing and decides the request, and a two-thirds concurring vote is needed to grant a variance. — appeal An aggrieved person may petition a court of record (circuit court) for a writ of certiorari, asking the court to review whether the board's decision was illegal. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful use that existed when a zoning ordinance was adopted may continue even though it no longer conforms. If the nonconforming use is discontinued for more than one year, any later use must conform to the current ordinance. — Municipal Planning and Zoning SDCL § 11-4-17 — South Dakota Municipal League — South Dakota has no single statewide zoning code; cities zone under SDCL chapter 11-4 and counties under chapter 11-2, so the local ordinance controls most details, including what counts as a nonconforming use. — Dakota Plains Legal Services

p: Tennessee Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Tennessee
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Tennessee — variance test varies — no single statewide test The statute blends both tests in one clause, speaking of peculiar and exceptional practical difficulties or undue hardship from the lot's shape, size, or topography. Local boards and courts also require a showing that strict enforcement would deprive the owner of any reasonable use of the land. — how to apply Apply to the local board of zoning appeals, which holds a public hearing after notice to nearby owners. You must show the hardship comes from conditions unique to your lot, not from something you did or from conditions shared by the whole neighborhood. — appeal A board of zoning appeals decision is reviewed by a petition for writ of certiorari in chancery or circuit court, which reviews the record rather than holding a new trial on the facts. deadline 60 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful use that predates a zoning change may generally continue, but local ordinances usually bar expanding it or changing it to a different nonconforming use, and discontinuing it can end the protection. — Municipal Zoning Tenn. Code Ann. § 13-7-207 — Tennessee Municipal League — Tennessee counties zone under a separate part of the same chapter (Tenn. Code Ann. title 13, chapter 7, part 3), and the board must tell parties in writing of their right to seek judicial review under title 27, chapter 9. — Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands

p: Texas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Texas
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Texas — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance requires unnecessary hardship: due to special conditions, literal enforcement would cause unnecessary hardship, the variance is not against the public interest, and the spirit of the ordinance is observed. Since 2021 the board may treat very high compliance costs or a large loss of buildable area as grounds for hardship. — how to apply Apply to the city's board of adjustment, which holds a public hearing and decides the request; a 75 percent concurring vote of the board is needed to grant a variance. The board cannot grant a variance that allows a land use the ordinance otherwise prohibits. — appeal An aggrieved person, a taxpayer, or a municipal officer may file a verified petition in district court, county court, or county court at law, and the court may issue a writ of certiorari to review the board's decision. deadline 10 days — nonconforming use varies — it depends on local law Chapter 211 sets no single statewide rule for grandfathered uses, so protection depends on the city's ordinance; a lawful nonconforming use is commonly allowed to continue but not expand, and a city may phase some uses out over time. Separately, Chapter 245 protects vested rights in a pending permit application. — Municipal Zoning Authority Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 211.009 — Texas Municipal League — Cities may zone only inside their city limits: a city cannot zone land in its extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ), where it may regulate subdivision and platting but not the use, height, bulk, or density of buildings. Texas counties have no general zoning power, and Houston has no comprehensive zoning ordinance. — Lone Star Legal Aid

p: Utah Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Utah
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Utah — variance test unnecessary hardship Utah uses an unreasonable-hardship test with five required findings, including special circumstances tied to the property and that the variance is essential to enjoy a substantial property right others in the zone have. A hardship that is self-imposed or purely economic does not count, and a use variance may not be granted at all. — how to apply Apply to the local appeal authority (a hearing officer, board, or other body the city or county designates), which decides the variance after a hearing. All five statutory findings must be made in the applicant's favor for the variance to be valid. — appeal After exhausting the local appeal-authority process, an adversely affected person may petition the district court for review; the court presumes the decision is valid and asks only whether it was arbitrary, capricious, or illegal. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A nonconforming use or noncomplying structure may continue and pass to a future owner, and a structure destroyed by fire or other calamity may generally be rebuilt unless the use was abandoned. A city may end a use by amortization over a reasonable time to recover the investment, or for abandonment. — Municipal Land Use, Development, and Management Act Utah Code § 10-9a-702 — Utah League of Cities and Towns — Utah also has a Property Rights Ombudsman in the Department of Commerce that gives free help on land-use disputes, and a landowner can ask it to arbitrate a takings claim, which pauses the 30-day court deadline. — Utah Legal Services

p: Vermont Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Vermont
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Vermont — variance test unnecessary hardship Vermont has a strict five-part unnecessary-hardship test: unique physical conditions on the lot, no possibility of developing in strict conformity, hardship not created by the applicant, no harm to the neighborhood's character or neighbors, and the smallest variance possible. — how to apply Apply to the local board of adjustment or development review board, which holds a hearing and must make written findings on all five hardship factors. A separate, easier test applies only to structures that are primarily renewable-energy structures. — appeal An interested person who participated in the local proceeding may appeal to the Environmental Division of the Superior Court; Act 250 decisions of a District Environmental Commission are appealed the same way, also to the Environmental Division. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful use that predates a zoning bylaw may continue, but local bylaws limit enlarging or changing it, and abandoning it can end the protection. A nonconforming use is separate from Act 250 approval, which a project may still need. — Municipal and Regional Planning and Development Act Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 24, § 4469 — Vermont League of Cities and Towns — Vermont is two-track: town zoning under 24 V.S.A. chapter 117 is only half the story, because Act 250 (10 V.S.A. chapter 151) requires a separate state land-use permit from a District Environmental Commission for larger developments, judged against ten criteria. Recent housing laws require towns to allow duplexes where single-family homes are allowed and have narrowed Act 250 review in town centers. — Vermont Legal Aid (via VTLawHelp.org, with Legal Services Vermont)

p: Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Virginia
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Virginia — variance test unnecessary hardship A variance is granted only if strict application would unreasonably restrict use of the property or if a physical condition of the property causes hardship, and the applicant must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence. The hardship must not be self-created, the variance cannot allow a prohibited use or change the zoning classification, and no other local process may offer the same relief. — how to apply Apply to the local board of zoning appeals, which holds a public hearing and decides the request; the board's members are appointed by the circuit court. The applicant carries the burden of proof on every part of the variance test. — appeal An aggrieved person may file a petition in the circuit court for the county or city, and the court reviews the board's decision by certiorari, with the board's findings of fact presumed correct unless rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful nonconforming use may continue, but it generally cannot be enlarged, extended, or rebuilt after substantial destruction for the nonconforming use, and local ordinances commonly treat about two years of disuse as abandonment that ends the protection. — Virginia Zoning Enabling Act (Code of Virginia, Title 15.2, Chapter 22) Va. Code § 15.2-2309 — Virginia Municipal League — Virginia also has a separate vested-rights statute (Va. Code § 15.2-2307) protecting a landowner who made substantial expenditures in good faith under a valid permit before a zoning change, and Virginia has nine regional legal aid programs rather than one statewide provider. — Virginia Legal Aid Society

p: Washington Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Washington
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Washington — variance test varies — no single statewide test Washington has no single statewide variance test; county and city enabling laws speak of special circumstances that deprive the property of rights enjoyed by nearby properties in the same zone, and each local ordinance sets its own test, so some use an unnecessary-hardship test and others a practical-difficulty test. — how to apply Apply to the local board of adjustment or hearing examiner, depending on the city or county's system, which holds a hearing and decides whether the special circumstances and no-detriment conditions in the local ordinance are met. — appeal An individual variance decision is challenged by filing a land use petition in superior court under the Land Use Petition Act (LUPA), which replaced certiorari for local land-use decisions. A challenge to the zoning rules themselves, rather than one property's variance, goes to the Growth Management Hearings Board. deadline 21 days — nonconforming use varies — it depends on local law There is no single statewide grandfathering rule; local ordinances generally let a lawful nonconforming use continue but bar expanding it or changing it to another nonconforming use, and discontinuing it for the period the ordinance sets can end the protection. — Growth Management Act RCW 36.70A — Washington State Department of Commerce — Growth Management Services — The Growth Management Act (RCW 36.70A) requires fast-growing counties and cities to adopt comprehensive plans and development regulations, and the Growth Management Hearings Board hears petitions that a plan or regulation violates the Act, filed within 60 days of publication. A variance itself is not a Growth Management Hearings Board matter. — Northwest Justice Project

p: West Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in West Virginia
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in West Virginia — variance test unnecessary hardship The board of zoning appeals may grant a variance only where, owing to special conditions, literal enforcement would result in unnecessary hardship, the variance is not against the public interest, and the spirit of the ordinance is observed with substantial justice done. — how to apply Apply to the local board of zoning appeals on the board's form; the board must set a hearing within 10 days of receiving the appeal and hold it within 45 days, then issue a written decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law within 30 days after the hearing. — appeal A board of zoning appeals decision may be reviewed by the circuit court of the county where the property is located on a verified petition for a writ of certiorari. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful use that predates a zoning ordinance may generally continue, but local ordinances limit expanding or changing it, and abandoning it can end the protection. — Land Use Planning (West Virginia Code, Chapter 8A) W. Va. Code § 8A-8-9 — West Virginia Municipal League — Many West Virginia counties and smaller towns have never adopted zoning at all, so the first question for a homeowner is often whether any zoning ordinance covers the property; where one exists, Chapter 8A supplies the board, hearing, and appeal framework. — Legal Aid of West Virginia

p: Wisconsin Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Wisconsin
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Wisconsin — variance test varies — no single statewide test Wisconsin splits the test by type: an area variance (setback, height, lot size) requires showing strict compliance would unreasonably prevent a permitted use or be unnecessarily burdensome, while a use variance requires showing strict compliance would leave no reasonable use of the property. In both cases the hardship must come from conditions unique to the property, not the owner. — how to apply Apply to the local board of appeals (cities) or board of adjustment (counties), which holds a public hearing and must state its reasoning on the record for why the statutory criteria are or are not met. The owner bears the burden of proving unnecessary hardship. — appeal An aggrieved person, a taxpayer, or a municipal officer may commence an action in circuit court seeking the remedy available by certiorari, and the court may reverse, affirm, or modify the board's decision. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue A lawful nonconforming use may continue, but repairs or alterations over 50 percent of the structure's assessed value for the nonconforming use may be barred, and if the use is discontinued for 12 months any future use must conform to the ordinance. — City Planning and Zoning (Wisconsin Statutes, section 62.23) Wis. Stat. § 62.23(7)(hb) — League of Wisconsin Municipalities — Counties zone under a parallel statute, Wis. Stat. § 59.69, which carries the same 50-percent repair limit and 12-month discontinuance rule for nonconforming uses, and Wisconsin's shoreland zoning rules add separate limits near navigable waters. — Legal Action of Wisconsin

p: Wyoming Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Zoning, variances & land use in Wyoming
t: zoning variances land use variance nonconforming use grandfathered — Zoning, variances & land use in Wyoming — variance test unnecessary hardship Wyoming's municipal test is hardship framed as loss of reasonable use: strict application must deprive the owner of the reasonable use of the land or building because of a physical condition or special circumstances peculiar to the property, and the adjustment granted must be the minimum needed. — how to apply Apply to the city or town board of adjustment, which fixes a reasonable time for a public hearing, gives notice to interested parties, and decides the request; a majority concurring vote is needed to reverse an official's decision or grant an adjustment. — appeal A board of adjustment decision is reviewed by petition to the district court under the Wyoming Rules of Appellate Procedure, which govern judicial review of local land-use decisions. deadline 30 days — nonconforming use protected — the use may continue An existing lawful use may continue after a zoning resolution is adopted, and a county may not end it merely because the use no longer conforms. Altering or adding to it is limited, and a use that is discontinued loses its protected status. — Municipal Zoning (Wyoming Statutes, Title 15, Chapter 1, Article 6) Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 15-1-608 — Wyoming Association of Municipalities — Wyoming has no statewide zoning code: cities zone under Title 15, Chapter 1, Article 6, counties zone unincorporated areas under Title 18, Chapter 5, Article 2, and much rural land is unzoned, so the local ordinance or resolution is decisive. — Legal Aid of Wyoming

p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Alabama — notification deadline 45 days Notice must go out as fast as possible and without unreasonable delay, and no later than 45 days after the company determines a breach happened that is reasonably likely to cause substantial harm. Law enforcement can ask for a delay if notice would interfere with a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Only if more than 1,000 Alabama residents must be notified — then the company must also tell the Attorney General and the consumer reporting agencies within 45 days. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, so set one up with each bureau if your information was exposed. — Alabama Data Breach Notification Act of 2018 Ala. Code § 8-38-1 et seq. — Office of the Attorney General of Alabama — Alabama's law is harm-based: if the company investigates and documents that harm is not reasonably likely, it may skip notifying you — but it must first send that written determination to the Attorney General. — Legal Services Alabama

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Alaska — notification deadline without unreasonable delay The law sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expeditious time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to figure out the scope of the breach and fix the system. Police can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice no — the law does not require it No. Alaska does not require the company to notify the Attorney General about a breach. If more than 1,000 residents are affected, the company must notify the nationwide credit bureaus instead. The AG only gets a written notice if the company claims no harm is likely and skips notifying you. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue limited — only in some situations — freeze your credit Alaska's own freeze law sits in the same act, and federal law makes freezes free: you can freeze your credit file with each of the three bureaus at no cost and lift it for free when you apply for credit. — Personal Information Protection Act Alaska Stat. § 45.48.010 et seq. — Alaska Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General — Alaska has no fixed deadline in days and no duty to tell the Attorney General, so if you hear nothing, check your credit reports and consider a freeze rather than waiting for an official notice. — Alaska Legal Services Corporation

p: Arizona Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Arizona — notification deadline 45 days The clock starts when the company's investigation determines a breach occurred. Notice must be made in the most expedient manner possible and without unreasonable delay, and in any case within 45 days after that determination. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Only if the breach requires notifying more than 1,000 people — then the company must also notify the Attorney General and the director of the Arizona Department of Homeland Security in writing, within the same 45 days. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name. — Arizona Data Breach Notification Law A.R.S. §§ 18-551–18-552 — Arizona Attorney General's Office — Arizona is unusual in also requiring notice to the state homeland security director for big breaches, and the breach notice itself must include the toll-free numbers for the three credit bureaus and the FTC. — Community Legal Services

p: Arkansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Arkansas — notification deadline without unreasonable delay Arkansas sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expedient time and manner possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. No notice is needed at all if the company determines after investigation that there is no reasonable likelihood of harm. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Only if the breach affects the personal information of more than 1,000 individuals — then the company must tell the Attorney General at the same time it notifies you, or within 45 days after determining harm is reasonably likely, whichever comes first. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name. — Personal Information Protection Act Ark. Code Ann. § 4-110-101 et seq. — Office of the Arkansas Attorney General — Arkansas has no fixed number of days for notifying you, and notice can be skipped entirely if the company decides harm is not reasonably likely — so watch your accounts and credit reports yourself. — Legal Aid of Arkansas

p: California Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in California — notification deadline 30 days Since January 1, 2026, notice must go out within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the breach, with delays allowed only for law enforcement needs or to determine the scope and restore the system. The notice must be in plain language, titled 'Notice of Data Breach,' with set headings. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches If more than 500 California residents must be notified from a single breach, the company must electronically send a sample copy of the notice to the Attorney General within 15 calendar days after notifying consumers. The Attorney General publishes these notices. — credit monitoring required — the company must pay for it — can you sue limited — only in some situations — freeze your credit Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and California law also gives you a free freeze right. A freeze is the strongest step you can take — it stops new accounts from being opened in your name. — California Data Breach Notification Law Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82 — California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General — California is the strongest of these ten states: a 30-day deadline, a sample notice to the Attorney General for breaches over 500 people, and a required offer of at least 12 months of free identity-theft prevention services if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed and the company was the source of the breach. Note the Legal Aid Association of California is a statewide association, not a law firm — it points you to your local legal aid office. — Legal Aid Association of California

p: Colorado Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Colorado — notification deadline 30 days Notice must go out in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches If the breach is reasonably believed to have affected 500 or more Colorado residents, the company must also notify the Attorney General within 30 days of determining the breach occurred. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name. — Notification of Security Breach Colo. Rev. Stat. § 6-1-716 — Colorado Attorney General's Office (Colorado Department of Law) — Colorado's 30-day deadline is one of the shortest in the country, and the breach notice must include the toll-free numbers for the credit bureaus and the FTC plus a statement about fraud alerts and security freezes. — Colorado Legal Services

p: Connecticut Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Connecticut — notification deadline 60 days Notice must go out without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery of the breach, unless a shorter time is required under federal law. If more affected residents turn up after 60 days, the company must still notify them as quickly as possible. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach will not likely cause harm. — attorney general notice yes — for every breach Yes — for every breach, with no minimum number of people. The company must notify the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies affected residents. — credit monitoring required — the company must pay for it — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus. Connecticut's breach notice must also tell you how to place a freeze on your credit file. — Breach of Security Involving Computerized Data Containing Personal Information Conn. Gen. Stat. § 36a-701b — Connecticut Office of the Attorney General — Connecticut is one of only three states in this set that require free identity-theft help: if your Social Security number was involved, the company must offer you at least 24 months of free identity-theft prevention and mitigation services, and the Attorney General must be told about every breach, not just big ones. — Connecticut Legal Services

p: Delaware Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Delaware — notification deadline 60 days Notice must be made without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the company determines a breach occurred, unless federal law requires a shorter time or law enforcement asks for a delay. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach is unlikely to harm you. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Only if more than 500 Delaware residents must be notified — then the company must tell the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies residents. — credit monitoring required — the company must pay for it — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and Delaware's own law requires the breach notice to include information on how to place a freeze on your credit file. — Computer Security Breaches 6 Del. C. § 12B-101 et seq. — Delaware Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General — If your Social Security number was in the breach, Delaware requires the company to offer you one year of free credit monitoring and to explain how to freeze your credit — take them up on both. — Community Legal Aid Society, Inc. (CLASI)

p: Florida Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Florida — notification deadline 30 days Notice to you must go out as expeditiously as practicable and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred or has reason to believe one did. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation, and the company can get 15 extra days if it shows good cause in writing to the Department. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Yes — the notice goes to the Department of Legal Affairs (the Attorney General's office). Any breach affecting 500 or more Floridians must be reported to the Department within 30 days, and even a 'no harm' determination must be sent to the Department within 30 days. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name. — Florida Information Protection Act of 2014 Fla. Stat. § 501.171 — Florida Attorney General, Department of Legal Affairs — Florida has one of the tightest deadlines (30 days) and makes the company report to the state even when it claims no harm will result — if you get a breach letter, check whether the company offered any free services, because Florida does not require it to. — Florida Legal Services

p: Georgia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Georgia — notification deadline without unreasonable delay Georgia sets no number of days. The company must notify you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice no — the law does not require it No. The notification statute never names the Attorney General, so a private company has no duty to tell the AG about a breach. If more than 10,000 Georgia residents must be notified at once, the company must instead notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Georgia has its own freeze law, and federal law makes freezes free at all three bureaus — place one if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed. — Georgia Personal Identity Protection Act O.C.G.A. § 10-1-910 et seq. — Georgia Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General — Georgia is the weakest timeline in this set: no deadline in days, no notice to the Attorney General, and no required credit monitoring — so act on your own fast: freeze your credit and watch your accounts yourself. — Georgia Legal Services Program

p: Hawaii Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Hawaii — notification deadline without unreasonable delay Notice must go out without unreasonable delay after discovery or notification of the breach, allowing time to find contact information, determine the scope, and restore the system. Hawaii sets no fixed number of days; law enforcement may ask for a delay in writing if notice would impede an investigation or jeopardize national security. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches Only if the business notifies more than 1,000 people at one time must it also notify, in writing and without unreasonable delay, the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (not the Attorney General directly) and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue yes — freeze your credit Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit. — Security Breach of Personal Information HRS § 487N-1 et seq. — Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs) — Hawaii is unusual in that breach reports go to the Office of Consumer Protection rather than the Attorney General, and only for breaches affecting more than 1,000 people. The breach notice itself must advise you to stay vigilant by reviewing account statements and checking your free credit reports. — Legal Aid Society of Hawaii

p: Idaho Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Idaho — notification deadline without unreasonable delay After a good-faith, prompt investigation finds that misuse of your information has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur, notice must go out as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay. Idaho sets no fixed number of days; notice may be delayed if law enforcement says it would impede a criminal investigation. — attorney general notice it depends — only for larger breaches A city, county, or state agency must notify the Idaho Attorney General within 24 hours of discovering a breach. A private business may report a breach to the Attorney General but is not required to do so. — credit monitoring not required by the breach law — can you sue no — freeze your credit Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit. — Disclosure of Breach of Security of Computerized Personal Information Idaho Code §§ 28-51-104 to 28-51-107 — Idaho Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division — Idaho's duty to tell you only kicks in after the investigation finds misuse happened or is reasonably likely — so a breach alone, with no likely misuse, may never trigger a notice to you. Only government agencies, not private companies, must tell the Attorney General, and they have just 24 hours to do it. — Idaho Legal Aid Services

p: Illinois Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: data breach response breach notification identity theft credit freeze — Data breach response in Illinois — notification deadline without unreasonable delay A data collector must notify you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovering or being told of the breach. p: Rhode Island Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Data breach response in Rhode Island
