p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Alabama — adverse possession 20 years Standard period is 20 years of continuous possession under the common-law rule (adverse possession by prescription). It drops to 10 years under Ala. Code § 6-5-200 if the claimant has a deed or other color of title recorded for 10 years, has listed the land for taxes for 10 years, or inherited it from someone already in possession. Possession must be actual, open and notorious, hostile (without the owner's permission), exclusive, continuous, and under a claim of right. Paying taxes is not required for the 20-year route. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement gives only the right to keep using someone else's land (for example, a driveway or road), not ownership of it. It takes 20 years of use that is adverse to the owner, under a claim of right, exclusive, continuous and uninterrupted, with the owner's actual or presumed knowledge. Use of a private road is presumed to be permissive in Alabama, so the claimant carries a heavy burden to prove the use was hostile. A 10-year route under Ala. Code § 6-5-200 exists only in limited cases (recorded color of title, tax listing, or descent). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Alabama courts recognize easements by necessity and by implication where there is genuine necessity (not mere convenience) and the two parcels were once under common ownership. Separately, Ala. Code § 18-3-1 lets a landlocked owner get a right-of-way up to 30 feet wide through probate court, paying the neighbor for the land taken. — Adverse Possession — Ala. Code § 6-5-200 Ala. Code § 6-5-200 — Alabama State Bar — Lawyer Referral Service — Alabama has one of the longest standard periods in the country (20 years) alongside a separate 10-year statutory shortcut, plus its own probate-court process for landlocked access. — Legal Services Alabama

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Alaska — adverse possession 10 years Standard period is 10 years of uninterrupted, adverse, notorious possession based on a good faith but mistaken belief that the land lies within the boundaries of adjacent land the claimant already owns (Alaska Stat. § 09.45.052(a)). It is 7 years if the claimant holds color and claim of title (a document that looks like title, even if defective). Since a 2003 law change, a knowing squatter cannot win — good faith is required. No claim can be made against land owned by the state or the United States, and the general 10-year limit for recovering real property is AS 09.10.030. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road or path), not ownership. It takes 10 years of continuous, uninterrupted, adverse, open and notorious use under AS 09.10.030. Unlike adverse possession for ownership, the 2003 good-faith amendments do not apply to prescriptive easements, so a knowing user can still gain an easement. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Alaska courts recognize easements by necessity and implied easements for landlocked parcels (see Williams v. Fagnan). The access must be genuinely necessary, not just more convenient, and the owner seeking it generally must pay for it and maintain it. — Adverse Possession — Alaska Stat. § 09.45.052 Alaska Stat. § 09.45.052 — Alaska Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — Alaska's 2003 reform made it one of the hardest states for adverse possession — bad-faith squatters are barred — and lands owned by Alaska Native corporations have extra federal protection against such claims. — Alaska Legal Services Corporation

p: Arizona Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Arizona — adverse possession 10 years Standard period is 10 years of peaceable, adverse possession while cultivating, using and enjoying the land (A.R.S. § 12-526; definition in § 12-521). It drops to 5 years if the claimant holds a duly recorded deed and has paid the taxes on the property (§ 12-525), and a 5-year rule also applies to city lots claimed under a recorded deed (§ 12-524). Possession must be actual and visible, continuous, hostile, and under a claim of right inconsistent with the owner's claim, and cannot cover more than 160 acres. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a driveway), not ownership. It takes 10 years of actual and visible use that is open, notorious, hostile (without permission), continuous, and under a claim of right. Unlike adverse possession, the use does not have to be exclusive — the owner may keep using the land too. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Arizona courts recognize an implied easement (way) of necessity when land is sold with no outlet, if the parcels were once under common ownership and the need existed when they were split. Separately, A.R.S. § 12-1202 lets a landlocked owner condemn a private way of necessity across a neighbor's land through court, but the owner must pay fair compensation for the strip taken. — Adverse Possession — A.R.S. §§ 12-521, 12-526 A.R.S. § 12-526 — Arizona Courts — Self-Service Center, Obtaining Legal Services — Arizona is unusual in offering two routes for a landlocked owner: a free implied easement if the land was landlocked when it was split, and a paid condemnation route under A.R.S. § 12-1202 if it became landlocked later. — Community Legal Services (Arizona)

p: Arkansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Arkansas — adverse possession 7 years Standard period is 7 years under Ark. Code Ann. § 18-11-106, but the claimant must hold color of title (a deed, will, or other document that appears to give title, even if defective) AND have paid the property taxes for those 7 years. For wild and unimproved land, paying taxes for 15 years can itself establish color of title. A second route covers land next to (contiguous to) land the claimant holds under color of title, also 7 years with taxes paid on the contiguous land. Possession must also be actual or constructive, hostile, exclusive, open and notorious, and continuous. People or entities exempt from property taxes do not have to meet the tax requirement. — prescriptive easement 7 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road), not ownership. Arkansas courts apply the same 7-year period as adverse possession: the use must be adverse to the true owner and under a claim of right for 7 years, with some open act that puts the owner on notice. Use that starts with permission cannot ripen into a prescriptive easement unless the user clearly shows the owner that the use is now adverse. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Arkansas courts recognize common-law easements by necessity and by implication for landlocked parcels (see Powell v. Miller), requiring that both tracts were once owned by one person, the titles were split, and the easement is necessary both when split and when used. Separately, Ark. Code Ann. § 27-66-401 lets a landlocked owner petition the county court to lay out a private road (no more than 50 feet wide) to a public road. — Adverse Possession — Ark. Code Ann. § 18-11-106 Ark. Code Ann. § 18-11-106 — Arkansas Judiciary — Self-Help Resources — Arkansas has one of the shortest clocks in the country (7 years), but the color-of-title-plus-taxes requirement makes claims harder than the short period suggests. — Legal Aid of Arkansas

p: California Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in California — adverse possession 5 years Period is 5 years of continuous occupation and claim under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325, and the claimant must have timely paid ALL state, county, and municipal taxes levied on the land for those 5 years, proven by certified county tax collector records. Without a written instrument (deed, judgment, or decree), the land must also have been protected by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved. Possession must be actual, open and notorious, hostile (without permission), exclusive, and under color of title or a claim of right. No claim can be made against land owned by a public entity or dedicated to public use (Civ. Code § 1007). — prescriptive easement 5 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, crossing a driveway), not ownership. It takes 5 years of open, notorious, continuous, adverse use under a claim of right (Code Civ. Proc. § 321; Civ. Code § 1007). Unlike adverse possession for ownership, no tax payment is required unless the easement was separately assessed. An owner can prevent one by posting signs reading 'Right to pass by permission, and subject to control, of owner: Section 1008, Civil Code' (Civ. Code § 1008). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. California recognizes easements by necessity: when land once under common ownership is divided in a way that leaves a parcel landlocked, a court may imply an access easement even though nothing was written in the deed. No 5 years of use is needed — the claim turns on the history of the split and strict necessity for access. — Adverse Possession — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325 Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325 — LawHelpCA — California legal aid directory — California's 5-year period looks short, but the tax-payment rule defeats most claims — especially for a small strip of a neighbor's lot, which is almost never taxed separately, so the claimant cannot prove they paid its taxes. — LawHelpCA

p: Colorado Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Colorado — adverse possession 18 years Period is 18 years of adverse possession under Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-41-101, which is conclusive evidence of ownership. For claims where title vests on or after July 1, 2008, the claimant must prove every element by clear and convincing evidence AND show a reasonable, good-faith belief that they were the actual owner; if they win, the court may order them to pay the former owner the property's fair market value plus taxes the owner paid. Possession must be hostile, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, and continuous. No claim can be made against land owned by the state, a county, a city, or other public body. — prescriptive easement 18 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a driveway or path), not ownership. Under Lobato v. Taylor, it takes 18 years of use that is (1) open or notorious, (2) continued without effective interruption for 18 years, and (3) either adverse or under an attempted but ineffective grant. The 2008 good-faith and compensation rules for ownership claims do NOT apply to prescriptive easements, and the use does not have to be exclusive. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Colorado recognizes easements by necessity: when an owner splits a tract and leaves one part with no access except across the other, a court will imply an easement if (1) one owner held the whole tract, (2) the necessity existed when it was split, and (3) the necessity is great (Thompson v. Whinnery). The easement ends if another route to the land later becomes available. — Adverse Possession — Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-41-101 Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-41-101 — Colorado Judicial Branch — Legal Help Center (LawHelp Colorado) — Colorado tightened its law in 2008 after a well-known Boulder County case, adding a good-faith requirement and possible compensation for ownership claims — but those changes deliberately do not apply to prescriptive easements. — Colorado Legal Services

p: Connecticut Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Connecticut — adverse possession 15 years Period is 15 years under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-575: the record owner must assert ownership within 15 years after being ousted, or lose the right to re-enter. Possession must be open, visible, and exclusive, uninterrupted for 15 years, hostile and under a claim of right, with the intent to use the property as one's own and without the owner's consent. No color of title or tax payment is required. Two owner defenses are unusual: paying the property taxes in full prevents the 15-year clock from starting and counts as an interruption, and the owner can also interrupt the clock by serving and recording a written notice disputing possession. — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a right-of-way or driveway), not ownership. Under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-37, no one can acquire a right-of-way or other easement by adverse use unless the use has continued uninterrupted for 15 years. The use must be open, visible, continuous and uninterrupted, and under a claim of right; use with the owner's permission does not count. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Connecticut recognizes easements by necessity (and implied easements generally) for landlocked parcels: when a property has no access to a road or public space, the law supplies the needed right-of-way across a neighbor's land, typically where the parcels were once under common ownership. — Adverse Possession — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-575 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-575 — Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection — Legal Assistance — Connecticut is unusual in letting the record owner stop the clock simply by paying the property taxes in full, or by serving and recording a written notice that disputes the possession. — Connecticut Legal Services

p: Delaware Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Delaware — adverse possession 20 years Period is 20 years under 10 Del. C. § 7901: no person may enter land more than 20 years after their right to do so first arose, and § 7902 bars any action to recover land unless the owner or a predecessor had actual possession within the last 20 years. Court cases supply the elements: possession must be actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, and hostile (without the owner's permission — hostility means acting as owner, not ill will). No color of title, deed, or tax payment is required, and none shortens the period. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a shared driveway), not ownership. Delaware courts require open, notorious, exclusive, continuous, and hostile use for at least 20 years (see Tubbs v. E E Flood Farms, L.P.), proved by clear and convincing evidence — a higher standard of proof than Delaware requires for adverse possession itself. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Delaware recognizes easements by necessity: when a parcel is landlocked with no other access, the owner may get a right-of-way across a neighbor's land so the property can be reached and used. — Adverse Possession — Del. Code Ann. tit. 10, § 7901 10 Del. C. § 7901 — Delaware Legal Help Link (Delaware Bar Foundation) — Delaware's 20-year period is among the longest in the country, and its statute is written as a deadline on the owner's right to sue rather than as a list of elements — the elements come from court decisions, and a prescriptive easement is actually harder to prove than ownership. — Community Legal Aid Society, Inc. (CLASI)

p: Florida Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Florida — adverse possession 7 years Period is 7 years of actual, continuous possession, with or without color of title. With color of title (a document that appears to give title, even if defective), Fla. Stat. § 95.16 applies; without color of title, Fla. Stat. § 95.18 applies and the claimant must also pay the taxes and file a return describing the property with the county property appraiser. Possession must be open, notorious, exclusive, hostile (without permission), continuous, and under a claim of title, and the land must be cultivated, improved, enclosed, or otherwise actually used. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road or path), not ownership. Florida uses the common-law period of 20 years of continuous and uninterrupted use — much longer than the 7 years for ownership (see J.C. Vereen & Sons v. Houser). The claimant must prove the use was open, notorious, adverse, hostile, continuous and uninterrupted, with the knowledge and acquiescence of the landowner. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Florida recognizes easements by necessity and by implication, and Fla. Stat. § 704.01 provides a statutory way of necessity for a landlocked parcel, generally where the parcels share unity of title from a common source other than the original grant from the state or the United States. — Adverse Possession — Fla. Stat. §§ 95.16, 95.18 Fla. Stat. § 95.18 — FloridaLawHelp.org — statewide legal aid directory — Florida is unusual in running the two clocks in opposite directions from what most people expect: ownership by adverse possession takes only 7 years, but a prescriptive easement takes 20. — Florida Legal Services

p: Georgia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Georgia — adverse possession 20 years Standard period is 20 years of possession meeting O.C.G.A. § 44-5-161, which confers good title by prescription (§ 44-5-163). It drops to 7 years if the possession is under color of title (§ 44-5-164) — a deed or writing that appears to give title, even if defective, held in good faith. Possession must be in the right of the possessor and not of another, must not have originated in fraud, must be public, continuous, exclusive, uninterrupted, and peaceable, and must be accompanied by a claim of right. Possession that starts with permission cannot found a claim until the user gives the owner actual notice of an adverse claim. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement (called a private way in Georgia) gives only a right to use someone else's land, not ownership. The general rule is 20 years of adverse use, or 7 years with color of title (Smith v. Clay). For a private way under O.C.G.A. § 44-9-1, the period is 7 years of uninterrupted use through improved lands, or 20 years through wild lands — and under § 44-9-54 the user must stay on the same route (no more than 20 feet wide) and keep the way in repair, which also serves as notice to the owner that the use is adverse. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. O.C.G.A. § 44-9-1 recognizes a private way by implication of law when access is necessary to enjoy lands granted by the same owner, and Georgia also allows a landlocked owner to get a private way by compulsory purchase through the superior court. — Adverse Possession (Prescription) — O.C.G.A. §§ 44-5-161, 44-5-163, 44-5-164 O.C.G.A. § 44-5-163 — Georgia Attorney General — Consumer Protection (Ask Ed) — Georgia's private-way rules are unusually specific: the path cannot shift, the user must keep it in repair, and it is capped at 20 feet wide. (Atlanta Legal Aid Society, at https://atlantalegalaid.org/about-us/our-work/, serves the five-county metro Atlanta area; GLSP serves the other 154 counties.) — Georgia Legal Services Program

p: Hawaii Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Hawaii — adverse possession 20 years A person must possess land openly, notoriously, exclusively, continuously, and hostilely (without the owner's permission) for 20 years under Haw. Rev. Stat. section 657-31. Hawaii adds a strict limit in section 657-31.5: a claim can only be made for land of five acres or less, and only if the claimant has not asserted a similar claim in good faith within the past 20 years. The statute sets no shorter period for color of title (a document that looks like a deed but is defective) or for paying taxes. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a driveway or path) without owning it. Hawaii courts use the same elements as adverse possession: the use must be adverse, continuous, and uninterrupted for the 20-year statutory period. Unlike adverse possession, a prescriptive easement does not transfer ownership and does not require exclusive possession — the owner can keep using the land too. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Hawaii recognizes implied easements by necessity, for example when a parcel is landlocked. The 20-year limitations period in section 657-31 does not bar a claim for an implied easement by necessity, and the parcels must once have shared a common owner. — Hawaii Revised Statutes, Chapter 657, Limitation of Actions Haw. Rev. Stat. sections 657-31, 657-31.5 — Hawaii State Bar Association — Lawyer Referral and Information Service — Hawaii is one of the strictest states for adverse possession: claims are limited to parcels of five acres or less, and minor encroachments within the measurement limits of Haw. Rev. Stat. section 669-11 can never ripen into an adverse possession claim. — Legal Aid Society of Hawaii

p: Idaho Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Idaho — adverse possession 20 years A claimant must possess land openly, notoriously, exclusively, continuously, and hostilely for 20 years under Idaho Code section 5-203. Two extra requirements apply: under section 5-210 the claimant must have paid all taxes levied on the land for the whole 20 years, and a claim based on a written instrument (color of title) is governed by section 5-207 — but the period is still 20 years; color of title does not shorten it. Idaho lengthened the period from 5 years to 20 years in 2006. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a road) without owning it. Idaho Code section 5-203 sets the period at 20 years. The claimant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the use was (1) open and notorious, (2) continuous and uninterrupted, (3) adverse and under a claim of right, (4) with the actual or imputed knowledge of the owner, (5) for the statutory period. Use with the owner's permission can never ripen into a prescriptive easement. Before 2006 the period was 5 years. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Idaho recognizes easements by necessity for landlocked parcels. The parcels must once have been under common ownership, the need for access must have existed when they were separated, and Idaho requires a 'great present necessity' — mere inconvenience is not enough. The easement lasts only as long as the necessity exists. — Idaho Code, Title 5, Chapter 2, Limitation of Actions Idaho Code sections 5-203, 5-207, 5-210 — Idaho Court Assistance Office (Court Self-Help) — Idaho changed both the adverse possession and prescriptive easement periods from 5 years to 20 years in 2006, so older claims may still be judged under the old 5-year period. Paying the property taxes for the full 20 years is mandatory for an adverse possession claim. — Idaho Legal Aid Services

p: Illinois Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Illinois — adverse possession 20 years A claimant must possess land actually, openly and notoriously, exclusively, hostilely (without permission), and continuously for 20 years under 735 ILCS 5/13-101. There is a shorter 7-year path: under 735 ILCS 5/13-109, a person who possesses land under color of title (a deed that appears valid but is defective) made in good faith and pays all legally assessed property taxes for seven straight years is treated as the owner. Registered (Torrens) land cannot be acquired by adverse possession. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a path or driveway) without owning it. Illinois requires 20 years of use that is adverse, uninterrupted, exclusive, continuous, and under a claim of right (Petersen v. Corrubia, 1961; National Financial, LP v. Pobuda, 2014 IL 116717). 'Exclusive' here means the user's claim does not depend on someone else's right — the owner may still use the land. Mere permission to use land can never ripen into a prescriptive right, no matter how long it lasts. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Illinois recognizes easements by necessity as one of the two kinds of implied easement (the other is an easement implied from prior use). A landlocked parcel typically gets a right of way across neighboring land to reach a public road. — Illinois Code of Civil Procedure, Article XIII, Limitations 735 ILCS 5/13-101 et seq. — Illinois State Bar Association — Illinois Lawyer Finder — Illinois offers a 7-year shortcut with color of title plus tax payment, but the standard period is 20 years. Prairie State Legal Services covers 36 counties in northern and central Illinois; Land of Lincoln Legal Assistance covers southern Illinois. — Prairie State Legal Services

p: Indiana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Indiana — adverse possession 10 years A claimant must possess land continuously for 10 years under Ind. Code sections 32-21-7-1 and 34-11-2-11, and must also have paid all property taxes and special assessments they reasonably and in good faith believed were due on the land for the entire 10 years — paying taxes does not shorten the period. Indiana courts (Fraley v. Minger) require clear and convincing proof of control, intent to claim ownership, notice to the owner, and duration. Color of title is not required and does not shorten the period. Note: a 2025 law (Senate Enrolled Act 157) created a fast process for removing squatters; check current law before starting a new claim. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a private road) without owning it. Under Ind. Code section 32-23-1-1, the use must be uninterrupted for at least 20 years — double Indiana's 10-year adverse possession period — and must be actual, hostile, open, notorious, continuous, and under a claim of right. The owner can interrupt the clock by serving or posting a written notice disputing the claim (Ind. Code sections 32-23-1-2 to 32-23-1-4). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Indiana recognizes easements by necessity — for example, when a parcel has no access to a public road — as well as easements implied from prior use. An easement by necessity cannot arise if the property is not landlocked. — Indiana Code, Title 32, Property Ind. Code sections 32-21-7-1 and 34-11-2-11 (adverse possession); Ind. Code section 32-23-1-1 (prescriptive easements) — Indiana Courts — Self-Service Legal Center — Indiana is unusual: its prescriptive easement period (20 years) is twice as long as its adverse possession period (10 years). Paying property taxes for the full 10 years is mandatory for an adverse possession claim. — Indiana Legal Services

p: Iowa Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Iowa — adverse possession 10 years A claimant must prove hostile, actual, open, exclusive, and continuous possession under a claim of right or color of title for at least 10 years, by clear and positive proof. Iowa Code section 564.1 sets the 10-year period for claiming an easement by adverse possession; the 10-year period for claiming title to land itself comes from Iowa case law. Paying rent defeats a claim, because a tenant occupies with permission. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a driveway) without owning it. Under Iowa Code section 564.1 and Iowa case law, the use must be under a claim of right or color of title, open, notorious, continuous, and hostile for 10 years or more, and each element must be strictly proved. Iowa is unusual: just using the land is not evidence that the user claimed it as a right — the claimant needs separate evidence, and the owner must have had express notice of the adverse claim. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Iowa recognizes easements by necessity when a parcel has no access to a public road — the landlocked condition itself is enough, with no need to prove prior visible use. The easement ends if the parcel later gains road access. Iowa also lets a landlocked owner condemn (force a purchase of) a right-of-way under Iowa Code section 6A.4(2). — Iowa Code, Chapter 564, Easements Iowa Code section 564.1 — Iowa State Bar Association — Find-A-Lawyer — Iowa requires express notice to the owner for a prescriptive easement — merely using a path or driveway for 10 years is not enough by itself. A landlocked owner can also use condemnation to get road access, which is rare among states. — Iowa Legal Aid

p: Kansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Kansas — adverse possession 15 years Under Kan. Stat. Ann. section 60-503, a claimant must have been in open, exclusive, and continuous possession for 15 years, either under a claim knowingly adverse or under a good-faith belief of ownership. Kansas law does not require the claimant to pay property taxes, and there is no shorter period for color of title. The statute replaced the old common-law 'hostility' element with the two options above, and the claimant must prove every element by clear and convincing evidence. — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a private road) without owning it. Kansas courts measure prescriptive easements by the same 15-year period in K.S.A. 60-503 (Pyle v. Gall, 317 Kan. 499 (2023)). The use must be (1) open, (2) exclusive — meaning unique to the person claiming it, not that no one else uses the land, (3) continuous, (4) for at least 15 years, and (5) adverse. Use with the owner's permission can never ripen into an easement. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Kansas recognizes easements by necessity: when a landowner conveys a parcel that is landlocked, the law implies a right of access across the remaining land (Horner v. Heersche, 1968; McCoy v. Barr, 2012). The necessity must be strict, not mere convenience. — Kansas Statutes Annotated, Chapter 60, Article 5, Limitations of Actions Kan. Stat. Ann. section 60-503 — Kansas Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — Kansas requires no tax payments for adverse possession, and its statute drops the usual 'hostile' element in favor of either a knowingly adverse claim or a good-faith belief of ownership. — Kansas Legal Services

p: Kentucky Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Kentucky — adverse possession 15 years A claimant must possess land actually, hostilely, exclusively, openly and notoriously, and continuously for 15 years under Ky. Rev. Stat. section 413.010. There is a shorter 7-year path under section 413.060: a person with a connected chain of title deducible of record from the Commonwealth (color of title) who actually occupies the land by settling on it under that title for seven years cannot be sued for it. The claimant must prove all elements by clear and convincing evidence, and adverse possession does not run against government-owned land. — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a driveway) without owning it. Kentucky requires the use to be open, notorious, exclusive, adverse, and continuous for at least 15 years. Occasional or permissive use does not count — if the landowner gave informal permission, no prescriptive easement can form (Cole v. Gilvin) — and if the owner interrupts the use, the 15-year clock resets. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Kentucky recognizes ways of necessity for landlocked parcels (Stephens v. Hamblin, 1922). Kentucky also has a statute, Ky. Rev. Stat. section 178.405, under which a private road used openly by the public for at least 15 years may be treated as dedicated to public use. — Kentucky Revised Statutes, Chapter 413, Limitations of Actions Ky. Rev. Stat. sections 413.010, 413.060 — Kentucky Bar Association — Find a Lawyer / Legal Aid — Kentucky's 7-year color-of-title path is narrow: it requires a connected chain of title traceable in the public records back to the Commonwealth, not just any deed. Kentucky Legal Aid serves south-central and western Kentucky; AppalReD Legal Aid, Legal Aid of the Bluegrass, and the Legal Aid Society cover the rest of the state. — Kentucky Legal Aid

p: Louisiana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Louisiana — adverse possession 30 years Louisiana is a civil-law state and does not use common-law adverse possession. Its equivalent is 'acquisitive prescription.' Under La. Civ. Code articles 3473-3475, a person who possesses land as owner, in good faith and under 'just title' (a written document that looks like a valid transfer of ownership), can acquire ownership after 10 years. Without just title or good faith, ownership can still be acquired after 30 years of possession under article 3486 — but only for the land actually possessed. In both cases the possession must be continuous, public, peaceful, and unequivocal (not violent, secret, interrupted, or unclear). — prescriptive easement 30 years Louisiana does not call them prescriptive easements — it calls them 'predial servitudes,' and they can be acquired by prescription only if they are 'apparent,' meaning visible, such as a road, path, or ditch (La. Civ. Code articles 740, 742). An apparent servitude may be acquired by peaceable, uninterrupted possession of the right for 10 years in good faith and by just title, or by uninterrupted possession for 30 years without title or good faith. A hidden servitude, such as a buried pipe with no visible sign, cannot be acquired by prescription. A prescriptive servitude gives only a right to use the land, not ownership of it. — easement by necessity landlocked Louisiana does not use the common-law easement by necessity, but its Civil Code reaches the same result: under article 689, the owner of an 'enclosed estate' — land with no access to a public road — may claim a right of passage over neighboring land to the nearest public road. Unlike the common-law version, the owner must pay the neighbor for the right of passage. — Louisiana Civil Code, Book III, Title XXIV (Prescription) and Title IV (Predial Servitudes) La. Civ. Code articles 3473-3475, 3486 (acquisitive prescription); La. Civ. Code articles 689, 740, 742 (servitudes) — Louisiana State Bar Association — Find Legal Help — Louisiana is the only civil-law state in the U.S.: it has acquisitive prescription instead of adverse possession and predial servitudes instead of easements. Only visible ('apparent') servitudes can be gained by long use, and a landlocked owner must pay for the right of passage. — Southeast Louisiana Legal Services

p: Maine Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Maine — adverse possession 20 years A claimant must prove possession that is actual, open, visible, notorious, hostile, under a claim of right, continuous, and exclusive for 20 years under 14 M.R.S. section 801. Maine has a special rule for uncultivated land in incorporated places (14 M.R.S. section 816): the claimant must also hold a recorded deed and have paid all taxes on the land for the 20-year period. Title cannot be acquired by adverse possession against the State. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a right-of-way) without owning it. Under 14 M.R.S. section 812, no right-of-way or other easement can be acquired by adverse use unless the use continues uninterrupted for 20 years. Maine courts require continuous use for at least 20 years, under a claim of right adverse to the owner, with the owner's knowledge and acquiescence (or use so open and notorious that knowledge is presumed). A landowner can stop a prescriptive easement from forming by posting a written notice on the land for 6 successive days under section 812. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Maine recognizes easements by necessity (Morrell v. Rice, 1993): when a parcel is landlocked because of a division by a common grantor, the law implies a right of way over the neighboring parcel. The easement covers all reasonable uses needed to enjoy the land, including installing utilities. — Maine Revised Statutes, Title 14, Chapter 205, Limitation of Actions 14 M.R.S. sections 801, 812, 816 — Maine State Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — Maine lets a landowner block a prescriptive easement by posting a written notice on the property for six days (14 M.R.S. section 812), and uncultivated land inside towns has a special deed-plus-taxes rule (section 816). — Pine Tree Legal Assistance

p: Maryland Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Maryland — adverse possession 20 years Under Md. Code, Courts and Judicial Proceedings section 5-103, a landowner has 20 years from when the right to sue first arises to file an action to recover land or re-enter it. Maryland courts require the claimant to prove the possession was actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile, under a claim of title or ownership, and continuous for the full 20 years. A 10-year path is reported where the claimant holds color of title and has paid the property taxes (Md. Code, Tax-Property section 14-108); verify that provision before relying on it. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a permanent right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, crossing it to reach a road) without owning it. Section 5-103 expressly preserves the common-law doctrine of prescription for easements. Maryland courts require the use to be adverse (without permission), exclusive (the claim must not depend on someone else's right), and uninterrupted and continuous for 20 years (Turner v. Bouchard, 202 Md. App. 428 (2011)). One wrinkle: use across unenclosed woodland or wild land is presumed to be permissive, not adverse, so the claimant carries a harder burden there. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Maryland recognizes easements by necessity (Gunfeld Coal Co. v. Carey, 2022): the claimant must show the parcels once shared a single owner, a division separated them, and the easement was necessary both when the land was divided and when it is used. — Maryland Code, Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. section 5-103 — Maryland Courts — Finding Legal Help — Maryland's adverse possession statute expressly preserves the common-law doctrine of prescription for easements, so the two doctrines sit side by side in one statute. Use across unenclosed woodland is presumed permissive, which defeats many rural prescriptive easement claims. — Maryland Legal Aid

p: Massachusetts Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Massachusetts — adverse possession 20 years The owner has 20 years to sue to recover land; after that, a person who has actually used the land openly and visibly, without the owner's permission, exclusively (as their own), and continuously for the full 20 years can claim ownership. 'Hostile' means without permission, not angry or aggressive. Having a flawed deed (color of title) or paying taxes does not shorten the 20 years in Massachusetts. Land registered with the Land Court (registered/Torrens land) can never be taken by adverse possession, and the 20-year limit does not bar a nonprofit land conservation organization from recovering conservation land. Statute: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 21. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is a right to keep using someone else's land for a specific purpose (for example, a driveway or path), not ownership of it. It requires open and obvious use, without permission, continuously and without interruption for 20 years. Unlike adverse possession, the use does not have to be exclusive — the user does not have to keep everyone else out. It cannot be gained over registered Land Court land. Statute: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 187, § 2. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, Massachusetts recognizes easements by necessity, but necessity alone is not enough: the two parcels must once have had the same owner, the split must have created the landlocked parcel, and the facts must show the parties would have intended access. The easement lasts only while the necessity lasts. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 260, Section 21 (adverse possession); Chapter 187, Section 2 (easements by prescription) Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 21; ch. 187, § 2 — Mass.gov — Massachusetts law about adverse possession — Massachusetts is distinctive for its two land systems: adverse possession and prescriptive easements do not apply at all to land registered with the Land Court. — Greater Boston Legal Services

p: Michigan Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Michigan — adverse possession 15 years A person must show actual possession that was continuous, open and notorious (visible, not hidden), exclusive, and hostile (without permission, under a claim of right) for 15 uninterrupted years. Color of title does not shorten the period in Michigan — it is 15 years either way. The claim must be proved in a court action to quiet title; simply occupying the land does not automatically change the deed. Statute: Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5801. — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a driveway or parking area), not ownership of it. It requires use that is open, notorious, adverse (without permission), and continuous for 15 years. It differs from adverse possession in one key way: the use does not have to be exclusive — the user and the owner may both use the land. Once it vests after 15 years it runs with the land to later owners. Statute: Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5801(4). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Michigan recognizes an easement by necessity when an owner splits land so that one resulting parcel is landlocked except for access across the other parcel; the court implies access because the parties are assumed to have intended it. For this type of easement, strict necessity is required — no other way to reach the land. — Michigan Compiled Laws, Section 600.5801 MCL 600.5801 — Michigan Legal Help (Michigan Supreme Court self-help program) — Michigan courts have held that a prescriptive easement vests automatically once the 15 years run, even if no lawsuit was ever filed, and it then passes with the land to the next owner. — Lakeshore Legal Aid

p: Minnesota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Minnesota — adverse possession 15 years The owner has 15 years to sue to recover real estate. To claim ownership, a person must prove by clear and convincing evidence actual, open, hostile, continuous, and exclusive possession for the full 15 years. For land that is separately assessed for taxes, the claimant (or their predecessors) must also have paid the taxes on it for at least five consecutive years during the claimed period — but that tax rule does not apply to boundary-line disputes or to land that is not assessed for taxes. No title to registered (Torrens) land can be gained by adverse possession. Statute: Minn. Stat. § 541.02. — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a driveway or farm road), not ownership of it. It uses the same elements as adverse possession — actual, open, continuous, exclusive, and hostile use for 15 years — but courts judge continuity less strictly for a use (such as seasonal farm access) than for full possession. Statute: Minn. Stat. § 541.02, as applied in Rogers v. Moore, 603 N.W.2d 650 (Minn. 1999). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Minnesota courts recognize implied easements by necessity for landlocked parcels: when a single parcel is split and one part is left with no access, a court may imply an easement across the other part if there was common ownership before the split and the access is reasonably necessary. — Minnesota Statutes, Section 541.02 — Recovery of Real Estate, 15 Years Minn. Stat. § 541.02 — Minnesota Judicial Branch — Self-Help / Help Topics — Minnesota is unusual in tying adverse possession to tax payment: for separately assessed land, five consecutive years of tax payments during the claim period are required, except in boundary disputes. — LawHelpMN

p: Mississippi Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Mississippi — adverse possession 10 years Ten years of actual adverse possession, continued without interruption, vests full title in the occupant. The claimant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the possession was under a claim of ownership, actual or hostile, open, notorious and visible, continuous and uninterrupted for 10 years, exclusive, and peaceful. Permission from the owner defeats the claim. Paying taxes does not shorten the period, but a record owner who pays the property taxes on an assessed parcel is treated as occupying it for that year, which can block a claim. A landowner who finds a fence or driveway built without permission can file a written notice with the chancery clerk within the 10 years to stop the claim from maturing. Statute: Miss. Code Ann. § 15-1-13. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road or driveway across it), not ownership. Mississippi courts apply the same 10-year period and the same elements as adverse possession: open, notorious and visible, hostile, under a claim of ownership, exclusive, peaceful, and continuous and uninterrupted use for 10 years. Use that started with permission can never become adverse, no matter how long it lasts. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Mississippi recognizes easements by necessity when a parcel becomes landlocked after a commonly owned tract is split; the law assumes the common owner impliedly granted access. Mississippi uses a reasonable-necessity standard, not strict necessity, and the easement lasts only as long as the necessity exists. — Mississippi Code, Section 15-1-13 — Ten Years' Adverse Possession Gives Title Miss. Code Ann. § 15-1-13 — The Mississippi Bar — Free and Low-Cost Legal Help in Mississippi — Mississippi's tax-payment rule is a trap for claimants: if the record owner pays the taxes on the assessed parcel, that payment counts as the owner's occupancy for that year. — Mississippi Center for Legal Services

p: Missouri Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Missouri — adverse possession 10 years The owner has 10 years to sue to recover land. To gain title, the claimant must prove possession that was hostile (under a claim of right, without permission), actual, open and notorious, exclusive, and continuous for 10 years. Failing on even one element defeats the claim, and title is established through a court action to quiet title. Paying taxes or having a deed does not shorten the 10 years. Statute: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.010. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a driveway), not ownership of it. It requires continuous, uninterrupted, visible, and adverse use for at least 10 years. Once open, continuous, visible, uninterrupted use for 10 years is shown, courts presume the use was adverse, and the landowner must show it was actually permissive. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, in two ways. Missouri recognizes a common-law easement by necessity when land is split and one parcel is left landlocked, and it also has a private-road statute (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 228.342) letting a landlocked owner ask a circuit court for a private road — but only on a showing of strict necessity, meaning the land cannot be used at all without it, not merely that access would be more convenient. — Revised Statutes of Missouri, Section 516.010 — Actions for Recovery of Lands Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.010 — Missouri Courts — Existing Pro Bono Programs / Legal Services Programs — Missouri has no single statute listing the elements of adverse possession — the 10-year period comes from § 516.010, and the five elements come from Missouri court decisions. — Missouri Legal Services

p: Montana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Montana — adverse possession 5 years Montana has one of the shortest periods in the country — 5 years — but it has a hard extra requirement: in no case is adverse possession established unless the land was occupied and claimed continuously for 5 years AND the claimant (and predecessors) paid all taxes legally levied and assessed on the land during that period. The possession must also be actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile (without permission), and continuous. Statute: Mont. Code Ann. §§ 70-19-401, 70-19-411. — prescriptive easement 5 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road for grazing, farming, or timber access), not ownership. Montana courts require open, notorious, exclusive, adverse, continuous and uninterrupted use for the full 5-year statutory period. Unlike adverse possession, the tax-payment requirement in § 70-19-411 applies to claiming ownership, not to claiming a right of use — but simply being a friendly neighbor who lets someone cross the land does not count as adverse use. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Montana recognizes an implied easement by necessity, but it requires (1) unity of ownership — the parcels were once one tract — and (2) strict necessity at the time that unified tract was split. A landlocked owner with no common-ownership history generally cannot get one, and neighborly permission alone cannot ripen into a prescriptive easement either. — Montana Code Annotated, Sections 70-19-401 and 70-19-411 — Occupancy and Payment of Taxes Necessary to Prove Adverse Possession Mont. Code Ann. § 70-19-411 — Montana Legislature — Montana Code Annotated, Section 70-19-411 — Montana's 5-year period looks easy, but the mandatory tax-payment rule is the real barrier — many claims fail because the claimant never paid the taxes on the disputed land. — Montana Legal Services Association

p: Nebraska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Nebraska — adverse possession 10 years A person must prove by a preponderance of the evidence actual, continuous, exclusive, notorious, and adverse possession under a claim of ownership for the full 10 years. Use by earlier owners can be added together (tacking) to reach 10 years. No shorter period applies for color of title or tax payment under this statute. Statute: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-202. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road), not ownership of it. Nebraska courts apply the same 10-year period as adverse possession: the use must be exclusive, adverse, under a claim of right, continuous and uninterrupted, and open and notorious for the full 10 years, proved by clear, convincing, and satisfactory evidence. 'Exclusive' here does not mean only one person ever used it — it means the use did not depend on a similar right held by others. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Nebraska recognizes easements by necessity and easements implied from prior use. An easement by necessity requires a greater degree of necessity than an implied easement from prior use, and for an easement claimed by the grantor (by reservation) strict necessity is required, while reasonable necessity is enough for one claimed by the grantee. — Nebraska Revised Statutes, Section 25-202 — Actions for the Recovery of Title or Possession of Real Estate Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-202 — Nebraska Supreme Court — Online Legal Self-Help Center — Nebraska courts treat prescriptive easements as 'not looked upon with favor,' so the claimant faces a higher standard of proof (clear, convincing, and satisfactory evidence) than for an ordinary civil claim. — Legal Aid of Nebraska

p: Nevada Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Nevada — adverse possession 5 years Nevada has a 5-year period: the owner must have been in possession of the land within 5 years before suing to recover it. To claim ownership, a person must also show 5 years of continuous occupation plus payment of all taxes levied on the land during that time (NRS 11.150), and the land must have been protected by a substantial enclosure or cultivated or improved in the usual way. The possession must be open, continuous, and hostile (without permission). Statute: Nev. Rev. Stat. §§ 11.070, 11.080, 11.150. — prescriptive easement 5 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a road across it), not ownership. Nevada courts require adverse, continuous, open, and peaceable use for a 5-year period, proved by clear and convincing evidence. Long use that the owner simply never noticed is not necessarily adverse, and use with the owner's express or implied permission is a license, not a prescriptive easement. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Nevada recognizes easements by necessity and easements by implication: when a parcel is landlocked and needs access across another property to reach a public road, a court may imply an easement, based on the parties' intent when the properties were divided and on reasonable necessity. — Nevada Revised Statutes, Chapter 11 — Limitation of Actions (Sections 11.070, 11.080, 11.150) NRS 11.070; NRS 11.080; NRS 11.150 — Nevada Legislature — Nevada Revised Statutes, Chapter 11 — Nevada pairs a short 5-year clock with a strict tax-payment rule for adverse possession, and it separately criminalizes unlawful occupancy of a home — occupying a house without permission is not a safe path to ownership. — Nevada Legal Services

p: New Hampshire Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in New Hampshire
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in New Hampshire — adverse possession 20 years No action to recover real estate may be brought after 20 years from when the right to recover first accrued. To gain title, the claimant must prove by a balance of probabilities 20 years of adverse, continuous, and uninterrupted use, in a way that gives reasonable notice to the record owner that an adverse claim is being made, plus exclusive use. 'Adverse' means use without license or permission — it is trespassory in nature, and permission defeats the claim. The claimant must get a court judgment (usually a petition to quiet title). No person can gain title to state lands by adverse possession. Statute: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 508:2. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a path or driveway), not ownership. New Hampshire requires 20 years of adverse, continuous, and uninterrupted use. The scope of the easement is limited to the kind of use that actually happened over those 20 years — for example, a footpath used for 20 years does not automatically become a right to drive vehicles over it. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, but narrowly. New Hampshire recognizes easements by necessity as a type of implied easement, arising from the presumed intent of the parties when land was subdivided — but necessity alone is not enough. The surrounding circumstances must show the parties intended an easement, including that both parcels were once under one ownership and the split created the access problem. — New Hampshire Revised Statutes Annotated, Section 508:2 — Real Actions N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 508:2 — New Hampshire Judicial Branch — Legal Assistance Resources — New Hampshire courts stress that the claimant carries the burden of proof throughout — even after showing acts that look non-permissive — and that a later agreement making the use permissive can break the 20-year clock. — New Hampshire Legal Assistance

p: New Jersey Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in New Jersey
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in New Jersey — adverse possession 30 years New Jersey's standard period is 30 years of actual possession — and 60 years for woodlands or uncultivated tracts. Title does not vest until the full 30 (or 60) years have passed. The claimant must prove possession that was adverse or hostile, exclusive, continuous, uninterrupted, visible, and open and notorious. Older sources sometimes say 20 years, because two other statutes (§§ 2A:14-6 and 2A:14-7) use 20 years for bringing a real-estate action, but the New Jersey Supreme Court in J & M Land Co. v. First Union National Bank, 166 N.J. 493 (2001), held that the 30- or 60-year period governs adverse possession. Statute: N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 2A:14-30, 2A:14-31. — prescriptive easement 30 years A prescriptive easement gives only a right to use someone else's land (for example, a shared driveway), not ownership. New Jersey requires adverse or hostile, exclusive, continuous, uninterrupted, visible, and open and notorious use for 30 years (the same period as adverse possession for developed land). It differs from adverse possession on exclusivity: for a prescriptive easement, the claimant's use may be shared with the record owner and still count, while adverse possession requires use exclusive of everyone, including the owner. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. New Jersey recognizes easements by necessity as a subset of implied easements: when a parcel is landlocked with no reasonable access to a public road and the parcels were once under common ownership, courts will grant access across a neighboring property. The easement lasts only as long as the necessity exists. — New Jersey Statutes Annotated, Sections 2A:14-30 and 2A:14-31 — Adverse Possession N.J.S.A. 2A:14-30; N.J.S.A. 2A:14-31 — State of New Jersey — Legal Aid / Legal Services of New Jersey — New Jersey has the longest standard period in this set — 30 years, or 60 for woodlands and uncultivated land — and its courts have warned that the 20-year figure found in some older guides is the wrong statute for adverse possession. — Legal Services of New Jersey

p: New Mexico Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in New Mexico
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in New Mexico — adverse possession 10 years 10 years of continuous, actual and visible possession in good faith under color of title (a written document that looks like it gives title, even if flawed), with a claim of right hostile to the true owner. Unlike most states, New Mexico also requires the claimant (or predecessors) to have continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes on the land for the whole 10 years. If the owner sues within the 10 years, the clock stops. Governed by N.M. Stat. Ann. Section 37-1-22. — prescriptive easement 10 years 10 years of use that is open and obvious, continuous and without the owner's permission (adverse). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway or road — it does not transfer ownership of the land. Unlike adverse possession, the user does not have to show exclusive control or pay taxes. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. New Mexico recognizes easements by necessity and implied easements when a division of land leaves a parcel landlocked. The necessity is judged at the time the land was divided — simply becoming landlocked later is not enough on its own. — New Mexico Statutes, Title in Fee Simple by Adverse Possession N.M. Stat. Ann. § 37-1-22 — State Bar of New Mexico — Civil Legal Service Providers — New Mexico is unusually strict: the 10-year claim requires BOTH color of title and continuous payment of all property taxes — missing either one defeats the claim. — New Mexico Legal Aid

p: New York Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in New York
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in New York — adverse possession 10 years 10 years of possession that is actual, open and notorious (visible enough that a reasonable owner would notice), exclusive, continuous, and hostile (without permission), under a claim of right. Since 2008 amendments, the claimant must also show a reasonable basis for believing the land was theirs, and small non-structural encroachments (a fence, hedge, shed) are treated as permissive, not adverse. Paying taxes is not required, and having a deed (color of title) does not shorten the 10 years. — prescriptive easement 10 years 10 years of use that is open, notorious, hostile (without permission) and continuous, proved by clear and convincing evidence. A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway — it does not transfer ownership. Unlike adverse possession, the user does not have to exclude the owner from the land. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. New York recognizes easements by necessity when a single owner divides land and one parcel is left with no access to a public road. The easement lasts only as long as the necessity lasts. — New York Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law, Article 5 (Adverse Possession) N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law §§ 501 et seq.; N.Y. C.P.L.R. § 212(a) — New York State Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — New York tightened its law in 2008: a claimant must now show a reasonable basis for believing the land was theirs, so knowingly squatting on land you know belongs to someone else will not work. The Legal Aid Society listed here serves New York City; upstate residents can use LawHelpNY to find their local legal aid. — The Legal Aid Society

p: North Carolina Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in North Carolina
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in North Carolina — adverse possession 20 years 20 years is the standard period: possession must be actual, exclusive, open and visible, hostile (without permission), and continuous, within known and visible boundary lines. The period drops to 7 years if the possessor holds color of title (for example, a faulty deed). Paying taxes is not required, though listing and paying taxes can be evidence of possession. Government-owned land is generally immune. Governed by N.C. Gen. Stat. Sections 1-40 (20 years) and 1-38 (7 years under color of title). — prescriptive easement 20 years 20 years of use that is adverse or under a claim of right, open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, and following the same definite route the whole time. Note this is longer than the 7-year color-of-title shortcut for adverse possession — the shortcut does not apply to prescriptive easements. A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using the land for a specific purpose, such as a road, not ownership of it. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. North Carolina recognizes easements by necessity when commonly owned land is divided and the split leaves one parcel with no access to a public road. All the elements must exist at the time of the split. If there was never common ownership, the remedy is a statutory cartway proceeding instead. — North Carolina General Statutes, Chapter 1, Article 4 (Limitations, Real Property) N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 1-38, 1-40 — North Carolina Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — North Carolina has two very different clocks: 20 years normally, but only 7 years with color of title for full ownership — while a prescriptive easement always takes 20 years. — Legal Aid of North Carolina
