h: Adverse possession & easements in North Dakota
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in North Dakota — adverse possession 20 years 20 years of open, hostile, exclusive and continuous possession. The period drops to 10 years if the possessor holds color of title (a document that looks like title, such as a contract for deed) AND has paid all taxes and assessments on the land for those 10 years (N.D. Cent. Code Section 47-06-03). Without a written instrument, only land that was protected by a substantial enclosure (fenced) or usually cultivated or improved counts (Section 28-01-11). A 2025 law also makes unlawfully occupying someone's home a felony. — prescriptive easement 20 years 20 years of use that is adverse, continuous and uninterrupted (Fischer v. Berger, 2006 ND 48). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a road to reach pasture — it does not transfer ownership, and the user does not have to exclude the owner. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, in principle: North Dakota follows the common-law rule that courts can imply an easement by necessity when a division of land leaves a parcel landlocked, but no North Dakota-specific statute or case on easements by necessity was verified in this research pass, so confirm with a local attorney before relying on it. — North Dakota Century Code, Title 28, Chapter 28-01 and Title 47, Chapter 47-06 N.D. Cent. Code §§ 28-01-04, 47-06-03 — State Bar Association of North Dakota — North Dakota has one of the longest standard periods in the country (20 years), and without a deed only fenced or farmed land counts. Since 2025, unlawfully occupying a home is a crime, separate from the civil adverse possession rules. — Legal Services of North Dakota

p: Ohio Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Ohio — adverse possession 21 years 21 years of possession that is actual, open and notorious, hostile (without permission), exclusive and continuous, proved by clear and convincing evidence (Grace v. Koch, 1998). Neither color of title nor paying taxes shortens the 21 years, and neither is required. The 21 years comes from the deadline for an owner to sue to recover land (Ohio Rev. Code Section 2305.04). Government-owned land cannot be taken this way. — prescriptive easement 21 years 21 years of use that is open, notorious, adverse (without permission) and continuous, proved by clear and convincing evidence. A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway — it does not transfer ownership, and unlike adverse possession the user does not have to exclude the owner from the land. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, but Ohio applies a strict test: a court will imply a way of necessity only when a parcel is truly landlocked with no other means of getting in or out, not merely when another route would be inconvenient (Trattar v. Rausch, 1950). Ohio also has a separate statutory route: a landowner with no road access can petition the county for a public road (Ohio Rev. Code Sections 5553.41–5553.43). — Ohio Revised Code, Actions to Recover Title to or Possession of Real Property Ohio Rev. Code § 2305.04 — Ohio State Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Services — Ohio's 21 years is tied for the longest adverse possession period in this set, and it is a firm rule — no deed or tax payments can shorten it. Ohio has no single statewide legal aid firm, so Ohio Legal Help is the statewide starting point that connects people to their local legal aid. — Ohio Legal Help (statewide legal-aid finder)

p: Oklahoma Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Oklahoma — adverse possession 15 years 15 years of possession that is hostile, under a claim of right or color of title, actual, open, notorious, exclusive and continuous. No tax payment is required and color of title does not shorten the 15 years — it is a flat rule. A shorter 5-year period applies only to challenges involving tax deeds or certain judicial sales (Okla. Stat. tit. 12, Section 93). Once the 15 years run, occupancy confers title by prescription (tit. 60, Section 333). — prescriptive easement 15 years 15 years of use that is open, continuous and uninterrupted, adverse (without permission) and under a claim of right (Nokes v. Padgett, 1953). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a shared driveway — it does not transfer ownership of the land. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Oklahoma recognizes easements by necessity, but only if the two parcels were once owned by the same person and the necessity existed at the time the title was split (Blackwell v. Mayes County Utility Services Authority). — Oklahoma Statutes, Title 12, Section 93 (Limitation of Real Actions) and Title 60, Section 333 (Title by Prescription) Okla. Stat. tit. 12, § 93(4); tit. 60, § 333 — Oklahoma Bar Association — Legal Resources — Oklahoma's 15-year rule is flat: no deed, tax payment or other shortcut changes it, which makes it simpler than most states — but also means there is no faster path even with a faulty deed. — Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma

p: Oregon Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Oregon — adverse possession 10 years 10 years of actual, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous possession — plus an extra requirement most states do not have: the claimant must prove an honest belief that they were the actual owner when they first entered the land, that the belief had an objective basis, was reasonable, and lasted the whole 10 years. Every element must be proved by clear and convincing evidence. Paying taxes is not required and is not mentioned in the statute (Or. Rev. Stat. Section 105.620). — prescriptive easement 10 years 10 years of use that is open, notorious, adverse to the owner's rights, and continuous and uninterrupted, proved by clear and convincing evidence (Thompson v. Scott). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a road — it does not transfer ownership, and the user does not have to show exclusive use. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes, and Oregon is unusual in having a statutory process for it: ORS 376.150–376.200 lets a landowner with no access petition for a way of necessity, but the petitioner must pay the affected landowners' costs and reasonable attorney fees. Common-law implied easements by necessity are also recognized, though Oregon courts view implied easements skeptically. — Oregon Revised Statutes, Acquiring Title by Adverse Possession Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.620 — Oregon State Bar — Lawyer Referral Service — Oregon has among the strictest adverse possession rules in the country because of the honest-belief requirement — someone who knew the land was not theirs cannot claim it, no matter how long they used it. — Legal Aid Services of Oregon

p: Pennsylvania Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Pennsylvania — adverse possession 21 years 21 years is the standard period: possession must be actual, continuous, exclusive, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile for the full 21 years (42 Pa.C.S. Section 5530). There is one shorter path: 10 years for an occupied single-family home on a lot of one-half acre or less (Section 5527.1, added 2019). Paying taxes is not required and color of title alone does not shorten the period outside that home exception. — prescriptive easement 21 years 21 years of use that is adverse, open, notorious, continuous and uninterrupted (Walley v. Iraca). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a right-of-way — it does not transfer ownership. Unlike adverse possession, the use does not have to be exclusive (the owner may use the same path), and the continuity test is less strict than for full ownership. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Pennsylvania courts imply a right-of-way by necessity when a split leaves a parcel with no access to a public road, on a showing of reasonable necessity (Burns Mfg. Co. v. Boehm). Separately, the Private Road Act (36 P.S. Section 2731) lets a landlocked owner petition the court for a private road to the nearest public road. — Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes, Title 42, Twenty-One Year Limitation and Ten-Year Limitation 42 Pa.C.S. §§ 5527.1, 5530 — Pennsylvania Bar Association — Find a Lawyer (Lawyer Referral Service) — Pennsylvania's 10-year shortcut is narrow — it applies only to an occupied single-family home on a half-acre or less, not to vacant land or larger parcels, which still need the full 21 years. — Pennsylvania Legal Aid Network

p: Rhode Island Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in Rhode Island
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Rhode Island — adverse possession 10 years 10 years of uninterrupted, quiet, peaceful and actual possession, claiming the land as one's own, that is actual, open, notorious, hostile, under a claim of right, continuous and exclusive — each element proved by clear and convincing evidence (R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-7-1). Paying taxes is not required and color of title does not shorten the period. Unusually, the record owner can interrupt a claim by giving the occupant written notice of intent to dispute it (Section 34-7-6). Public land cannot be taken this way. — prescriptive easement 10 years 10 years of use that is actual, open, notorious, hostile and continuous under a claim of right, proved by clear and convincing evidence (Burke-Tarr Co. v. Ferland Corp.). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using part of someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway — it does not transfer ownership of the land. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. Rhode Island recognizes implied easements by necessity for access when a parcel is landlocked (see Prentiss v. Cadenazzi, R.I. Super. 2006). The easement covers only what is actually necessary for access, and it ends when the necessity ends. — Rhode Island General Laws, Chapter 34-7, By Possession and Prescription R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-7-1 — Rhode Island Bar Association — Lawyer Referral Service — Rhode Island gives owners a special defense most states lack: a written notice of intent to dispute the claim can interrupt adverse possession before the 10 years run out. — Rhode Island Legal Services

p: South Carolina Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in South Carolina
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in South Carolina — adverse possession 10 years 10 years of continuous possession that is actual, open, notorious, hostile (without permission) and exclusive. The owner's deadline to sue to recover land is 10 years (S.C. Code Section 15-3-340), and the adverse possession statute presumes an occupant is acting under the owner's authority unless the occupation has been adverse for 10 years (Section 15-67-210). Color of title (a faulty deed) can extend the claim to the full tract the deed describes. Paying taxes is not required. Courts also recognize a 20-year period that can support a presumed grant of title. — prescriptive easement 20 years 20 years — double the adverse possession period. The claimant must identify the exact thing enjoyed (for example, a specific road) and show use that was open, notorious, continuous, uninterrupted and contrary to the true owner's rights for 20 years (Simmons v. Berkeley Electric Cooperative, 2016). A prescriptive easement only gives the right to keep using the land for that specific purpose, not ownership of it. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes. South Carolina recognizes easements by necessity when a sale splits commonly owned land and leaves one parcel with no legal access to a public road (Kennedy v. Bedenbaugh). The owner must prove prior common ownership, the split, and genuine necessity — mere inconvenience is not enough. — South Carolina Code of Laws, Title 15, Chapter 3 and Chapter 67 (Recovery of Real Property) S.C. Code Ann. §§ 15-3-340, 15-67-210 — South Carolina Bar — Get Legal Help / Lawyer Referral Service — South Carolina is backwards from most states: full ownership takes only 10 years, but a mere right to use the land (a prescriptive easement) takes 20 years. — South Carolina Legal Services

p: South Dakota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in South Dakota
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in South Dakota — adverse possession 20 years Possession must be actual, open and notorious (visible), exclusive, continuous, and hostile (without the owner's permission) for 20 years. The period drops to 10 years if the claimant has color of title (a deed or other document that looks like ownership but is legally flawed) AND has paid the property taxes for those 10 years. The claim is not automatic — the claimant must go to court to quiet title. Governed by S.D. Codified Laws §§ 15-3-1, 15-3-15 and 15-3-16. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is the right to keep using someone else's land for a specific purpose (such as driving on a road or path) after 20 years of open, visible, continuous, unmolested use without the owner's permission. Unlike adverse possession, it gives only a right to use the land, not ownership of it. You cannot get a prescriptive easement against government-owned land. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — South Dakota recognizes easements by necessity. If a parcel is landlocked with no legal access to a public road, a court may grant an easement across a neighbor's land so the property can be reached, even if the neighbor objects. — South Dakota Codified Laws, Chapter 15-3 (Adverse Possession and Limitation of Actions to Recover Real Estate) S.D. Codified Laws §§ 15-3-1, 15-3-15, 15-3-16 — South Dakota Unified Judicial System — Legal Self-Help — South Dakota's 20-year period is among the longest in the country, and it is one of the few states where paying taxes plus holding a deed actually shortens the clock. Western South Dakota is served by a separate program, Dakota Plains Legal Services, and the statewide intake portal is SD Law Help. — East River Legal Services

p: Tennessee Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Tennessee — adverse possession 20 years Possession must be actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, hostile (without permission), and under a claim of right for 20 years. The period drops to 7 years if the claimant holds color of title — a recorded deed or document that appears to give ownership but is legally defective — recorded for the full 7 years. A claimant who never pays property taxes is vulnerable: under Tenn. Code § 28-2-110, a person who fails to have the land assessed and pay taxes on it for more than 20 years is barred from recovering it. — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement is earned by 20 continuous years of open, adverse use of another person's land under a claim of right — for example, driving across a neighbor's land to reach your own. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Use with the owner's permission never counts, and simply using a road without objection is not enough without proof of a hostile claim of right. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Tennessee recognizes easements by necessity (and easements by prior use). A landlocked parcel can get court-ordered access over a neighbor's land, but the claimant must prove the access is genuinely necessary, not merely convenient, and the necessity must have existed when the land was divided (Cowan v. Hardeman County). — Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 28, Chapter 2 (Limitation of Actions — Real Property) Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 28-2-101 to 28-2-110 — Tennessee Bar Association — For the Public — Tennessee has four regional legal aid programs; the Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands is the state's largest nonprofit law firm, serving 48 counties. East Tennessee is served by Legal Aid of East Tennessee and West Tennessee by West Tennessee Legal Services and Memphis Area Legal Services. — Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands

p: Texas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Texas — adverse possession 10 years Texas has a ladder of periods, not one number. The standard period with no deed at all is 10 years of peaceable possession while cultivating, using, or enjoying the land (capped at 160 acres without a title document). It is 3 years with title or color of title, 5 years with a duly registered deed plus paying the property taxes, and 25 years in special cases (including claims against an owner under a legal disability). Possession must be actual and visible, hostile to the owner's claim, and continuous. Since 2021, the 5-year route does not apply to quitclaim deeds, forged deeds, or deeds signed under a forged power of attorney. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement is gained by at least 10 years of use that is open and notorious, continuous, exclusive, and adverse (without permission) — the same 10-year period as the general adverse possession statute. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose (such as a driveway), not ownership. Texas courts disfavor these claims and scrutinize every element strictly. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Texas recognizes easements by necessity, but being landlocked alone is not enough. The claimant must prove three things: the two parcels were once owned by the same person, the access is a true necessity (not a mere convenience), and the necessity existed when the parcels were split (Hamrick v. Ward, 2014). A landlocked owner can also ask the county commissioners court for a public access road under Texas Transportation Code § 251.053. — Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code, Chapter 16, Subchapter B (Limitations of Real Property Actions) Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 16.021–16.034 — State Bar of Texas — Texas has three main regional legal aid programs: Lone Star Legal Aid (Houston and East Texas, 72 counties), Legal Aid of NorthWest Texas (114 counties in North and West Texas), and Texas RioGrande Legal Aid (South Texas). The State Bar's Lawyer Referral & Information Service offers a 30-minute consultation for $20. — Lone Star Legal Aid

p: Utah Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Utah — adverse possession 7 years Utah requires 7 years of continuous, open, hostile possession — but with a strict condition most states do not impose: the claimant must have paid ALL property taxes levied and assessed on the land for the entire 7-year period (Utah Code § 78B-2-209). Color of title (a document that appears to convey ownership) is also part of the statutory scheme. The owner is presumed to be in possession until the claimant proves 7 years of adverse holding (§ 78B-2-208). — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement in Utah takes 20 years — much longer than the 7-year adverse possession period. The claimant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the use was open, notorious, adverse (without permission), and continuous for at least 20 years (Utah Code § 78B-2-206; Van Denburgh v. Sweeney Land Co.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Use shared with the general public is presumed permissive, not adverse. A separate statute covers prescriptive easements for water conveyances (§ 57-13a-102, also 20 years). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Utah recognizes easements by necessity for landlocked parcels. The claimant must show the two parcels were once under common ownership, the access is truly necessary (not merely convenient), and the necessity existed when the parcels were split. The easement ends if the necessity ends, for example if another public road reaches the property. — Utah Code, Title 78B, Chapter 2, Part 2 (Adverse Possession) Utah Code Ann. §§ 78B-2-208 to 78B-2-214 — Utah State Bar — Tips on Finding a Utah Attorney — Utah is unusual: its adverse possession period (7 years) is one of the shortest in the country, but its prescriptive easement period (20 years) is nearly three times longer. Since May 7, 2025, a Utah owner can also ask police to remove a trespasser on a verified complaint without a court case (S.B. 55, Utah Code § 78B-6-817). — Utah Legal Services

p: Vermont Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Vermont — adverse possession 15 years Possession must be open, notorious, hostile (without permission), exclusive, and continuous for 15 years (12 V.S.A. § 501). Vermont does NOT require color of title or payment of property taxes. The claimant must then file a quiet title action in Superior Court and prove every element; ownership does not transfer automatically. One exception: a buyer at a tax sale who records the deed, moves in, and pays taxes gives the former owner only 1 year to sue (32 V.S.A. § 5263). — prescriptive easement 15 years A prescriptive easement is established by open, notorious, continuous, and adverse use of another's land for 15 years, which creates a presumption of a claim of right (Russell v. Pare; Community Feed Store v. Northeast Culvert Corp.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose — for example, a road or a path to a lake — not ownership. Permission from the owner defeats the claim, and successive owners can combine (tack) their periods of use if there is privity between them. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Vermont recognizes easements by necessity (implied easements) for landlocked parcels. But there is a catch: in Gray v. Treder (2018), the Vermont Supreme Court held that an unrecorded easement by necessity can be wiped out by the state's Marketable Record Title Act, so an access easement should be recorded to survive. — Vermont Statutes Annotated, Title 12, Chapter 23 (Limitation of Time for Commencement of Actions) Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, § 501 — Vermont Bar Association — Vermont Legal Aid works together with Legal Services Vermont (formerly Law Line); both share the VTLawHelp.org intake system. The Vermont Bar Association's Lawyer Referral Service offers a 30-minute consultation for no more than $25. — Vermont Legal Aid

p: Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Virginia — adverse possession 15 years Possession must be actual, hostile, exclusive, visible (open and notorious), and continuous, under a claim of right, for 15 years (Va. Code § 8.01-236). The claimant must prove every element by clear and convincing evidence — a high bar — and Virginia courts presume that someone occupying another's land does so with permission. You cannot adversely possess land owned by the federal or state government. Successive possessors can combine (tack) their time only if there is privity, such as a deed connecting them. — prescriptive easement 20 years Virginia is unusual: a prescriptive easement takes 20 years, longer than the 15-year adverse possession period. The claimant must show use that was adverse, under a claim of right, exclusive, continuous and uninterrupted, with the landowner's knowledge, for at least 20 years (Craig v. Kennedy, 202 Va. 654; Powell v. Magee). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. A separate statute defines prescriptive easements for utility and communications providers as 20 years or more (Va. Code § 55.1-306.1). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Virginia recognizes easements by necessity for landlocked parcels. The claimant must show the two parcels were once under common ownership, the land became landlocked when the land was divided, and there is currently no other way in or out. Mere convenience is not enough, and if another route later becomes available the neighbor can ask a court to end the easement. — Code of Virginia, Title 8.01, Chapter 4 (Limitation of entry on or action for land) Va. Code § 8.01-236 — Virginia State Bar — Legal Help — Virginia has several regional legal aid programs (Central, Southwest, Eastern Virginia, Northern Virginia, Blue Ridge); Virginia Legal Aid Society serves 20 counties and 6 cities in Central, Southside, and Western Tidewater Virginia. Virginia also has a court process to relocate a longstanding easement (10 years or older) under Va. Code § 55.1-304. — Virginia Legal Aid Society

p: Washington Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Washington — adverse possession 10 years Possession must be hostile (without permission), actual, exclusive, open and notorious, and continuous for 10 years (RCW 4.16.020). The period drops to 7 years if the claimant holds the land under color of title (a deed that appears valid) or has paid the property taxes (RCW 7.28.070). No adverse possession claim can be made against state or other government-owned land, and forestland claims also require substantial improvements that stayed on the land for at least 10 years (RCW 7.28.085). — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement requires 10 years of use that is open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, over a uniform route, adverse to the owner, and with the owner's knowledge at a time when the owner could have enforced their rights (Gamboa v. Clark, 183 Wn.2d 38). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. Washington presumes that a neighbor's use of a road is permissive (neighborly accommodation), so the claimant must overcome that presumption. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Washington recognizes easements by necessity (ways of necessity) for landlocked land, but the bar is strict necessity, not reasonable necessity — poor access alone does not qualify. Washington also has a private condemnation statute (RCW 8.24.010) letting a landlocked owner condemn a private way of necessity and pay the neighbor for it. — Revised Code of Washington, Title 4, Chapter 4.16 and Title 7, Chapter 7.28 (Adverse Possession) RCW 4.16.020; RCW 7.28.050; RCW 7.28.070 — Washington State Bar Association — Find Legal Help — Washington's free legal help runs through the CLEAR intake line (outside King County) and 211 (inside King County), both coordinated by the Northwest Justice Project, which also runs WashingtonLawHelp.org. The state bar itself does not refer people to private attorneys; it points to county bar referral services instead. — Northwest Justice Project

p: West Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Adverse possession & easements in West Virginia
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in West Virginia — adverse possession 10 years Possession must be hostile (adverse), actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, and under claim of title or color of title for 10 years (W. Va. Code § 55-2-1; Elder v. Smith). If the true owner was a minor or mentally incapacitated when the occupation began, they get 5 extra years after the disability ends to sue (§ 55-2-3). A 2025 bill to abolish adverse possession (HB 2924) was introduced but did not become law, so the 10-year rule still stands. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement requires open, continuous and uninterrupted use of a road or path over another's land, under a bona fide claim of right and without the owner's objection, for 10 years (Holland v. Flanagan; O'Dell v. Stegall). The claimant must prove each element by clear and convincing evidence, including the reasonably precise location, width, and purpose of the use. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership, and use with the owner's permission never counts. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — West Virginia recognizes easements by necessity, called a 'way of necessity.' Under Cobb v. Daugherty, the claimant must prove four things: both properties were once under common ownership, a conveyance split them apart, the easement was strictly necessary for the landlocked parcel at the time of the split, and the necessity continues today. The easement ends when the necessity ends, such as when a new road reaches the property. — West Virginia Code, Chapter 55, Article 2 (Limitation of Actions and Suits) W. Va. Code § 55-2-1 — West Virginia Lawyer Referral Service (West Virginia State Bar) — West Virginia's 2025 Stop Squatters Act (W. Va. Code §§ 55-3C-1 to 55-3C-6, in effect July 10, 2025) lets a property owner ask police to remove a squatter on a verified complaint without an eviction case; squatting is treated as criminal trespass, not a tenancy. Legal Aid of West Virginia is the state's primary civil legal aid provider, with 12 offices statewide. — Legal Aid of West Virginia

p: Wisconsin Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Wisconsin — adverse possession 20 years The standard period with no deed is 20 years of uninterrupted adverse possession, and the land must be actually occupied and either protected by a substantial enclosure (such as a fence) or usually cultivated or improved (Wis. Stat. § 893.25). It drops to 10 years with a recorded written instrument (color of title, § 893.26) and to 7 years with color of title plus payment of taxes (§ 893.27). There is no good-faith requirement for the 20-year route. No adverse possession against state or local government land except after 20+ years on a mutually agreed fence line (§ 893.29). — prescriptive easement 20 years A prescriptive easement requires continuous adverse use of another person's land for at least 20 years (Wis. Stat. § 893.28(1)). The use must be hostile and inconsistent with the owner's rights, visible, open and notorious, under an open claim of right, and continuous and uninterrupted for the full 20 years (Bauer v. Wisconsin Energy Corp.). It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. A shorter 10-year period applies only to certain utilities and cooperatives (§ 893.28(2)), and use of a way over unenclosed (wild, unimproved) land is presumed permissive, not adverse (§ 893.28(3)). Once the right accrues, the holder must record it within 30 years or lose it (§ 893.33(2)). — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Wisconsin recognizes a common-law way of necessity for landlocked parcels, but it is granted through the circuit court's discretion, not automatically as a matter of law (McCormick v. Schubring, 2003 WI 149). A landlocked owner can also apply to the town board to have a public highway laid out to the property under Wis. Stat. § 82.27, with the owner paying the cost. — Wisconsin Statutes, Chapter 893, Subchapter III (Adverse Possession and Prescription) Wis. Stat. §§ 893.25, 893.26, 893.27, 893.28 — State Bar of Wisconsin — Lawyer Referral Service — Legal Action of Wisconsin merged with Judicare Legal Aid on January 1, 2026, so it is now the single statewide civil legal aid intake for the whole state. The State Bar's Lawyer Referral Service charges no more than $20 for a first 30-minute consultation. — Legal Action of Wisconsin

p: Wyoming Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: adverse possession easements prescriptive easement easement by necessity landlocked property boundary — Adverse possession & easements in Wyoming — adverse possession 10 years Possession must be actual, open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile (adverse to the owner's interest) for 10 years (Wyo. Stat. § 1-3-103). Wyoming has no shortcut: the statute does not shorten the period for paying taxes or holding a deed, so a claimant with no paperwork is on the same 10-year clock as anyone else. A 2025 bill that would have stopped the clock while the owner paid all property taxes (HB 123) passed the House but died in a Senate committee, so the flat 10 years stands. — prescriptive easement 10 years A prescriptive easement in Wyoming takes 10 years of use that is continuous and uninterrupted, open and notorious, and adverse (without permission) — the same period as adverse possession. It gives only the right to keep using the land for that purpose, not ownership. The 10-year period is codified for water conveyances in Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-158 (2023), which also lets the holder file a notice of the easement with the county clerk. — easement by necessity landlocked Yes — Wyoming recognizes implied easements, including easements by prior use where a road or path was openly used before the land was split (Hansuld v. Lariat Diesel Corp.). Wyoming also has a statutory private road remedy: a landlocked owner can petition the court for a private road of necessity under Wyo. Stat. § 24-9-101, paying the neighbor damages — confirmed in Wagonhound Land & Livestock Co. v. Little Medicine Creek Ranch (2026). — Wyoming Statutes, Title 1, Chapter 3 (Limitation of Actions — Recovery of Real Property) Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-3-103 — Wyoming State Bar — Since July 1, 2025, Wyoming law (SF 6, Enrolled Act 20) lets a property owner apply to law enforcement to remove an unauthorized occupant from a residence without first going to court. Legal Aid of Wyoming runs a free Legal Aid Hotline staffed by licensed attorneys, and Equal Justice Wyoming (equaljustice.wy.gov) is the state's legal-help website. — Legal Aid of Wyoming

p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Alabama — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage, from the moment a ride is accepted until the passenger is dropped off — uninsured underinsured motorist No separate UM/UIM amount is set for rideshare in the TNC statute; the statute requires all other state-mandated motor vehicle coverage, and Alabama law requires UM coverage to be offered at minimum limits of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident, though a driver may reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While the driver is logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's personal policy is first in line if it covers TNC activity, but most personal policies exclude commercial use, and Alabama law requires the TNC's coverage to step in from the first dollar if the driver's policy lapses or does not cover the claim. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first regardless of the driver's personal coverage. — Alabama Code §§ 32-7C-1 to 32-7C-36 (Transportation Network Company Act); insurance requirements at Ala. Code § 32-7C-2 — deadline to file 2 years The two-year clock under Ala. Code § 6-2-38 starts on the date of the crash, is tolled while the injured person is a minor, and claims against a city require written notice within 6 months. — Alabama Public Service Commission — Alabama's TNC law (2018) requires every TNC to hold a permit from the Public Service Commission, and the statute bars any contract between a TNC and its drivers or riders from reducing the required insurance. The Commission also runs a TNC complaint process and requires a zero-tolerance drug and alcohol policy. — Legal Services Alabama

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Alaska — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car) — uninsured underinsured motorist UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods as required by AS 21.96.020 and AS 28.20.440, at Alaska's minimums of $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident; Alaska law requires UM coverage to be offered but allows the policyholder to reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's personal policy pays first if it covers TNC driving, but Alaska law expressly lets personal insurers exclude all coverage while a driver is logged on or giving a prearranged ride. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar and defend the claim, and the TNC's coverage may not be conditioned on the personal insurer denying the claim first. During a prearranged ride (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays. — Alaska Statutes §§ 28.23.010-28.23.180 (Transportation Network Companies and Drivers); insurance at AS 28.23.050 and AS 21.96.018 — deadline to file 2 years The two-year clock under AS 09.10.070 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and is tolled while the injured person is a minor. — Alaska Department of Administration, Division of Motor Vehicles — Alaska's TNC law (2017) requires no state TNC permit or registration; companies must comply with the statute's insurance, background-check, and vehicle-inspection rules on their own. Distinctive rules: a TNC vehicle may be no more than 12 years old, and drivers are independent contractors by statute (AS 28.23.080). — Alaska Legal Services Corporation

p: Arizona Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Arizona — waiting for a ride Period 1 $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident for bodily injury or death, $20,000 property damage (state statutory minimum; Uber and Lyft in practice provide higher Period 1 limits of $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident, with $25,000 property damage from Uber and $20,000 from Lyft) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 Period 2 (en route to pickup): $250,000 per incident primary commercial liability. Period 3 (passenger in the vehicle): $1,000,000 per incident primary commercial liability (raised from $250,000 by HB 2729 in 2024). — uninsured underinsured motorist Arizona requires commercial UM coverage in the rideshare context: $250,000 per incident while the driver is en route to a pickup, and $25,000 per person / $75,000 per incident while a passenger is in the vehicle (A.R.S. § 28-4038, as amended by HB 2729 in 2024). Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the state floor. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), coverage may come from the driver's policy, the TNC's policy, or a combination, and the TNC must provide coverage from the first dollar if the driver's policy excludes TNC activity or falls short. Once a ride is accepted, the TNC's commercial policy is primary: $250,000 while en route to the pickup and $1,000,000 once a passenger is in the car. Most personal auto policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common and does not leave the injured person without coverage in Periods 2 and 3. — Arizona Revised Statutes Title 28, Chapter 30, §§ 28-9551 et seq. (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at A.R.S. § 28-4038 — deadline to file 2 years The two-year clock under A.R.S. § 12-542 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and a claim against a public entity requires a notice of claim within 180 days. — Arizona Department of Transportation, Motor Vehicle Division — Arizona is unusual in splitting Periods 2 and 3: the $1,000,000 floor applies only once a passenger is in the car, while the drive to the pickup is capped at a $250,000 statutory minimum (though Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 for both periods under their own policies). TNCs must hold an ADOT permit, drivers must be at least 19, and public airports may still regulate TNC pickups. — Community Legal Services

p: Arkansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Arkansas — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car) — uninsured underinsured motorist The TNC statute does not set a separate UM/UIM amount for rideshare; Arkansas law requires UM coverage to be offered at minimum limits of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident, and a driver may reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's policy pays first if it covers TNC driving, but the TNC must provide coverage from the first dollar if the driver's policy excludes the activity or does not meet the minimums. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Most personal policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common and triggers the TNC's first-dollar duty. — Arkansas Code §§ 23-13-701 to 23-13-719 (Transportation Network Company Services Act); insurance requirements at Ark. Code § 23-13-709 — deadline to file 3 years The three-year clock under Ark. Code § 16-56-105 starts on the date of the crash and is tolled while the injured person is a minor. — Arkansas Public Service Commission — Arkansas was an early TNC regulator (2015): every TNC must hold a permit from the Public Service Commission, and Arkansas gives crash victims three years to file, longer than most states in this set. The statute also states that a TNC driver is an independent contractor, not an employee of the company. — Legal Aid of Arkansas

p: California Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in California — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and personal injury, $30,000 property damage (primary coverage), plus $200,000 per occurrence in excess coverage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability for death, personal injury, and property damage from the moment a ride is accepted until the ride is complete — uninsured underinsured motorist UM/UIM coverage of $60,000 per person / $300,000 per incident is required while a passenger is in the vehicle, under Public Utilities Code § 5433(b)(2) as amended by SB 371 (2025), effective January 1, 2026; this is a sharp cut from the $1,000,000 UM/UIM floor that applied before. Uber and Lyft still advertise $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the new state floor. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the TNC's coverage is primary at $50,000/$100,000/$30,000, with $200,000 in excess coverage on top. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary commercial policy pays first. California law requires the TNC to tell drivers in writing that their personal policy may not cover TNC driving, and most personal policies exclude it, so a personal insurer's denial is expected and does not block the TNC coverage. — California Public Utilities Code §§ 5430-5445, Article 7 (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5433 — deadline to file 2 years The two-year clock under Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and a claim against a government entity requires a written claim within 6 months. — California Public Utilities Commission — California created the TNC category and is the only state in this set where the regulator (the CPUC) issues TNC permits and sets detailed rules in General Order 157. Proposition 22 (2020) keeps rideshare drivers as independent contractors, and California's $30,000 Period 1 property-damage floor is higher than the $25,000 used in most other states. — LawHelp California

p: Colorado Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Colorado — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $30,000 property damage (primary coverage) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability per occurrence while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car) — uninsured underinsured motorist UM coverage of at least $200,000 per person / $400,000 per occurrence is required for the driver and each rider during a prearranged ride, under C.R.S. § 40-10.1-604(2.5), in effect since August 10, 2022. No UM coverage is required during Period 1, so UM protection while waiting depends on the driver's own policy or the TNC's policy terms. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies, at Colorado's $25,000/$50,000/$15,000 minimums. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$30,000 that recognizes TNC driving. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Colorado law states that nothing in the TNC statute requires a personal policy to cover time logged into the app, so a personal insurer's denial for commercial use is common and the TNC coverage fills the gap. — Colorado Revised Statutes §§ 40-10.1-601 to 40-10.1-608 (Transportation Network Company Act); insurance requirements at C.R.S. § 40-10.1-604 — deadline to file 3 years Colorado's general personal injury limit is 2 years, but motor vehicle accident injuries get 3 years under C.R.S. § 13-80-101(1)(n), starting on the date of the crash, and a claim against a government entity requires notice within 182 days. — Colorado Public Utilities Commission — Colorado was the first state in the country to regulate TNCs (SB 14-125, 2014), and it has one of the strongest rideshare UM mandates in this set at $200,000 per person / $400,000 per occurrence during a ride. SB 24-075 added fare-transparency and driver-pay rules enforced by the Department of Labor and Employment. — Colorado Legal Services

p: Connecticut Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Connecticut — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident for bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability per accident for bodily injury, death, or property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car) — uninsured underinsured motorist UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 38a-336, at Connecticut's minimums of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the state floor. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 plus UM/UIM, and the TNC's coverage steps in from the first dollar if the driver's policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Connecticut law preserves personal-policy exclusions for vehicles used to carry passengers for a fee, so a personal insurer's denial for commercial use is common. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 13b-116 to 13b-120, Chapter 244c (Transportation Network Company Vehicles); insurance requirements at Conn. Gen. Stat. § 13b-120 — deadline to file 2 years The two-year clock under Conn. Gen. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 113L (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 228(c)-(d)); Uber and Lyft also provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3 under their company policies. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. In Period 1 the required coverage may be held by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of both, and in practice Uber/Lyft provide contingent coverage at the Period 1 limits. If the driver's own insurance has lapsed, failed to provide the required coverage, or denied the claim, the TNC's insurance must provide the required coverage from the first dollar of the claim and defend it (ch. 175, § 228(e)), so a personal-insurer denial for commercial use does not leave the injured person without coverage while the driver is logged on. — Mass. Laws ch. 175, § 228 (TNC insurance requirements); 220 CMR 274.00 — deadline to file 3 years The clock normally starts on the crash date under Mass. Gen. p: Michigan Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Michigan — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus PIP and property protection insurance as required by the Insurance Code — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 combined single limit for all bodily injury or property damage, plus PIP and property protection insurance as required by the Insurance Code — uninsured underinsured motorist Michigan's TNC statute (MCL 257.2123) does not require UM/UIM coverage, and UM/UIM is optional in Michigan generally; Uber and Lyft company policies do provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3, but that is a company benefit, not a state mandate. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In Periods 1-3 the required coverage may be held by the driver, the TNC, or both, and if the required insurance lapses or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar and defend the claim (MCL 257.2123(5)). TNC coverage is not dependent on the personal insurer denying the claim first (MCL 257.2123(6)), so a personal policy's commercial-use exclusion does not block the TNC policy. Michigan is a no-fault state, so an injured passenger usually claims PIP medical benefits from their own (or a resident relative's) policy first. — Limousine, Taxicab, and Transportation Network Company Act, 2016 PA 345, MCL 257.2101 et seq.; insurance requirements at MCL 257.2123 — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the injury under MCL 600.5805(2), with tolling for minors, but no-fault PIP benefit claims have a separate 1-year deadline under MCL 500.3145 and claims against a public transit authority can require written notice within 60 days. — Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), Corporations, Securities and Commercial Licensing Bureau — Michigan's no-fault system makes it distinctive: TNCs must elect higher PIP levels ($250,000, $500,000, or unlimited), yet an injured passenger's own PIP policy is usually the first payer, with the TNC's PIP applying only when no other policy is available. Michigan also requires an annual vehicle inspection only for TNC vehicles five years old or older. — Michigan Legal Help

t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Minnesota — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 for two or more persons bodily injury or death, $30,000 property damage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,500,000 combined single limit for death, injury, or destruction of property of others, plus a separate TNC-provided personal-injury policy of at least $1,000,000 per incident for the driver — uninsured underinsured motorist Primary uninsured motorist and underinsured motorist coverage are required in Period 1 and in Periods 2-3 where required by Minn. Stat. § 65B.49, subdivisions 3a and 4a (Minn. Stat. § 65B.472, subd. 2(b)(3)), at Minnesota's statutory UM/UIM minimums. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In Periods 1-3 the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that expressly recognizes rideshare use. If the driver's coverage lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance steps in from the first dollar. Minnesota is a no-fault state, so basic economic loss (medical and wage-loss) benefits are also part of the required coverage in Period 1. — Minn. Stat. § 65B.472 (Transportation Network Financial Responsibility) and Minn. Stat. ch. 181C (Transportation Network Companies, enacted 2024) — deadline to file 6 years For a negligence crash claim, the clock runs 6 years from the crash under Minn. Stat. § 541.05, subd. 1(5); note that some secondary sources cite the 2-year period in § 541.07(1), which applies to intentional torts such as assault and battery, not ordinary negligence, and claims against a government entity have separate shorter notice rules. — Minnesota Department of Commerce — Minnesota has the highest Period 2-3 liability minimum in this set at $1,500,000, not $1,000,000, and it is the only state here that also requires the TNC to provide a separate $1,000,000 personal-injury policy for the driver at no cost to the driver. Its 2024 TNC law (ch. 181C) also sets driver minimum pay and deactivation rules, enforced by the Department of Labor and Industry. — LawHelpMN

p: Mississippi Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Mississippi — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage — uninsured underinsured motorist Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both periods to the extent required by Miss. Code § 83-11-101; Mississippi requires UM coverage unless the insured rejects it in writing, at the statutory minimum limits. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that recognizes rideshare use, and the requirements may be met by the driver's policy, the TNC's policy, or a combination. Mississippi law expressly allows personal insurers to exclude coverage for losses while the driver is logged on or providing a prearranged ride, which is why the TNC's primary coverage is the payer in those periods. — Mississippi House Bill 1381 (2016), codified at Miss. Code §§ 63-15-39 to 63-15-43 (TNC insurance) and Miss. Code § 77-7-7 (TNC licensing) — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the crash under Miss. Code § 15-1-49, with tolling for minors and persons under a legal disability, and a shorter deadline applies to claims against a government entity. — Mississippi Department of Insurance (licenses transportation network companies) — Mississippi splits legal aid geographically: North Mississippi Rural Legal Services covers the northern counties and the Mississippi Center for Legal Services covers the central and southern counties, and both are reached through the statewide MSLegalServices.org portal. A TNC business-entity license in Mississippi carries a $5,000 annual fee. — Mississippi Legal Services (MSLegalServices.org)

Rev. Stat. § 379.203 (RSMo § 379.1702(2)(2) and (3)(2)). — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that recognizes rideshare use. If the driver's insurance has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar and defends the claim, and if the driver's policy covers the loss but below the required limits, the TNC provides excess coverage up to the required limits (RSMo § 379.1702(4)). — Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 387.400 to 387.440 (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 379.1700 to 379.1708 — deadline to file 5 years The clock starts on the date of the injury under Mo. Rev. Missouri is also unusual in splitting TNC regulation (Department of Revenue licensing) from TNC insurance rules (chapter 379). — Legal Services of Missouri

t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Montana — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury, and property damage — uninsured underinsured motorist Montana's TNC statute (MCA 69-12-343) does not expressly require UM/UIM coverage; Montana law requires insurers to offer UM coverage, which a driver may reject, and Uber and Lyft company policies provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3, but that is a company benefit, not a state TNC mandate. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary insurance recognizing rideshare use, and if the driver's policy lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance must cover the claim from the first dollar and defend it (MCA 69-12-343). Personal insurers in Montana may exclude all coverage, including UM/UIM and collision, for losses while the driver is logged on or providing a prearranged ride (MCA 69-12-345). — Mont. Code Ann. Title 69, chapter 12, §§ 69-12-341 to 69-12-345 (Transportation Network Carriers, Class E motor carriers; SB 396, 2015) — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the crash under Mont. Code Ann. § 27-2-204, with a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered and tolling for minors, and a shorter notice deadline applies to claims against a government entity. — Montana Public Service Commission — Montana is distinctive in calling rideshare companies 'transportation network carriers' and regulating them as Class E motor carriers that must hold a certificate of compliance from the Public Service Commission, and state law expressly bars local governments from regulating TNC services. Montana Legal Services Association is the state's sole statewide provider of general civil legal assistance. — Montana Legal Services Association

Rev. Stat. § 75-334), and UM/UIM coverage of at least $1,000,000 for both driver and passengers is required in the engaged and passengers-on-board stages (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 75-333). — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In the application-open stage (logged on, no ride accepted) the TNC or driver must maintain primary TNC insurance, and in the engaged and passengers-on-board stages the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary. Nebraska's Department of Insurance warns that personal auto policies typically exclude business use or being available for hire, so a personal insurer's denial in those stages is expected and the TNC policy is the payer. — Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-321 to 75-341 (Transportation Network Company Act; LB 629, 2015); insurance at Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-333 and 75-334 — deadline to file 4 years The clock starts on the date of the crash under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-207, with tolling for minors and a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered, and claims against a government entity require a tort claim notice within 1 year. — Nebraska Public Service Commission — Nebraska has the lowest Period 1 minimums in this set at $25,000/$50,000/$25,000, half the bodily-injury limits most other states require while waiting for a ride, while its engaged-stage UM/UIM requirement of $1,000,000 is among the strongest. Nebraska also uses its own stage names: application-open, engaged, and passengers-on-board. — Legal Aid of Nebraska

t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Nevada — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per crash bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 for bodily injury to or death of one or more persons and injury to or destruction of property of others in any one accident — uninsured underinsured motorist UM/UIM coverage is NOT required in Nevada's TNC insurance law; NRS 690B.470(6) says a TNC policy may include UM/UIM, medical payments, comprehensive and collision coverage, but none of it is required, and Uber and Lyft are reported not to provide UM/UIM coverage for drivers in Nevada. — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies, and Nevada's general minimums are $25,000/$50,000/$20,000. In Period 1 the TNC insurance is not contingent on the personal insurer denying first, and the TNC insurer has a duty to defend and indemnify (NRS 690B.470(7)-(8)). A personal insurer may exclude TNC activity entirely and then has no duty to defend or indemnify (NRS 690B.480), so the TNC policy is the payer once the driver is logged on. — Nev. Rev. Stat. ch. 706A (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Nev. Rev. Stat. § 690B.470 — deadline to file 2 years The clock starts on the date of the crash under Nev. Rev. Stat. § 11.190(4)(e), with a discovery rule for latent injuries and tolling for minors, and claims against a government entity have a shorter notice and filing deadline. — Nevada Transportation Authority — Nevada's trip-period minimum was $1,500,000 until AB 523 (2025) cut it to $1,000,000 effective October 1, 2025, so many older sources still quote $1,500,000 and the crash date decides which figure applies; the same 2025 law added NRS 706A.155 barring vicarious liability for TNCs. Nevada is also one of the few states here with no UM/UIM requirement at all in the rideshare context. — Nevada Legal Services

While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage, and if the driver's insurance has lapsed or falls short, the TNC's insurance provides the required coverage from the first dollar and defends the claim (RSA 359-U:8). TNC coverage is not dependent on the personal insurer denying the claim first (RSA 359-U:8), and personal insurers may exclude all coverage during TNC activity (RSA 359-U:10). — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. ch. 359-U (Transportation Network Company; RSA 376-A repealed and replaced by 2023 ch. 30, eff. July 1, 2023); insurance at RSA 359-U:8; rules at N.H. Admin. Rules Saf-C 5400 — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the act causing the injury under N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 508:4(I), or on discovery if the injury and its cause could not reasonably have been discovered then, with tolling for minors, and a shorter notice deadline applies to claims against a government entity. — New Hampshire Department of Safety, Division of Motor Vehicles — New Hampshire is the outlier in this set: its statutory minimum for a prearranged ride is only $300,000, not $1,000,000, so the $1,000,000 figure riders see comes from Uber and Lyft company policies, not state law. It is also the only state here where most drivers are not required to carry auto insurance at all, which makes the TNC policy especially important. — New Hampshire Legal Assistance

h: Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in New Jersey
t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in New Jersey — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus primary PIP — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,500,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus at least $10,000 in medical payments per person for the driver and $1,500,000 in UM/UIM coverage — uninsured underinsured motorist UM/UIM coverage is required in both stages: in Period 1 at the state minimum under N.J.S.A. 17:28-1.1 (now $35,000 per person / $70,000 per incident bodily injury and $25,000 property damage as of January 1, 2026), and in Periods 2-3 at least $1,500,000 (N.J.S.A. 39:5H-10). — who pays When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver, the TNC, or a combination must maintain the required primary coverage, and the TNC's coverage is primary, not a backstop. If the driver's coverage lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance must provide the required coverage from the first dollar. A New Jersey personal insurer may exclude any and all coverage while the driver is logged on or on a ride (N.J.S.A. 39:5H-12), so the TNC policy is the payer in those periods, and New Jersey's no-fault PIP system covers medical bills first. — Transportation Network Company Safety and Regulatory Act, P.L.2017, c.26, N.J.S.A. 39:5H-1 et seq.; insurance at N.J.S.A. 39:5H-10 — deadline to file 2 years The clock starts when the claim accrues, normally the crash date, under N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2, with a discovery rule for injuries discovered later and tolling for minors, and claims against a public entity require a notice of claim within 90 days under the Tort Claims Act. — New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission — New Jersey has the strongest rideshare insurance package in this set: $1,500,000 in liability and $1,500,000 in UM/UIM coverage in Periods 2-3, plus $10,000 in medical payments for the driver, and it is a no-fault state, so PIP applies in Period 1 as well. A New Jersey appeals court has also held that the TNC act covers transport of people, not app-based food delivery. — Legal Services of New Jersey

t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in New York — waiting for a ride Period 1 $75,000 per person / $150,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured motorist coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,250,000 liability for bodily injury, death and property damage, plus $1,250,000 supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault) — uninsured underinsured motorist Uninsured motorist coverage is required in Period 1, and during a prearranged trip the policy must include $1,250,000 in supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage — far above the $25,000 minimum UM coverage on a regular New York auto policy. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at New York's $25,000/$50,000 minimums plus $50,000 no-fault PIP. Once logged on, the TNC must maintain a group policy that satisfies the limits above, and that TNC coverage is primary; a personal insurer's rideshare exclusion does not defeat the TNC coverage. No-fault PIP pays medical bills and lost wages first regardless of fault, and a claim for pain and suffering still requires a 'serious injury' under Insurance Law Section 5102(d). — Vehicle and Traffic Law Article 44-B, Transportation Network Company Services, Sections 1691-1699 (insurance requirements at Section 1693) — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the crash, but a no-fault (PIP) claim must be filed within 30 days of the crash, and a claim against a city or other government body requires a notice of claim within 90 days. — New York State Department of Financial Services — New York's limits are the highest in this group outside New York City ($1,250,000 per trip), but Article 44-B does not apply to trips originating in New York City, where Uber and Lyft cars are for-hire vehicles under Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) rules requiring at least $100,000/$300,000 bodily injury coverage. — The Legal Aid Society

t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in North Carolina — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage — uninsured underinsured motorist Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is required with the TNC policy under North Carolina's mandatory UM law; during Periods 2-3 Uber and Lyft carry $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage, and in Period 1 UM/UIM follows the state's mandatory uninsured motorist requirements. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Period 1, Uber and Lyft provide contingent liability coverage that only pays if the driver's personal policy denies the claim or is exhausted, which is where most coverage disputes arise. Once a ride is accepted, the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary, and the driver's personal insurer may exclude rideshare use entirely. — Transportation Network Companies Act, N.C.G.S. Article 10A, Sections 20-280.1 to 20-280.10 (insurance requirements at Section 20-280.4) — deadline to file 3 years The clock starts on the date of the crash, or when a hidden injury is or should have been discovered, with a 10-year outer limit; the period is paused while the injured person is a minor. — North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles — North Carolina is one of the few states that still uses contributory negligence, so any fault on the injured person's part, no matter how small, can bar recovery entirely. TNCs must get a permit from the Division of Motor Vehicles and renew it annually. — Legal Aid of North Carolina

Chapter 39-34, and TNC insurance, N.D.C.C. Chapter 26.1-40.1 (Sections 26.1-40.1-03 and 26.1-40.1-04), as amended by 2023 HB 1440 — deadline to file 6 years The clock starts on the date of the crash and is paused for minors until age 18, but a wrongful-death claim has a shorter 2-year deadline. — North Dakota Department of Transportation — North Dakota's 6-year personal injury deadline is among the longest in the country, and its no-fault PIP system means medical bills are paid through PIP regardless of fault. t: rideshare accidents uber lyft transportation network company TNC insurance periods — Rideshare accidents (Uber & Lyft) in Oregon — waiting for a ride Period 1 $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists) — on the way passenger in the car Periods 2-3 $1,000,000 combined single limit primary liability (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists) — uninsured underinsured motorist Oregon law (ORS 742.502) requires UM/UIM coverage equal to the bodily injury liability limits on every auto policy, including TNC coverage; the statewide TNC law also requires personal injury protection of at least $15,000 in medical expenses plus up to $3,000 per month in wage loss for up to 52 weeks for drivers, passengers and pedestrians struck by the vehicle. — who pays With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Portland, the TNC must maintain primary coverage for all periods, with the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 tier while waiting and $1,000,000 once a ride is accepted, so there is no coverage gap. Outside Portland there is no statewide tiered liability law, so coverage depends on the city, the TNC's own policy, and whether the driver's personal policy has a livery exclusion, which can leave a gap in Period 1. — Oregon Revised Statutes Sections 742.518 and 742.520 (TNC personal injury protection, HB 2393 of 2021); Portland City Code Chapter 16.40, Section 16.40.230 (insurance tiers) — Oregon has no statewide TNC operating statute — deadline to file 2 years The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered, with a 10-year outer limit under ORS 12.115; a claim against a government body needs a tort-claim notice within 180 days. — Portland Bureau of Transportation (Private For-Hire Transportation program) — Oregon is unusual in having no comprehensive statewide TNC law: the only statewide TNC-specific statute requires PIP benefits, and permits, background checks and the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 and $1,000,000 insurance tiers are set by individual cities, with Portland's Chapter 16.40 as the model. Oregon uses modified comparative fault with a 51% bar under ORS 31.600. — Legal Aid Services of Oregon
