p: New York Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in New York
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in New York — what counts as a service animal New York law covers guide dogs, hearing dogs, and service dogs. Civil Rights Law Section 47-b defines a service dog by reference to the federal ADA regulations: a dog under the control of the person using or training it that has been or is being individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including psychiatric disabilities. The state statute speaks only of dogs; it does not include miniature horses in its own definition. — public access No person may be denied admittance to or equal use of any public facility because they are accompanied by a guide, hearing, or service dog, including restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, schools, government buildings, and all public and private transportation and housing accommodations. Under the ADA, staff may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the dog is a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. New York goes beyond the ADA by expressly counting all forms of public and private housing as public facilities. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under either New York law or the ADA, because they provide companionship rather than trained tasks, so they have no right to enter stores, restaurants, or other public places. They may still be protected in housing as a reasonable accommodation under the New York Human Rights Law and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty New York has no general criminal penalty for falsely claiming a pet is a service animal. An emotional support animal may also be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with documentation if the need is not apparent. — New York Civil Rights Law, Article 4-B, Sections 47 to 47-c; New York Executive Law Section 296(14); Agriculture and Markets Law Section 118 — New York State Division of Human Rights — New York expressly gives trainers the same public-access rights as handlers while training a dog (Civil Rights Law Section 47-b(3)), and denying access is an unlawful discriminatory practice under Executive Law Section 296(14). Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. North Dakota goes beyond the ADA by making it a Class A misdemeanor to deny or interfere with admission or enjoyment of those places (Section 25-13-04). — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under North Dakota law or the ADA, because their sole function is comfort or emotional support rather than trained tasks, so they have no public-access rights. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under state and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Infraction under N.D. Cent. Code Section 25-13-02.2: a person is guilty of an infraction if, in an attempt to gain admission to a public place or obtain a reasonable housing accommodation under Section 47-16-07.5, the person knowingly makes a false claim that a pet is a service animal. Sources disagree on the dollar amount: the 2019 bill text set a maximum fine of $100, while other sources report the general infraction maximum of $1,000; the text of Section 25-13-02.2 itself states no dollar amount. — housing A service animal must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under N.D. Cent. Code Section 47-16-07.5, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation if the disability or need is not apparent, and knowingly providing fraudulent disability documentation for a housing accommodation can lead to eviction and a damage fee of up to $1,000 under Section 47-16-07.6. — North Dakota Century Code, Chapter 25-13 (Blind and Disabled Persons' Activities), Sections 25-13-01.1 to 25-13-06; N.D. Cent. Code Section 47-16-07.5 (housing) — North Dakota Department of Labor and Human Rights, Human Rights Division — Trainers have express public-access rights: a trainer with a service animal in training may enter public places if the trainer notifies the onsite manager, wears a photo ID issued by a nationally recognized service animal training program, and accepts financial responsibility for damage (Section 25-13-02.1). Denying access to a service animal team is a Class A misdemeanor, a stronger penalty than in most states. — Legal Services of North Dakota — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Ohio Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Ohio
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Ohio — what counts as a service animal Ohio uses the term 'assistance dog': a dog trained by a nonprofit or for-profit special agency as a guide dog (for a blind person), a hearing dog (for a deaf or hearing-impaired person), or a service dog (for a person with a mobility impairment), including dogs still in training. A broader term, 'animal assistant,' is used in public-accommodation and housing rules and means any animal which aids a person with a disability. (Ohio Rev. Code Sections 955.011 and 955.43; Ohio Admin. Code 4112-5-02) — public access A person who is blind, deaf, hearing impaired, or has a mobility impairment, or a trainer of an assistance dog, is entitled to full and equal access to all public conveyances, hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, institutions of education, and other places the general public is invited, and may take the dog into those places. No fee or charge may be made for the dog, though the dog may not occupy a seat on a public conveyance and must be leashed on a common carrier. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. Ohio's broader 'animal assistant' definition can cover animals beyond dogs in public-accommodation and housing contexts. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not assistance dogs under Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 955 and have no public-access rights as service animals. They may still qualify as an 'animal assistant' or assistance animal in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Ohio and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Ohio has no targeted fake service dog or misrepresentation statute; general fraud laws could theoretically apply, but there is no specific service-animal misrepresentation offense. By contrast, recklessly denying access to or charging a fee for an assistance dog is a misdemeanor of the fourth degree under Ohio Rev. Code Section 955.43, punishable by up to 30 days in jail and a fine of up to $250. — housing An assistance animal or animal assistant must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent. — Ohio Revised Code Sections 955.011, 955.43, and 955.99; Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4112 (Ohio Civil Rights Act); Ohio Admin. Code 4112-5-02 — Ohio Civil Rights Commission — Ohio's definition of a person with a mobility impairment was significantly expanded by HB 33, effective October 3, 2023. Ohio also designates the last week of July as Service Dog Awareness Week, and killing an assistance dog is a third-degree felony under Ohio Rev. Code Section 2921.321. — Ohio Legal Help — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Oklahoma Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Oklahoma
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Oklahoma — what counts as a service animal Under Title 4, Section 801, as amended by HB 1178 effective November 1, 2025, a service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, matching the ADA definition, and it does not include an emotional support animal or a therapy animal. The older Title 7, Section 19.1 law is narrower: a guide dog, signal dog, or service dog, with 'service dog' defined only for a physically handicapped person, and a signal dog must wear an orange identifying collar. — public access A person with a disability accompanied by a guide, signal, or service dog may not be denied admittance to streets, sidewalks, common carriers, hotels, motels, lodging, public buildings, educational facilities, restaurants, or any other place of public accommodation, amusement, convenience, or resort, with no extra charge for the dog, though the handler is liable for damage. Trainers from a recognized training center have the same access while training. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. Oklahoma is distinctive in requiring businesses to post signage about service animal rights and in requiring an orange collar for signal dogs. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals and therapy animals are expressly excluded from the definition of a service animal under Title 4, Section 801, so they have no public-access rights in Oklahoma. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Oklahoma and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Misdemeanor under 4 Okla. Stat. Section 801(E) and (F), as amended by HB 1178 effective November 1, 2025: knowingly presenting any animal or therapy animal as a service animal, or intentionally misrepresenting entitlement to an animal as a qualified service animal to obtain disability rights or benefits, is a misdemeanor upon conviction. The statute sets no dollar fine amount in that section. Denying access under Title 7, Section 19.2 is also a misdemeanor. — housing A service dog must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under 41 Okla. Stat. Section 113.1, with no extra charge or pet deposit for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need if it is not readily apparent, and a knowingly false disability claim or fraudulent documentation to obtain a housing accommodation can lead to eviction remedies and damages of up to $1,000 under Section 113.2. — Oklahoma Statutes, Title 4, Section 801 (Public Accommodations and Service Animals, as amended by HB 1178, 2025); Title 7, Sections 19.1 to 19.2; Title 41, Section 113.1 (housing) — Oklahoma Attorney General, Office of Civil Rights Enforcement (successor to the Oklahoma Human Rights Commission) — HB 1178, enacted in 2025 by legislative veto override and effective November 1, 2025, aligned Oklahoma's definition with the ADA, added the misrepresentation misdemeanors, and requires public accommodations to post signage about service animal rights. Oklahoma's employment anti-discrimination law applies to employers with just one or more employees. — Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Oregon Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Oregon
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Oregon — what counts as a service animal Oregon uses the term 'assistance animal': a dog or other animal designated by administrative rule that has been individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability. Oregon Administrative Rule 839-006-0345 designates dogs and miniature horses as assistance animals. An 'assistance animal trainee' is an animal undergoing training to do work or tasks directly related to the person's disability. (ORS 659A.143) — public access A place of public accommodation or of access to state government services, programs, or activities may not deny a person with a disability or an assistance animal trainer the right to be accompanied by an assistance animal or trainee in any area open to the public or business invitees, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings. No fee or admission charge may be imposed for the animal, and no documentation may be required. A business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required due to a disability, and what work or task it is trained or being trained to perform; it may not ask about the nature or extent of the disability. Oregon goes beyond the ADA by expressly covering trainees and by barring any documentation demand in the statute itself. — emotional support animals Emotional support, therapy, comfort, and companion animals are not assistance animals under Oregon law or the ADA, because they are not individually trained to do work or tasks, so they have no public-access rights. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Oregon and federal fair housing law, where the definition is broader. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Oregon has no targeted fake service dog or misrepresentation statute; bills in 2019 (HB 2758 and HB 3098) failed to pass. Interfering with an assistance animal is a separate offense, a Class A misdemeanor under ORS 167.352, punishable by up to 364 days in jail and a fine of up to $6,250. — housing An assistance animal must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under ORS 659A.145, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage it causes. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent, and in housing the term can include emotional support animals that qualify as a reasonable accommodation. — Oregon Revised Statutes Section 659A.143 (Assistance animals); ORS 659A.139, 659A.141, 659A.145; Oregon Admin. Rule 839-006-0345 — Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries, Civil Rights Division — Oregon's disability definition carries an express 'construe broadly' mandate (ORS 659A.139), directing courts and agencies to interpret disability protections more expansively than the ADA. Oregon also exempts assistance animal owners from dog license fees (ORS 609.105) and allows civil penalties of up to $50,000 for a first discrimination violation and up to $100,000 for later violations. — Legal Aid Services of Oregon — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Pennsylvania Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Pennsylvania
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Pennsylvania — what counts as a service animal A 'service, guide or support dog' is a dog that is trained or is being trained to work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, consistent with federal and state law related to service animals. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission uses a similar definition covering a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability. (18 Pa.C.S. Sections 5531 and 7325) — public access It is a summary offense for the proprietor, manager, or employee of a theater, hotel, restaurant, or other place of public accommodation to refuse access to a person using a service, guide, or support dog or other aid animal, including trainers of such dogs. Service animals must be allowed in restaurants, retail stores, hotels, theaters, hospitals, professional offices, and public transportation, in all areas customers are normally allowed. Under the ADA, staff may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the dog is a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; no certification or license is required. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act also makes denial an unlawful discriminatory practice. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals, because they are not trained to perform a specific task, so they cannot be taken into stores, restaurants, or other public accommodations as service dogs. They are, however, protected in housing as assistance animals that qualify as a reasonable accommodation under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Pennsylvania's misrepresentation penalties apply to housing only, under the Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act, Act 118 of 2018 (68 P.S. Sections 405.5 to 405.6). Misrepresenting a disability or disability-related need for an assistance or service animal in housing, or making materially false statements to obtain documentation, is a misdemeanor of the third degree, punishable by up to one year in prison and a fine of up to $2,500. Misrepresenting an animal as an assistance or service animal in housing, including with a false document or by fitting it with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, is a summary offense with a fine of up to $1,000. There is no general public-access misrepresentation offense. — housing A service or assistance animal, including an emotional support animal that qualifies as a reasonable accommodation, must be allowed in housing with no pet deposit or extra fee, though the handler is liable for damage. Under the Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act (68 P.S. Section 405.3), a landlord may request documentation of the disability and disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent or known to the landlord. — Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, 43 P.S. Sections 951 to 963; 18 Pa.C.S. Section 7325 (discrimination on account of guide, signal or service dog); Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act, Act 118 of 2018, 68 P.S. Sections 405.1 to 405.7 — Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission — Pennsylvania is distinctive in targeting its fraud penalties at housing rather than public places, and in giving the Human Relations Commission detailed guidance distinguishing service animals, assistance animals, and emotional support animals across housing, public accommodations, education, and employment. Trainers of service, guide, or support dogs have the same public-access rights as handlers under 18 Pa.C.S. Section 7325. — Pennsylvania Legal Aid Network — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Rhode Island Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Rhode Island
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Rhode Island — what counts as a service animal A service animal is a dog that has been, or is being, specifically trained to assist an individual with a disability, including a guide dog specially trained to aid a person who is blind or visually impaired, a hearing dog specially trained to aid a person who is deaf or hard of hearing, and a service dog specially trained to aid a person with another type of disability. The state definition covers dogs only; miniature horses are covered only through the ADA. (R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-1.1) — public access Every person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in any place listed in R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-1, including public streets, buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants, theaters, and all other places to which the general public is invited, with no extra charge for the animal, though the handler is solely liable for damage it causes. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not ask about the disability or demand certification. Rhode Island also expressly covers trainers and puppy raisers of service animals. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under Rhode Island law or the ADA, so they have no public-access rights. They are, however, expressly protected in housing: state regulations cover the presence or desired presence of a personal assistive animal or emotional support animal for a person with disabilities in housing. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Civil violation under R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-3.1: it is a violation to expressly represent that a pet or other animal is a service animal to gain access to a public area, when the person knew or should have known the animal did not meet the definition. The penalty is up to 30 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities. There is no fine in the enacted text; a proposed $500 fine appeared in the bill only and was not enacted. — housing A person with a disability who has a guide dog or other personal assistive animal has full and equal access to covered housing, with no extra charge for the animal (R.I. Gen. Laws Sections 40-9.1-1(c), 40-9.1-2, and 34-37-4(e)). An emotional support animal may also be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with documentation if the disability or need is not apparent. — Rhode Island General Laws, Chapter 40-9.1 (Equal Rights of Blind and Deaf Persons to Public Facilities), Sections 40-9.1-1 to 40-9.1-5; R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-37-4(e) (housing) — Rhode Island Commission for Human Rights — Rhode Island's misrepresentation law, added in 2019, is unusual in using community service rather than a fine, and it directs the Commission for Human Rights to provide businesses with a decal stating that service animals are welcome and that misrepresentation is a violation of Rhode Island law. Trainers and puppy raisers have the same access rights as handlers under Section 40-9.1-2.1. — Rhode Island Legal Services — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: South Carolina Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in South Carolina
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in South Carolina — what counts as a service animal A service animal or service animal-in-training is an animal trained or being trained to do work or perform tasks for an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability. The definition is limited to a dog or a miniature horse, and emotional support, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks. No vest, marking, or documentation is required for an animal to qualify. (S.C. Code Section 47-3-920) — public access A person with a disability has the same right as anyone else to full and free use of public places and full and equal accommodations, including common carriers, hotels, lodging, restaurants, retail establishments, and places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, accompanied by an assistance dog with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage. Trainers of assistance or guide dogs have the same access while engaged in training. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. South Carolina's Layla's Law lets places of public accommodation set their own rules for non-service animals, including emotional support animals (Section 47-3-990). — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under South Carolina law or the ADA, because emotional support, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks, so they have no public-access rights, and businesses may set their own rules for them. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under South Carolina and federal fair housing law. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Civil fine, not a criminal offense, under S.C. Code Section 47-3-980 (2019 Act No. 44): intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal-in-training to obtain a right or privilege provided to a disabled person is unlawful, with a fine of up to $250 for a first offense, up to $500 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for a third or later offense. No custodial arrest may be made except on a warrant for failure to appear or failure to pay the fine. Earlier bill drafts had proposed misdemeanor fines of $350 to $5,000, but the enacted law uses the lower civil fines above. — housing A person with a disability who has an assistance dog has full and equal access to covered housing, with no extra charge for the animal (S.C. Code Section 43-33-70(d)). Under Section 31-21-70, added by 2019 Act No. 44, a landlord may ask certain questions about a tenant's or prospective tenant's animal for a reasonable accommodation, following a codified two-question process; no pet deposit or fee may be charged for an assistance animal. — South Carolina Code, Title 47, Chapter 3, Article 15, Layla's Law, Sections 47-3-910 to 47-3-990; S.C. Code, Title 43, Chapter 33, Sections 43-33-20, 43-33-40, and 43-33-70 — South Carolina Human Affairs Commission — South Carolina is unusually strict toward businesses that deny access: interfering with a person's service-animal access rights is a misdemeanor under Section 43-33-40, and the state guide reports penalties of up to 3 years imprisonment for denying access. The state also designates October 15 as White Cane Safety Day, and its service-animal rules are split between two parts of the code, the older Title 43 access law and the newer Title 47 Layla's Law. — South Carolina Legal Services — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: South Dakota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in South Dakota
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in South Dakota — what counts as a service animal South Dakota's public-access law (SDCL 20-13-23.2) covers a person who is totally or partially physically disabled, blind, deaf, or has a psychiatric or mental disability, accompanied by a specially trained service animal, without limiting the term to dogs in that section. The misrepresentation law (SDCL 22-35-9) defines a service animal more narrowly as a dog trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to the person's disability; crime-deterrent effects and emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship do not count as work or tasks. A service animal in training is a dog that has completed basic obedience training and is housebroken (SDCL 20-13-1(17)), and its trainer must be affiliated with a nationally recognized training program. — public access A person with a disability may be accompanied by a specially trained service animal in hotels, lodging, public accommodations, amusement or resort places, and other places open to the public (SDCL 20-13-23.1 and 20-13-23.2), with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage the animal causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not demand certification or proof of training. Denying access is a Class 2 misdemeanor, and service animals in training have public access if they wear a collar and leash, harness, or cape identifying them as in training. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in South Dakota. In housing, however, SDCL 43-32-33 defines 'service animal' broadly to include emotional support animals, therapy animals, and assistance animals. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Class 2 misdemeanor under SDCL 22-35-9, enacted by 2026 Senate Bill 82 (signed March 9, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) — intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal in a place of public accommodation to obtain rights the person knows they are not entitled to. A Class 2 misdemeanor carries up to 30 days in jail and/or a fine of up to $500. — housing A landlord may not prohibit by lease or otherwise the keeping of a service animal in a rented or leased residence (SDCL 20-13-23.4, violation a Class 2 misdemeanor), and no extra charge may be imposed for the animal. Under SDCL 43-32-33 through 43-32-36, a landlord may require reliable supporting documentation from a licensed health care provider confirming the disability and the disability-related need, unless the need is readily apparent or already known, and may not accept documentation from a provider who operates in the state solely to provide service or assistance animal certifications. — South Dakota Human Relations Act, SDCL Chapter 20-13, especially SDCL 20-13-23.1, 20-13-23.2, and 20-13-23.4; misrepresentation at SDCL 22-35-9; housing documentation at SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36 — South Dakota Department of Labor and Regulation, Division of Human Rights — South Dakota is distinctive in explicitly covering psychiatric and mental disabilities in its public-access statute and in making it a criminal offense for a landlord to deny a service animal. Its 2018 housing law was an early anti-letter-mill law, and its 2026 misrepresentation law (SB 82) is new, so older guides that say South Dakota has no fake-service-animal penalty are out of date. — East River Legal Services — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Tennessee Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Tennessee
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Tennessee — what counts as a service animal Tennessee uses different definitions by context. Public access (Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112) uses the older term 'dog guide' for a blind, physically disabled, or deaf or hard-of-hearing person led or accompanied by a dog guide. Housing (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111) defines a service animal as a dog or miniature horse individually trained to work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. Criminal law (Tenn. Code Ann. 39-14-216) is broader, covering any animal individually trained or being trained to do work for a person with a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability. — public access A proprietor of a place of public accommodation, amusement, or recreation — including inns, hotels, restaurants, stores, public conveyances, theaters, and public educational institutions — may not refuse entry to a person accompanied by a dog guide (Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112). The business may not require documentation such as proof the dog guide is certified, trained, or licensed, and may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious; the dog must be under the handler's control and may be removed only if out of control or not housebroken. Dog guides in training have public access when led by an employee or puppy raiser from a recognized training agency or school, wearing a harness and on a leash. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Tennessee; a 2024 law (Tenn. Code Ann. 68-14-729) expressly bars live animals whose sole function is comfort or emotional support from indoor areas of food service establishments, while trained service animals are excepted. In housing, Tennessee defines a 'support animal' (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111) to include an animal prescribed or recommended by a health care provider to provide emotional support that alleviates identified symptoms of a disability. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Class B misdemeanor under Tenn. Code Ann. 39-16-304 for knowingly misrepresenting a service or support animal, including false claims or false documentation to a landlord or to an employee of a place of public accommodation. For misrepresentation of a service animal, the court must also impose 100 hours of community service to be completed within six months. — housing Under Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111 and 66-28-406, a tenant or prospective tenant with a disability may request an exception to a no-pets policy or pet fees for a service or support animal as a reasonable accommodation, with no extra payment for the animal. A landlord may request reliable documentation from a health care provider with actual knowledge of the disability; Tennessee's 2024 amendment bars documentation from websites whose primary function is selling ESA certificates, and landlords are not liable for injuries caused by a permitted service or support animal. — Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112 (public access, dog guides); Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111 and 66-28-406 (housing, service and support animals); Tenn. Code Ann. 39-16-304 (misrepresentation); Tenn. Code Ann. 68-14-729 (animals in food service establishments) — Tennessee Human Rights Commission — Tennessee is unusual in having three different service-animal definitions depending on whether the issue is public access, housing, or criminal law, and in expressly banning emotional support animals from indoor restaurant areas while giving them strong housing protection. Its 2024 anti-letter-mill provision and landlord liability shield are recent additions. — Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Texas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Texas
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Texas — what counts as a service animal Texas defines a service animal (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.002) as a canine specially trained or equipped to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability and used by a person with a disability — dogs only, with no miniature horses in the state definition. The statute's disability definition is broad and expressly includes mental or physical disabilities, intellectual or developmental disabilities, hearing or speech impairments, visual impairments, deafness, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and health conditions requiring special ambulatory devices. Animals in training have public access when with an approved trainer. — public access A person with a disability who has or obtains an assistance animal is entitled to full and equal access to all public facilities, including streets, transportation, aircraft, lodging, government buildings, retail establishments, educational facilities, and food service locations (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.002 and 121.003), with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not demand proof of certification or training. Texas goes beyond the ADA by providing both criminal penalties and civil remedies for access denial, including a $300 minimum damages presumption. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Texas. Texas law uses the broader term 'assistance animal,' which includes an animal that provides emotional support alleviating medically identified symptoms of a disability, and that broader term is what gives housing protection — not public-access rights. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Misdemeanor under Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.006, as strengthened by HB 4164 (2023): intentionally or knowingly representing that an animal is an assistance or service animal when it is not specially trained is punishable by a fine of not more than $1,000 and 30 hours of community service for a governmental entity or nonprofit serving persons with disabilities, to be completed within one year. Older sources citing a $300 maximum fine reflect the pre-2023 law. — housing A person with a disability who has or obtains an assistance animal is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations and may not be required to pay extra compensation or make a deposit for the animal, though the person is liable for damage the animal does beyond reasonable wear and tear (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.003(h)). A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need for an assistance animal where the need is not apparent. — Texas Human Resources Code Chapter 121 (Persons with Disabilities), especially Sections 121.002, 121.003, 121.004, and 121.006 — Texas Workforce Commission, Civil Rights Division — Texas has one of the most detailed state frameworks: it expressly names PTSD as a qualifying disability, gives service dogs in training public access, and has tiered felony penalties for harming a service animal — up to a third-degree felony for killing one (Tex. Penal Code 42.091). Its 2023 increase of the fake-service-animal fine from $300 to $1,000 is recent, so older guides understate the penalty. — Lone Star Legal Aid — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require proof of certification. Denying or interfering with that access is a class C misdemeanor, and trainers of service animals in training have the same public-access rights. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Utah. Utah law separately defines a 'support animal' for housing purposes as an animal that provides emotional support alleviating identified symptoms of a disability, and support animals are protected in housing as a reasonable accommodation, not in public places. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Class C misdemeanor under Utah Code 26B-6-805 (formerly 62A-5b-106) for intentionally and knowingly falsely representing that an animal is a service animal or support animal, knowingly misrepresenting a material fact to a health care provider to obtain documentation for that designation, or, for a person without a disability, using an animal to gain treatment or benefits provided only to a person with a disability. The statute section reviewed states no specific fine amount. Older sources calling this a class B misdemeanor reflect the pre-2019 law; HB 43 (2019) lowered it to class C. — housing In housing, a person with a disability may keep a service animal or support animal as a reasonable accommodation even in no-pets housing, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may request reliable documentation from a health care provider confirming the disability and the disability-related need if the need is not readily apparent, and knowingly providing false documentation is a class C misdemeanor. — Utah Code Title 26B, Chapter 6, Part 8, Rights and Privileges of an Individual with a Disability (formerly Title 62A, Chapter 5b), especially Sections 26B-6-802, 26B-6-803, and 26B-6-805 — Utah Labor Commission, Utah Antidiscrimination and Labor Division (UALD) — Utah's chapter was renumbered from Title 62A, Chapter 5b to Title 26B, Chapter 6, Part 8, so citations to 62A-5b-102 and 62A-5b-106 in older guides are the same law under new numbers. Utah is also distinctive in criminalizing false statements made to a health care provider to obtain service or support animal documentation, not just false claims made to a business or landlord. — Utah Legal Services — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Vermont Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Vermont
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Vermont — what counts as a service animal Vermont's public-accommodations statute (9 V.S.A. 4502) uses the term 'service animal' without spelling out which species count in the statute itself. The Vermont Human Rights Commission's administrative rules define a service animal as any dog or miniature horse (meeting the qualifications in the rules) individually trained to do work or perform tasks that mitigate the limitations caused by the person's qualifying disability, including service dogs used by firefighters, law enforcement, and other rescue personnel. Individuals training an animal to perform as a service animal are expressly covered (9 V.S.A. 4502(b)(2)). — public access An owner or operator of a place of public accommodation — including schools, stores, restaurants, and other establishments offering goods or services to the general public — may not prohibit entry to a person with a disability accompanied by a service animal (9 V.S.A. 4502). A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require documentation, certification, a vest, or a harness. The animal must be under control and housebroken, and access may not be denied based on breed or size. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Vermont, and Vermont has no ESA-specific public-access statute. Under the Human Rights Commission's rules, an assistance animal (including one providing emotional support) is permitted as a reasonable accommodation in housing but in places of public accommodation only at the entity's discretion. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty No specific state penalty — no Vermont statute reviewed sets a penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. General fraud or false-pretenses laws could still apply to fabricated documentation, and misrepresentation in housing could violate 9 V.S.A. 4503, but Vermont has no dedicated fake-service-animal statute. — housing Under 9 V.S.A. 4503(a)(9), it is unlawful discrimination in the sale or rental of a dwelling to discriminate against a person because the person relies on specially trained animals, wheelchairs, or similar devices. A service animal or assistance animal must be allowed as a reasonable accommodation in housing, with no pet deposit or extra fee, and a landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only where the need is not apparent. — Vermont Fair Housing and Public Accommodations Act, 9 V.S.A. Chapter 139, especially 9 V.S.A. 4501, 4502, and 4503 — Vermont Human Rights Commission — Vermont is one of the more permissive states for service animals in training: 9 V.S.A. 4502(b)(2) expressly gives public-access rights to any individual training an animal to perform as a service animal, with no professional-trainer, harness, or identification condition stated in the statute. It is also one of the few states with no dedicated misrepresentation penalty at all. — Vermont Legal Aid — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Virginia
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Virginia — what counts as a service animal Virginia defines a 'service dog' (Va. Code 51.5-40.1) as a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a mobility-impaired or otherwise disabled person, where the work or tasks are directly related to the individual's disability or disorder — including guiding, pulling a wheelchair, assisting during a seizure, alerting to allergens, retrieving or carrying items, and providing physical support and assistance with balance. Emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks. Virginia covers guide dogs, hearing dogs, and service dogs, all dogs only, and dogs in training at least six months old are covered (Va. Code 51.5-44(E)). — public access A person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a trained guide dog, hearing dog, or service dog in the public places and accommodations listed in Va. Code 51.5-44(B), including public conveyances, hotels, restaurants, stores, theaters, and government buildings, with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage the dog causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious, and may not require certification; a hearing dog is identified by a blaze orange leash and a service dog by a harness, backpack, or vest identifying it. Virginia goes beyond the ADA by extending access to dogs in training at least six months old. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or Virginia law — Virginia expressly excludes emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship from the definition of work or tasks — and they have no public-access rights. In housing, an emotional support animal may qualify as an assistance animal and be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Virginia Fair Housing Law, with documentation of the disability-related need where the need is not apparent. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Class 4 misdemeanor under Va. Code 51.5-44.1 for knowingly and willfully fitting a dog with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, or using an identification card commonly used by a person with a disability, in order to represent that the dog is a service dog or hearing dog to fraudulently gain public access under Va. Code 51.5-44. — housing Under the Virginia Fair Housing Law, a housing provider must allow a service dog or other assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, and the handler is liable for damage the animal causes. A provider may request documentation confirming the disability-related need where the disability or need is not readily apparent. — Code of Virginia Title 51.5, Chapter 9, Rights of Persons with Disabilities, especially Va. Code 51.5-40.1, 51.5-44, and 51.5-44.1 — Office of Civil Rights, Office of the Attorney General of Virginia — Virginia is distinctive in requiring visible identification for its service dogs — a harness, backpack, or vest for a service dog and a blaze orange leash for a hearing dog — while still requiring no certification or state registration, and in covering dogs in training as young as six months old. Virginia has no separate human rights commission; disability discrimination complaints go to the Attorney General's Office of Civil Rights. — Virginia Legal Aid Society — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Washington Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Washington
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Washington — what counts as a service animal Washington defines a service animal (RCW 49.60.040) as any dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, where the work or tasks are directly related to the disability. A 2024 amendment (SB 5788) added definitions for a 'service animal trainee' — any dog or miniature horse undergoing training to become a service animal — and a 'service animal trainer.' Washington's broader disability definition covers sensory, mental, or physical impairments that are medically cognizable or exist as a record or perception. — public access It is an unfair practice under the Washington Law Against Discrimination (RCW 49.60.215) to deny, restrict, or charge more because a person uses a trained dog guide or service animal in places of public accommodation, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transportation, and government buildings. A business or enforcement officer may ask only the two ADA questions when the disability or the animal's work is not readily apparent — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require proof the animal is certified, trained, or licensed. Service animal trainees have public access under the 2024 amendment. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or Washington law and have no public-access rights. In housing, Washington's definition in RCW 49.60.040 expressly does not apply to the housing sections (RCW 49.60.222 to 49.60.227), which use a broader reasonable-accommodation framework under which an assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, may be allowed with documentation of the disability-related need. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Civil infraction under RCW 49.60.214 for expressly or impliedly representing that an animal is a service animal or service animal trainee to secure rights afforded to persons with a disability, when the person knew or should have known the animal did not meet the definition. The maximum penalty is $500 under RCW 7.80.120(1)(a)(iii), and the person must remove the animal from the place of public accommodation. Older sources citing $250 reflect the pre-2024 figure. — housing In housing, a provider must make reasonable accommodations for a person with a disability, including allowing a service animal or other assistance animal even in no-pets housing, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. Because the RCW 49.60.040 service-animal definition does not apply to housing, the housing framework is broader and can cover assistance animals beyond dogs and miniature horses; a provider may request documentation of the disability-related need where the need is not apparent. — Washington Law Against Discrimination, RCW Chapter 49.60, especially RCW 49.60.040, 49.60.214, 49.60.215, and 49.60.222 to 49.60.227; misrepresentation penalty at RCW 7.80.120 — Washington State Human Rights Commission — Washington goes further than the ADA in several ways: its disability definition is broader, the Law Against Discrimination applies to employers with as few as 8 employees (compared with the ADA's 15), and its 2024 amendment expressly covers service animal trainees and trainers. It also lets enforcement officers ask the two questions and treats refusal to answer as creating a presumption the animal is not a service animal. — Northwest Justice Project — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: West Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in West Virginia
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in West Virginia — what counts as a service animal West Virginia defines a service animal (W. Va. Code 5-15-3) as any guide dog, signal dog, or other animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability — including guiding individuals with impaired vision, alerting individuals with impaired hearing to intruders or sounds, providing minimal protection or rescue work, pulling a wheelchair, or fetching dropped items. The state wording is broader than the ADA because it says 'other animal' and is not limited to dogs, and it does not mention miniature horses specifically. — public access A person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in public places, transportation, lodging, restaurants, professional offices, hospitals, other public accommodations, amusement venues, and places of employment, with full and equal access and no extra charge (W. Va. Code 5-15-4). A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious, and no license, certification, or specific signage or labeling is required for the animal. The handler is liable for damage the animal causes unless another person provoked it. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in West Virginia. In housing, an emotional support animal may qualify as an assistance animal and be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the West Virginia Fair Housing Act, with documentation of the disability-related need where the need is not apparent. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Misdemeanor under W. Va. Code 5-15-9 for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal to obtain a right or privilege under W. Va. Code 5-15-4: a first offense is punishable by a fine of up to $200, up to 10 days in jail, or both, and a second or later offense by a fine of up to $1,000, up to 30 days in jail, or both. Note that the older text in W. Va. Code 5-15-3(d) states a fine of not more than $100 plus 30 hours of community service; the 5-15-9 figures above are the current misrepresentation penalties as amended in 2018. — housing A housing provider must allow a service animal as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, and the handler is liable for damage the animal causes. A provider may request documentation confirming the disability-related need where the disability or need is not readily apparent, and complaints about housing discrimination go to the West Virginia Human Rights Commission within 365 days. — W. Va. Code Chapter 5, Article 15, White Cane Law, especially W. Va. Code 5-15-3, 5-15-4, and 5-15-9; disability discrimination also under the West Virginia Human Rights Act, W. Va. Code Chapter 5, Article 11 — West Virginia Human Rights Commission — West Virginia's service-animal definition is one of the broadest in the country because it covers 'any guide dog, signal dog or other animal' rather than dogs alone, and its White Cane Law expressly states that service animals need not be licensed or certified by any state or local government and need no specific signage or labeling. — Legal Aid of West Virginia — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Wisconsin Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Wisconsin
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Wisconsin — what counts as a service animal Under the 2025 Wisconsin Act (AB 366), amending Wis. Stat. 106.52(1)(fm), a service animal is a dog that meets the definition of 'service animal' in 28 CFR 35.104 — a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability — and includes a miniature horse under the circumstances in 28 CFR 35.136(i), plus a service animal in training. The prior Wisconsin definition was broader, covering a guide dog, signal dog, or other animal individually trained or being trained to do work or perform tasks, including guiding a person with impaired vision, alerting a person with impaired hearing, providing minimal protection or rescue work, pulling a wheelchair, or fetching dropped items. — public access Under Wis. Stat. 106.52(3), places of public accommodation or amusement — including restaurants, hotels, theaters, stores, transportation, and government buildings — must allow service animals in all areas where the public is normally permitted, with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require documentation of certification or training. Service animals in training have public access, and denying access can draw a fine of $100 to $500 plus civil remedies. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Wisconsin; Wis. Stat. 106.52(1) defines an emotional support animal as an animal that provides emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship but is not trained to perform tasks for a person with a disability. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under Wis. Stat. 106.50, with documentation from a licensed health professional. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Under Wis. Stat. 106.52(6), created by 2025 Wisconsin Act (AB 366), a person who intentionally misrepresents that they are in possession of a service animal in a public place is subject to a forfeiture of $200 for a first violation and $500 for subsequent violations, and a court may substitute 20 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities in place of the forfeiture. Separately, a person who intentionally misrepresents a disability or the need for an emotional support animal to obtain housing, or provides false ESA documentation, forfeits not less than $500 under Wis. Stat. 106.50(2r). — housing Under Wis. Stat. 106.50, a housing provider must allow a service animal or an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability, with no extra charge for the animal. A provider may request reliable documentation of the disability-related need from a licensed health professional, and may also request a prescription or letter for the emotional support animal; a health professional who misrepresents a patient's disability or need for an ESA forfeits not less than $500. — Wis. Stat. 106.52 (public accommodations, service animals); Wis. Stat. 106.50 (housing, service and emotional support animals); 2025 Wisconsin Act (AB 366) — Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development, Equal Rights Division — Wisconsin's 2025 Act narrowed its formerly very broad service-animal definition (which covered any individually trained animal) to dogs and miniature horses meeting the ADA standard, and created the state's first dedicated fake-service-animal penalty. Legal Action of Wisconsin absorbed Judicare Legal Aid on January 1, 2026, and is now the single statewide civil legal-aid intake. — Legal Action of Wisconsin — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Wyoming Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Service animals & disability access in Wyoming
t: service animals disability access ADA emotional support animals ESA public access — Service animals & disability access in Wyoming — what counts as a service animal Wyoming defines a service animal (Wyo. Stat. 35-13-205) by reference to 28 CFR 35.104 — a dog, or in the ADA framework a miniature horse, individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, where the work or tasks are directly related to the disability. Wyoming separately defines an 'assistance animal' (Wyo. Stat. 35-13-205) as an animal that works, provides assistance, or performs tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, or provides emotional support that alleviates one or more identified symptoms or effects of the person's disability. — public access A person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in any facility of a public entity in accordance with 28 CFR 35.136 and any place of public accommodation in accordance with 28 CFR 36.302(c), including hotels, motels, lodging places, restaurants, public elevators, and other places to which the general public is invited, with no extra charge (Wyo. Stat. 35-13-201). A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious, and may not require identification, a vest, or a badge. A public accommodation that permits a service animal in good faith is not liable for damage or injury the animal causes. — emotional support animals Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Wyoming. Wyoming is unusual in expressly defining 'assistance animal' in statute to include an animal providing emotional support, and that definition is what gives ESAs housing protection — not public access. — faking a service animal misrepresentation penalty Misdemeanor under Wyo. Stat. 35-13-203(b) for knowingly and intentionally misrepresenting that an animal is a service animal or an assistance animal to obtain any rights or privileges under the article, punishable by a fine of not more than $750. Denying or interfering with admittance is also a misdemeanor with a fine of not more than $750 under Wyo. Stat. 35-13-203(a). Some secondary guides cite Wyo. Stat. 35-13-207 for the misrepresentation penalty; the official 2017 bill text and the Animal Law compilation place it at 35-13-203. — housing A person may not be discriminated against in leasing or renting residential property because the person has an assistance animal (Wyo. Stat. 35-13-201), and an assistance animal must be allowed as a reasonable accommodation with no pet deposit or extra fee. The person is liable for any damage the assistance animal causes to the leased or rented property, and a provider may request documentation of the disability-related need where the need is not apparent. — Wyo. Stat. Title 35, Chapter 13, Article 2, Protection and Rights of Blind and Disabled Persons (Assistance Animals), especially Wyo. Stat. 35-13-201, 35-13-203, and 35-13-205 — Wyoming Department of Workforce Services, Labor Standards Division (Wyoming Fair Employment Program) — Wyoming is one of the few states with a single unified chapter covering service animals and assistance animals (including ESAs) together, and its $750 misdemeanor penalty covers fake service animals and fake ESAs alike. Its Fair Employment Practices Act also applies to employers with as few as 2 employees, one of the lowest thresholds in the country. — Legal Aid of Wyoming — two questions business may ask no documentation no vest no extra charge

p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Digital assets after death in Alabama
t: digital assets after death RUFADAA fiduciary access email photos accounts — Digital assets after death in Alabama — the law Alabama has adopted RUFADAA as the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, Act 2017-316 (HB 138), effective January 1, 2018, codified at Ala. Code §§ 19-1A-1 through 19-1A-18. — what a fiduciary can get A fiduciary (personal representative, trustee, agent under a power of attorney, or conservator) can get the catalogue of electronic communications and other digital assets on a lighter showing, but the content of electronic communications only with the user's consent or a court order. The custodian may choose how to disclose: full account access, partial access, or a copy of the assets. It may demand a written request, a certified death certificate, proof of appointment such as letters testamentary, and the will, trust, or power of attorney showing consent, and it must comply within 60 days of a valid request. — who decides A user can direct disclosure through a custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. The priority order is: online tool first, then will, trust, or power of attorney, then the custodian's terms of service. — terms of service A direction made through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney overrides a contrary term in the custodian's terms of service. If the user left no direction at all, the terms of service govern, and the fiduciary then needs the user's consent in an estate document or a court order to reach the content of messages. — Ala. Code §§ 19-1A-1 through 19-1A-18 — Alabama Attorney General, Consumer Interest Division — Alabama's act sits in Title 19 on fiduciaries rather than as a standalone technology law, and its custodian-disclosure section gives the custodian sole discretion to choose full access, partial access, or a copy of the assets. — Legal Services Alabama — Google Inactive Account Manager Apple Legacy Contact Meta legacy contact catalogue content of electronic communications 60 days

p: Louisiana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Digital assets after death in Louisiana
t: digital assets after death RUFADAA fiduciary access email photos accounts — Digital assets after death in Louisiana — the law Has NOT adopted RUFADAA. Louisiana is one of the few states that never enacted it. House Bill 1118 in the 2016 Regular Session would have enacted RUFADAA as Revised Statutes sections 51:2701 to 51:2720; it passed the House and Senate in different forms but died in conference and was never signed. Instead, Louisiana has its own narrower 2014 law, Code of Civil Procedure Article 3191, paragraphs C through H, added by Acts 2014, Number 758. — what a fiduciary can get Under Article 3191, a succession representative (the executor or administrator, called a succession representative in Louisiana) has power to take control of, handle, continue, distribute, or terminate any digital account of the decedent, subject to any restriction in a valid testament or a court order. The holder of the account must transfer, deliver, or provide access or possession within 30 days after receiving the letters testamentary, letters of administration, or letters of independent administration, to the extent federal law permits. Federally insured financial institutions follow Revised Statutes sections 6:325 and 6:767 instead. The article covers only a succession representative; it has no equivalent provision for an agent under a power of attorney, a trustee, or a curator. — who decides Louisiana has no RUFADAA priority order, so there is no statute ranking an online tool first, then a will or trust, then terms of service. In practice, use the platform's own tool first, such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact or a Meta legacy contact, because the platform controls its own account. Then look to the decedent's testament for any restriction on the succession representative's power, since Article 3191(C) makes the representative's power subject to a restriction in a valid testament or a court order. A person planning ahead should also name a mandatary under a mandate and leave clear written instructions, since Article 3191 does not cover incapacity. — terms of service Article 3191(E) expressly supersedes any contrary provision in a service agreement, and treats the succession representative as an authorized user with the decedent's lawful consent for purposes of accessing or possessing the digital accounts. That is stronger than RUFADAA on this point. Even so, the duty applies only to the extent permitted by federal law, and the federal Stored Communications Act still limits when a provider may disclose the contents of electronic communications. — La. p: Massachusetts Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Digital assets after death in Massachusetts
t: digital assets after death RUFADAA fiduciary access email photos accounts — Digital assets after death in Massachusetts — the law Massachusetts has NOT adopted RUFADAA. No digital-assets act exists in the Massachusetts General Laws, and the probate code (M.G.L. c. 190B) has no digital-assets article. Bills to adopt it in the 194th General Court were reported favorably in 2025-2026 but have not been enacted. Massachusetts is one of only three states that have not adopted RUFADAA. — what a fiduciary can get There is no Massachusetts statute forcing a custodian to disclose an account to a fiduciary. A personal representative's authority comes only from the general probate duty to take possession of the decedent's property (M.G.L. c. 190B, section 3-709) and to inventory it (section 3-706), which runs to the property, not to the provider. In practice the custodian decides under its own terms of service, and the federal Stored Communications Act generally bars a provider from disclosing the contents of emails and messages without the user's consent or a court order. There is no statutory 60-day deadline for a custodian to respond. — who decides Because there is no state statute, the user's own planning does all the work: set up each platform's online tool (Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, Meta legacy contact), and put express digital-asset authority in the will, trust, or durable power of attorney, naming who may access which accounts. Without a statute there is no legally fixed priority order, so the platform's tool and the written documents should agree with each other. — terms of service Yes — in Massachusetts the custodian's terms of service effectively control, since no state law overrides them. If the user left no direction, the family must ask the custodian under its deceased-user process, and the custodian may refuse, delete, or memorialize the account as its terms allow. p: Oklahoma Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Digital assets after death in Oklahoma
t: digital assets after death RUFADAA fiduciary access email photos accounts — Digital assets after death in Oklahoma — the law No. Oklahoma has NOT adopted RUFADAA. Two independent sources confirm this: ProbatePedia's 2026 state-by-state table lists Oklahoma among the three states that have not adopted RUFADAA, and Law Commentary, citing the National Conference of State Legislatures, likewise names Oklahoma as a holdout, noting a RUFADAA bill has sat in the House Rules Committee since February 2020. The only state law is a narrow 2010 statute, Okla. Stat. tit. 58, Section 269, letting an executor or administrator take control of a deceased person's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts. — what a fiduciary can get There is no Oklahoma statute setting out the RUFADAA catalogue-versus-content rules or a 60-day deadline. Under the 2010 law, an executor or administrator may take control of, continue, or terminate the decedent's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts where otherwise authorized. For anything beyond that, access depends on the custodian's own policies, the user's own directions, and general probate law, and a court order is the usual fallback when a custodian refuses. — who decides Because Oklahoma has no RUFADAA priority ladder, there is no state-law rule that an online tool beats a will or that a will beats the terms of service. In practice, the platform's own tools still matter most: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta's legacy contact let the user name someone in advance, and a will or power of attorney that expressly grants digital-asset authority strengthens the fiduciary's request to the custodian. — terms of service Without RUFADAA, the custodian's terms of service carry much more weight in Oklahoma than in the other states in this batch. p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Life insurance claim denials in Alabama
t: life insurance claim denial denied beneficiary appeal complaint — Life insurance claim denials in Alabama — contestability period Two years from the date the policy is issued. After the policy has been in force during the insured's lifetime for two years, the insurer generally cannot contest it based on statements in the application, except for nonpayment of premiums (Ala. Code § 27-15-4). — grace period 30 days (or, at the insurer's option, one month of not less than 30 days) after a premium due date, during which the policy stays in full force (Ala. Code § 27-15-3). If the insured dies during the grace period, the insurer may deduct the unpaid premium from the payout. — common denial reasons Insurers may deny a claim if the insured made a material misstatement on the application and the death happened within the two-year contestability period. Other lawful reasons include the policy having lapsed for nonpayment of premiums, suicide within the policy's two-year suicide exclusion, or a death caused by an activity the policy specifically excludes. — bad faith Yes. Alabama recognizes a bad-faith tort against an insurer that intentionally refuses to pay a claim with no reasonably legitimate or arguable reason, knowing it has no such reason (Chavers v. National Security Fire & Casualty Co., 405 So. 2d 1 (Ala. 1981)). If the insurer had a debatable reason for the denial, there is no bad faith. — appeal Ask the insurer in writing for a full review of the denial and the exact policy language it relied on. If that fails, file a complaint with the Alabama Department of Insurance. You can also sue the insurer for breach of contract, but watch the time limit for suing in your policy and talk to a lawyer promptly. — complaint First contact the insurance company in writing and ask it to resolve the problem. If that does not work, file an online complaint with the Alabama Department of Insurance, giving your policy and claim numbers and a description of what happened; the department sends the complaint to the insurer, which must respond, and the department can require corrective action if the insurer broke the law. — Alabama Department of Insurance Legal Services Alabama — two years incontestable material misstatement suicide exclusion lapse nonpayment

t: life insurance claim denial denied beneficiary appeal complaint — Life insurance claim denials in Wyoming — contestability period Two years from the date of issue, while the insured is alive. After that the policy is incontestable except for nonpayment of premiums (Wyo. Stat. § 26-16-104). A reinstated policy can be contested again for fraud or misrepresentation about the reinstatement for the same period (Wyo. Stat. § 26-16-501). — grace period 30 days (or one month of at least 30 days, at the insurer's option; four weeks for industrial policies paid more often than monthly). The policy stays in force during the grace period (Wyo. Stat. § 26-16-103). — common denial reasons The insurer may deny for a material misstatement on the application during the first two years, for a lapsed policy after premiums went unpaid, or for suicide within two years of issue (in which case the insurer must pay at least the policy reserve, Wyo. Stat. § 26-16-119). After two years, misstatements alone cannot be used to deny the claim. — bad faith Yes. Wyoming allows a bad-faith claim, but punitive damages require proof of willful and wanton misconduct by the insurer. Attorney fees are available when the insurer unreasonably and without cause refuses to pay a covered loss (Wyo. Stat. § 26-15-124(c)). — appeal Ask the insurer in writing for the reason for the denial and the policy language behind it, and send any missing proof. Wyoming law requires life and health insurers to accept or reject a claim and pay it within 45 days after receiving proof of loss (Wyo. Stat. § 26-15-124(a)). If the denial stands, you can file a Department complaint and you can sue in court — your policy cannot cut the time to sue to less than three years (Wyo. Stat. § 26-16-119). — complaint Contact the insurance company first, state your dispute, and ask what it needs from you to review it. If that fails, file a complaint with the Wyoming Department of Insurance online through its consumer portal, or call to have a paper form mailed to you. The Department investigates complaints about improper denials and claim delays, but it cannot act as your lawyer, decide disputed facts, or force the company to pay your claim. — Wyoming Department of Insurance Legal Aid of Wyoming — two years incontestable material misstatement suicide exclusion lapse nonpayment

p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: timeshare exit cancel rescission cooling-off deed-back resale scam — Timeshare exit in Alabama — cooling-off window 5 calendar days after you sign the contract. If the fifth day falls on a Sunday, the deadline moves to Monday (Ala. Code § 34-27-53). — how to cancel Send a written cancellation notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the seller at the address listed in the contract. Keep the certified mail receipt and a copy of your letter as proof you cancelled on time. — after the window After the 5 days end, you can ask the resort about a deed-back (giving the timeshare back), try to sell or give it away, or pay off the loan and keep using it. p: Hawaii Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
t: timeshare exit cancel rescission cooling-off deed-back resale scam — Timeshare exit in Hawaii — cooling-off window 7 calendar days after the later of signing the contract or receiving the timeshare disclosure statement (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 514E-8). — how to cancel Send a written notice of cancellation to the seller, either by hand-delivering it to the address in the contract or by mailing it to that address. The notice counts on the day you hand-deliver or mail it, so keep a copy and proof of mailing. — after the window After the 7 days pass, ask the resort about a deed-back or surrender program, since many resorts will take the timeshare back if the loan is paid off and fees are current. t: timeshare exit cancel rescission cooling-off deed-back resale scam — Timeshare exit in Illinois — cooling-off window No current Illinois timeshare-specific cooling-off period. The former Real Estate Timeshare Act of 1999 gave buyers 5 calendar days after signing or receiving the public offering statement, whichever was later (765 ILCS 101/10-10), but that Act was repealed (P.A. 100-534), so a new purchase today has no statutory timeshare rescission right — check the cancellation clause in your own contract. — how to cancel Because there is no current timeshare rescission statute, follow whatever cancellation clause your contract contains, and send written notice exactly as the contract directs — the old law required hand delivery or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the address in the contract. Keep a copy of the notice and proof of mailing, and act immediately, since contract deadlines are often only a few days. — after the window After any contract cancellation window closes, ask the resort about a deed-back or surrender program, which usually requires the loan to be paid off and fees to be current. You can also try to resell or transfer the timeshare, but resale values are usually very low.
