p: Alabama Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Alabama
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Alabama — when youth age out No youth ages out of Alabama foster care before age 19, and all youth age out by their 21st birthday, under Ala. Code § 38-7-2(1) and Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-48-.05. The juvenile court keeps jurisdiction over a child until age 21 under Ala. Code § 12-15-117(a). — staying in care longer Yes. Youth may stay in DHR care until age 21, and youth ages 18 to 20 who already left care may ask to re-enter before age 21 if they are living in a situation that poses an identifiable risk of harm. To stay in an independent or transitional living placement, a youth must work full or part time and be in a diploma, GED, or vocational program. — help after leaving care Youth who age out can get help from DHR's Independent Living Program, which offers transitional and independent living placements, life-skills training, and education and employment support up to age 21. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, can apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) housing vouchers through DHR. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Alabama Department of Human Resources through its online foster care inquiry form or your county DHR office to start. Applicants must be at least 19, pass criminal background checks, complete a home study, and finish 30 hours of Trauma Informed Partnering for Permanence and Safety (TIPPS) training. — kinship care Yes. Under Ala. Code § 38-12-2, DHR must try to place a removed child with a relative first, and approved kinship foster parents can receive the full foster care rate. Relatives who foster for at least six months may also become kinship guardians and receive guardianship assistance. — Alabama Department of Human Resources (DHR) Legal Services Alabama — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Alaska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Alaska
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Alaska — when youth age out Youth generally age out of Alaska foster care at 18, when state custody normally ends. Under Alaska Stat. § 47.10.080, the court may extend custody one year at a time past 18, up to the 21st birthday, if continued custody is in the young person's best interests and the young person consents. — staying in care longer Yes. A young person who was in state custody at 18 may stay in care or ask the court to resume custody up to age 21, and must consent and sign a custody resumption agreement that includes actively working on a transition plan. Alaska also runs a Foster Care Transition Program under Alaska Stat. §§ 47.18.300-47.18.390 for young adults ages 18 to 21 who turned 18 in foster care. — help after leaving care OCS's Independent Living Program serves youth in care from age 16 and former foster youth up to age 21 with life-skills training, education and job help, and housing support. The Foster Care Transition Program can help with education and vocational training, housing and utility assistance, career and employment services, and mentoring, and former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26 and apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Office of Children's Services or the Alaska Center for Resource Families to start; applicants apply through OCS and work with a licensing worker. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks for all household members age 16 and older, complete required training, and pass a home safety inspection. — kinship care Yes. OCS looks for extended family or relatives first when a child needs out-of-home care, and relatives may be licensed foster parents or provide unlicensed relative care. Relatives must pass a criminal history screening, complete a relative study, and meet basic home safety standards, and the Alaska Center for Resource Families offers relative caregiver training and support. — Alaska Department of Family and Community Services, Office of Children's Services (OCS) Alaska Legal Services Corporation — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Arizona Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Arizona
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Arizona — when youth age out Youth age out of Arizona foster care at 18, when they may choose to leave care or stay. Under A.R.S. § 8-521.02, a youth who was in DCS custody as a dependent child at 18 can then choose extended foster care up to age 21. — staying in care longer Yes. Youth who turned 18 in DCS custody can stay in care voluntarily until age 21 by signing a voluntary extended foster care agreement and living in a DCS-approved supervised setting. They must also be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or job training, working at least 80 hours a month, in a program that removes barriers to employment, or unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition. — help after leaving care Youth who turn 18 in Arizona foster care are pre-enrolled in AHCCCS (Arizona Medicaid) through Young Adult Transitional Insurance, which has no income limit and runs until age 26. Former foster youth under 21 who were in foster care at age 16 or older can get Education and Training Voucher (ETV) funds for college or job training, and youth who leave at 18 can get aftercare help through the Transitional Independent Living Program (TILP), including help returning to care any time before age 21. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Arizona Department of Child Safety or one of its contracted licensing agencies to start; DCS contracts with private agencies to train, license, and supervise foster families. Applicants must be at least 21, pass FBI and local background checks and get a Level One Fingerprint Clearance Card, complete pre-service training, and pass a home study and home safety inspection. — kinship care Yes. Under A.R.S. § 8-514, DCS must place a child with a parent first, then a grandparent, then kinship care with another family member or a person with a significant relationship to the child, before non-relative foster care. A kinship foster parent must be at least 18, apply with DCS, pass criminal and central registry checks, and have a home visit; kinship caregivers who become licensed receive the same foster care payment as non-relative foster parents. — Arizona Department of Child Safety (DCS) Community Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Arkansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Arkansas
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Arkansas — when youth age out Youth age out of Arkansas foster care at 18, the legal age of majority. Under Ark. Code § 9-28-114 and 9 CAR § 40-905, youth who were in foster care at 18 may choose extended foster care up to age 21. — staying in care longer Yes. Youth ages 18 to 21 who were adjudicated dependent or dependent-neglected and were in foster care at 18 may choose the Extended Foster Care Program, which gives case management and help with room and board costs. To stay, the youth must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes employment, working at least 80 hours a month, have a viable plan to meet one of those, or be unable to do them because of a documented medical condition. — help after leaving care Youth who leave care at 18 can still get help from DCFS Transitional Youth Services, including help paying for school or job training, and Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) Housing Choice Vouchers are available in some counties for young adults ages 18 to 24. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, and Education and Training Vouchers can help pay for college or vocational training. — becoming a foster parent Submit an inquiry through Every Child Arkansas, the state's foster family network, or contact your local DCFS office; DCFS or a private licensed placement agency approves the home. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks, complete about 30 hours of pre-service training plus CPR and first aid, and complete a home study and home inspection. — kinship care Yes. Under 9 CAR § 40-708, DCFS treats safe and appropriate relatives and fictive kin as the best placements and gives them preferential consideration, aiming for a child's first placement to be with a relative when possible. Relatives can open as provisional resource homes and receive support payments while working toward full approval, and relatives caring for children outside the foster care system may qualify for the Kinship Care Subsidy Program. — Arkansas Department of Human Services, Division of Children and Family Services (DCFS) Legal Aid of Arkansas — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: California Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in California
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in California — when youth age out Youth age out of California foster care at 18, when juvenile court dependency normally ends. Under Assembly Bill 12 (AB 12), the California Fostering Connections to Success Act, eligible youth can instead stay in care as nonminor dependents until age 21. — staying in care longer Yes. Under AB 12, youth who had a foster care placement order on their 18th birthday can remain in Extended Foster Care until age 21 by signing a Mutual Agreement for Extended Foster Care (form SOC 162). They must meet one of five participation rules: be in high school or a GED program, be in college or vocational school, work at least 80 hours a month, be in a program that helps them find work or remove barriers to work, or be unable to do those things because of a medical or mental health condition. — help after leaving care Youth in Extended Foster Care keep foster care payments, Medi-Cal health coverage, and case management, and youth who leave at 18 can re-enter before age 21 through a Voluntary Re-Entry Agreement. After care ends, former foster youth can keep Medi-Cal until age 26, get Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for THP-Plus transitional housing and support services up to age 24, or 25 in counties that extended the program. — becoming a foster parent Contact your county child welfare agency or a licensed Foster Family Agency to start California's single Resource Family Approval (RFA) process, which covers fostering, adoption, and guardianship. Applicants must be at least 18, pass criminal background checks, complete at least 12 hours of pre-approval training, and pass a home environment assessment. — kinship care Yes. Relatives and nonrelative extended family members get preferential consideration for placement, and they go through the same Resource Family Approval process as other foster parents. Relatives who become legal guardians can receive Kinship Guardianship Assistance Payments (Kin-GAP), which AB 12 extended up to age 21 for eligible youth. — California Department of Social Services (CDSS) LawHelp California — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Colorado Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Colorado
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Colorado — when youth age out Youth generally age out of Colorado foster care at 18, and the juvenile court's jurisdiction normally continues only until age 18 and a half under Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-205. The court can keep jurisdiction until age 21 for youth who are not ready for independence or who are transitioning into adult disability services. — staying in care longer Yes. Under House Bill 21-1094, the Foster Youth in Transition program lets eligible youth voluntarily keep receiving child welfare services until the last day of the month of their 21st birthday through a voluntary services agreement with the county. To qualify, a youth must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or career and technical education, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition. — help after leaving care Colorado's Chafee program helps youth currently and formerly in foster care with education, employment, housing, and life skills, and Chafee services can run up to age 23. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, apply for Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, and get help through the Colorado Fostering Success Voucher Program for housing. — becoming a foster parent Contact your local county department of human services or a child placement agency, or start through CO4Kids, the CDHS statewide foster care initiative, and attend an information meeting. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks, complete 12 hours of core training plus 27 hours of pre-certification training and CPR and first aid, and complete a home study. — kinship care Yes. Relatives, friends, neighbors, and others with a significant relationship to the child can care for the child as kinship caregivers, and certified kinship foster homes receive the same daily payment as other foster homes. Colorado also runs the Colorado Kinnected navigator program for kinship families and a Kinship Adoption Program that offers free legal help with adoption for kinship caregivers in the metro Denver area. — Colorado Department of Human Services (CDHS) Colorado Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Connecticut Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Connecticut
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Connecticut — when youth age out Youth age out of Connecticut foster care at 18, when DCF custody normally ends. Under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 17a-11, a young person who was under DCF care at 18 may voluntarily stay under DCF supervision until age 21 if DCF decides further care would help. — staying in care longer Yes. Youth who were committed to DCF as abused, neglected, or uncared for at 18 can stay voluntarily in DCF's Services Post-Majority program until age 21, with a written care plan and regular reviews. To stay, they must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled full time in college or vocational school, or participating full time in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, though the commissioner can waive these rules for compelling reasons. — help after leaving care Youth who age out can get help with housing through DCF's Community Housing Assistance Program (CHAP) and Community Housing Employment Enrichment Resources (CHEER), plus education help through the Education and Training Voucher program and DCF post-secondary education assistance. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid coverage, and Chafee independent living services can run up to age 23; youth adopted from DCF care may get college help through DCF up to the semester of their 23rd birthday. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Connecticut Department of Children and Families or its partner, the Connecticut Alliance of Foster and Adoptive Families, to submit an inquiry and attend an information session. Applicants must be at least 21, pass federal, state, and local criminal history and DMV checks, complete about 30 hours of pre-licensing training, and complete a home study; licensing usually takes four months or more. — kinship care Yes. DCF must work to identify adult relatives of children in its care, and a relative can be placed with the child on an emergency basis while completing licensing, then receive the same foster care payment as a non-relative foster parent. After a relative has fostered a child for at least 12 months, the relative can ask DCF to transfer guardianship and receive a subsidized guardianship payment. — Connecticut Department of Children and Families (DCF) Connecticut Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Delaware Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Delaware
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Delaware — when youth age out Youth age out of Delaware foster care at 18, when they leave DFS custody. Under 29 Del. Code § 9015(f), DSCYF can still fund foster care supports, housing help, and stipends for young adults ages 18 to 21, and transitional and independent living services now run to age 23. — staying in care longer Delaware does not have a traditional extended foster care placement program that keeps youth in a foster home to age 21. Instead, under 29 Del. Code § 9015(f), DSCYF funds housing-related foster care supports, direct youth stipends through the ASSIST program (Achieving Self Sufficiency and Independence through Supported Transition), and independent living services for youth ages 18 to 21, and House Bill 271 (2022) extended transitional and independent living services to age 23. — help after leaving care Youth who age out at 18 can get voluntary transitional and independent living services to age 23, including life-skills training, mentoring, tuition help, transitional housing support, and need-based stipends through the ASSIST program. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26 and apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Division of Family Services Foster Care Program through DSCYF and attend a free 3-hour foster parent information session as the first step. Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint-based criminal background checks, complete about 27 hours of PRIDE pre-service training, and complete a home study and home assessment. — kinship care Yes. Delaware's Kinship Care Program under 31 Del. Code § 356 promotes placing children with relatives when a child needs out-of-home care, and relatives within the fifth degree of kinship can get kinship care benefits, a one-time emergency subsidy, and help through the Delaware Helpline. Relatives can also become licensed foster parents under the same standards and at the same payment rate as non-relative foster parents, or seek permanent guardianship through Family Court. — Delaware Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families (DSCYF), Division of Family Services Community Legal Aid Society, Inc. (CLASI) — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Florida Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Florida
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Florida — when youth age out Youth age out of Florida foster care at 18, when they would normally leave licensed care. Under Fla. Stat. § 39.6251, a young adult living in licensed care on their 18th birthday who has not reached permanency can choose to stay in care until age 21, or age 22 with a documented disability. — staying in care longer Yes. Under Fla. Stat. § 39.6251, young adults ages 18 to 21 who turned 18 in licensed care can stay in Extended Foster Care in a supervised living setting approved by DCF or the lead agency, such as a foster home, group home, college dorm, shared housing, or apartment. To stay, they must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a physical, intellectual, emotional, or psychiatric condition. — help after leaving care Florida's Independent Living programs include Extended Foster Care, Postsecondary Education Services and Support (PESS), which pays a monthly stipend of $1,720 to eligible youth in college or vocational school, and Aftercare Services for young adults up to age 23. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds can help with college or job training costs. — becoming a foster parent Contact Florida's Foster Information Center or your local community-based care lead agency, which handles licensing in your county. Applicants must be at least 21, attend an orientation, complete at least 21 hours of free pre-service training, pass fingerprint-based criminal background checks, and pass a home inspection and home study. — kinship care Yes. Relatives, nonrelatives, and fictive kin with an existing relationship to the child can seek Level I child-specific foster home licensure, which is designed for family or like-family caregivers. Relatives caring for a dependent child may also get help through Florida's Relative Caregiver Program under Fla. Stat. § 39.5085, which pays a monthly benefit and covers the child under Medicaid. — Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF) Florida Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Georgia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Georgia
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Georgia — when youth age out Youth age out of Georgia foster care at 18, when they may choose to leave care or stay. Under O.C.G.A. § 15-11-340, youth ages 18 to 21 can receive extended-care youth services through DFCS's Extended Youth Support Services (EYSS) program, known as Connected by 21. — staying in care longer Yes. Through the Connected by 21 / Extended Youth Support Services program, youth ages 18 to 21 who sign a voluntary placement agreement with DFCS can stay in foster care to age 21. They must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 120 hours a month (or 80 hours a month combined with school or another activity, or if a medical condition limits work), or unable to do those things because of a medical condition. — help after leaving care Georgia's Independent Living Program serves eligible youth ages 14 to 21 with help for education, employment, housing, life skills, and adult connections, and youth who leave at 18 can return to extended care within six months. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for a state tuition and fee waiver at Technical College System of Georgia schools under O.C.G.A. § 20-3-660. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Georgia Division of Family and Children Services or one of its more than 100 Child Placing Agencies to start; DFCS first completes a virtual information session with interested families. Applicants must be at least 21, complete pre-service training and a medical exam, pass child protective screenings and criminal record checks, and show proof of residence and financial stability. — kinship care Yes. DFCS looks for kinship care first when a child enters foster care, placing the child with a relative or fictive kin who has a long-standing bond with the child or family. Kinship caregivers get the same recruitment, training, and support as other caregivers, plus help from DFCS Caregiver Navigators, and can be approved by DFCS or a Child Placing Agency. — Georgia Department of Human Services, Division of Family and Children Services (DFCS) Georgia Legal Services Program — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Hawaii Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Hawaii
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Hawaii — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Hawaii Revised Statutes section 587A-35, the family court may keep jurisdiction only until the youth turns 19. — staying in care longer Yes. Hawaii's Imua Kakou program (Young Adult Voluntary Foster Care, Act 252 of 2013, Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 346) lets young adults voluntarily stay in foster care until age 21. To stay in, the youth must sign a voluntary care agreement, meet monthly with a case manager, and be finishing high school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition. — help after leaving care Hawaii was the first state to extend Medicaid coverage to former foster youth until age 26. Through Imua Kakou, youth up to 21 can get monthly living assistance payments, medical and dental coverage, a case manager, help finding housing, independent living training, and help with jobs and education. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Department of Human Services Child Welfare Services Branch, which works with its contracted partner to recruit resource families. Applicants complete a 15-hour pre-service training called HANAI, plus background and child abuse clearances, a home visit, references, and medical reports. — kinship care Yes. Hawaii's child welfare mission puts relative placement first, and relatives can become licensed resource caregivers for children in their family, including through child-specific licensing. — Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services Legal Aid Society of Hawaii — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Idaho Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Idaho
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Idaho — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Idaho Code section 16-1604, the court's jurisdiction over a child in need of care ends at the child's 18th birthday unless the court extends it. — staying in care longer Yes. Idaho offers extended foster care to age 23 under Idaho Code section 16-1622 as amended by 2025 House Bill 245. A youth who turns 18 in department custody can stay in Continuous Foster Care until 23, or re-enter through Voluntary Post-18 Foster Care before turning 23, as long as they are finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a medical condition. — help after leaving care Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and the department offers independent living services for youth ages 14 to 21, including help with education costs through the federal Education and Training Voucher program. The process starts with an information request and an orientation meeting, followed by an application, criminal background checks, pre-service training, and a home study. — kinship care Yes. Relatives can become licensed foster parents in Idaho, and a 2025 law (House Bill 245) gives the department more flexibility to license relatives, including expedited placement, limited variances, and separate licensing standards. — Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Idaho Legal Aid Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Illinois Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Illinois
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Illinois — when youth age out Youth in Illinois can remain in DCFS care until age 21. Under 705 ILCS 405/2-31, juvenile court wardship ends automatically when a youth turns 21. — staying in care longer Yes. Illinois provides child welfare services to youth in care past 18 until age 21, and a youth whose case closed can ask the court to reinstate wardship any time before turning 21. Youth in college with at least a C average can get assistance until 23, and a 2023 law (House Bill 1293) allows services to continue to 23 for a youth who is not yet able to care for themselves. — help after leaving care DCFS offers scholarships for youth in care, along with housing, counseling, employment, education, and life-skills services, and youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26. Federal Education and Training Voucher funds are also available to help former foster youth pay for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services by filling out the online foster parent interest form. Foster parents must be at least 21, pass criminal background checks for all household members, complete a home inspection and social assessment, finish 27 hours of PRIDE pre-service training, and complete a health screening. — kinship care Yes. Illinois prioritizes placing children with relatives, and the Kinship in Demand (KIND) Act, signed February 5, 2025 and effective July 1, 2025, lets DCFS certify relative caregivers under separate standards so relatives can care for children in DCFS custody and get support. — Illinois Department of Children and Family Services Illinois Legal Aid Online — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Indiana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Indiana
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Indiana — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18, when regular foster care ends. Under Indiana Code section 31-28-5.8, a youth who was in court-ordered foster care on their 18th birthday can then choose extended care. — staying in care longer Yes. Indiana's Collaborative Care program is voluntary extended foster care from age 18 until 21 for youth who were in court-ordered care on their 18th birthday. The youth signs a Voluntary Collaborative Care Agreement, works with a case manager, and must meet school, job training, or work requirements; youth who left care can re-enter before age 20, and Voluntary Services continue to age 23. — help after leaving care Through DCS Older Youth Initiatives, youth get independent living services starting at age 16, continued health insurance, case management, and help with housing, education, and jobs. Collaborative Care youth keep placement support and services to 21, Voluntary Services run to the day before turning 23, and federal Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Indiana Department of Child Services or a licensed child placing agency, starting with the inquiry form at IndianaFosterCare.org. Foster parents must be at least 21, pass fingerprint background checks, show they are financially stable, complete pre-service training plus first aid and CPR, and finish a home study; a foster home license lasts four years. — kinship care Yes. Relatives get priority as placements, and unlicensed relative or kinship homes can care for a child while working toward a foster license; DCS also runs Kinship Indiana support services for relative caregivers. — Indiana Department of Child Services Indiana Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Iowa Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Iowa
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Iowa — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Iowa Code section 234.1, a youth who is still in high school full time or in special education can still count as a 'child' for foster care purposes at age 18 or 19. — staying in care longer Iowa does not offer a general extended foster care program to age 21. Instead, a youth age 18 to 20 who was in court-ordered foster care at 18 and is at imminent risk of homelessness or of not graduating from high school can apply to HHS for extended foster care or supervised apartment living, and all former foster youth can use voluntary Aftercare services to age 21, with Extended Aftercare to age 22. — help after leaving care The Iowa Aftercare Services Network gives former foster youth ages 18 to 20 voluntary aftercare support, including a self-sufficiency advocate, life-skills help, and vendor payments, plus a monthly Preparation for Adult Living (PAL) stipend for youth in college, job training, or working full time. Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services or its foster recruitment contractors, Four Oaks Family Connections and Lutheran Services in Iowa. Foster parents must be at least 21, complete 30 hours of pre-service training, pass background checks, and finish a home study with home visits. — kinship care Yes. Iowa places children with adult relatives first, before other foster homes, and relatives can apply for a foster family license so they can receive foster care payments; relatives who take legal guardianship of a child from foster care may also qualify for the subsidized guardianship program. — Iowa Department of Health and Human Services Iowa Legal Aid — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Kansas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Kansas
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Kansas — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Kansas Statutes section 38-2203, court jurisdiction can continue until June 1 of the school year in which the youth turns 18 if they are still in high school, and until age 21 if there is no court-approved transition plan. — staying in care longer Kansas does not offer a general extended foster care placement program to age 21. Instead, the court can keep jurisdiction until age 21 when no transition plan has been approved, and youth who leave care at 18 get help through DCF's Independent Living and Self-Sufficiency Program until age 21, including a monthly subsidy, Chafee funds, and help with housing and education. — help after leaving care Former foster youth in Kansas keep Medicaid (KanCare) coverage until age 26, can get Education and Training Voucher funds for up to five years (to age 26), and can have college tuition and fees waived under the Kansas Foster Child Education Assistance Act. The Independent Living Program also offers a monthly subsidy, start-up funds for housing, and help with transportation and school costs until age 21. — becoming a foster parent Choose a licensed child placing agency, such as KVC, TFI Family Services, or Saint Francis Ministries, to sponsor your application, and DCF's Foster Care Licensing Division issues the license. Applicants must be at least 21, have enough income to meet their family's basic needs, pass background checks, complete 30 hours of pre-service (MAPP) training, and pass a family assessment and home inspection. — kinship care Yes. Relatives can become licensed foster parents in Kansas, with an accelerated process for relative and non-related kinship homes and waivers for some non-safety licensing rules; kinship caregivers complete a 30-hour Kinship Path training course within the first year of licensure. — Kansas Department for Children and Families Kansas Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Kentucky Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Kentucky
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Kentucky — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Kentucky Revised Statutes section 620.140, a commitment to the Cabinet cannot extend past age 18 unless the youth elects to extend it. — staying in care longer Yes. Kentucky's Extended Commitment program lets a youth who turns 18 in state care ask to stay in care until age 21 to receive transitional living support, including housing, help with daily needs, and case management. The youth must ask before turning 19, get court approval with the Cabinet's agreement, and be working full time (at least 30 hours a week), attending school full time, working part time while attending school part time, or have a documented disability that prevents work or school. — help after leaving care Through the KY RISE program, youth in care ages 16 to 21 get independent living help, and former foster youth can use the Tuition Waiver for Foster and Adopted Children, which waives tuition and mandatory fees at Kentucky's public universities and community and technical colleges. Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training. — becoming a foster parent Contact the local Department for Community Based Services office to start the process. Foster parents must be at least 21, attend an informational meeting, complete 15 hours of approved classroom training plus 15 hours of web-based pre-service training, pass FBI, sex offender registry, and child abuse registry background checks, and complete a home study; the process usually takes six to nine months. — kinship care Yes. Relatives and fictive kin can become foster parents for a child in their family, and relative or fictive kin foster parents need only be 18. Kentucky's KY KINS program offers peer support, training, and a kinship support line for relative caregivers, along with help such as child care assistance. — Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Department for Community Based Services Legal Aid of the Bluegrass — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Louisiana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Louisiana
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Louisiana — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Louisiana Children's Code Article 686, a judgment placing a child in foster care stays in force only until the child's 18th birthday. — staying in care longer Yes. Louisiana's Extended Foster Care program (Louisiana Revised Statutes section 46:288.3, signed into law in June 2019) lets youth who turn 18 in foster care voluntarily stay in care until age 21. The youth signs a voluntary placement agreement and must be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition; caseworkers use the Youth Villages LifeSet model for intensive, weekly support. — help after leaving care Louisiana's Chafee Foster Care Independence Program serves youth in and formerly in foster care up to age 26, with Education and Training Voucher help available until age 23, and youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26. Extended foster care youth get intensive LifeSet case management help with education, employment, housing, and independent living skills. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services or a licensed child-placing agency and attend an orientation meeting to start certification. Applicants must be at least 21, have enough income to meet their own family's needs, be in good physical, emotional, and mental health, pass fingerprint background checks, complete about 21 hours of pre-service training, and finish a home study. — kinship care Yes. When a child is removed, DCFS must make reasonable efforts to place the child with a relative for kinship foster care, and an approved kinship foster parent receives the full foster care rate under Louisiana Revised Statutes section 46:286.1; DCFS also runs a Kinship Navigator program for relative caregivers. — Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services Southeast Louisiana Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Maine Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Maine
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Maine — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18, but they can choose to keep receiving care and support by signing a voluntary agreement with the department under Maine Revised Statutes Title 22, section 4037-A. — staying in care longer Yes. Maine's Voluntary Extended Support (V9) agreement lets a youth who turned 18 in state care keep placement and supports until their 23rd birthday (extended from age 21 effective August 8, 2023). To stay in, the youth must be working toward a high school diploma or GED, enrolled in college or career training, in an employment support program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a documented medical or behavioral health condition, and can re-enter before 23 if they left earlier. — help after leaving care Maine's Youth Transition Services (Chafee Foster Care Independence Program) help youth with housing, education, employment, and life skills, and former foster youth keep MaineCare (Medicaid) coverage until age 26. Youth who were adopted or entered permanency guardianship at age 16 or older may also get Education and Training Voucher funds for college or training. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Office of Child and Family Services or its recruitment partner, A Family for ME, and attend an informational meeting before applying. Resource parents must be at least 21 and Maine residents, and licensing requires an application, background checks, a home inspection, a home study, and introductory training. — kinship care Yes. Whenever possible, OCFS places children with relatives first, and relatives can become licensed resource parents for a child in their family; relatives interested in caring for a child should contact the child's caseworker or A Family for ME. — Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Child and Family Services Pine Tree Legal Assistance — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Maryland Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Maryland
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Maryland — when youth age out Youth can remain in out-of-home placement under a voluntary placement agreement until age 21 under Maryland Family Law section 5-525. Court commitment as a Child in Need of Assistance ends at 18, but voluntary care continues past 18. — staying in care longer Yes. Maryland offers extended foster care to age 21 through a voluntary placement agreement: eligible youth stay in placement automatically for 180 days after turning 18, and longer if the juvenile court finds it is in their best interest. To stay in, the youth must be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a medical condition, and former foster youth can re-enter care before age 20 and 6 months. — help after leaving care Maryland's Ready by 21 program serves youth in care from age 14 to their 21st birthday with help in education, employment, housing, finances, health care, and mentors, plus independent living aftercare services for ages 18 to 21. Former foster youth can also use the Tuition Waiver for Foster Care Recipients at Maryland public colleges, keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and get Education and Training Voucher funds for college or training. — becoming a foster parent Contact the local Department of Social Services in the county where you live to start the process of becoming a resource parent. Applicants must be at least 21 and a U.S. citizen or legal resident, complete 27 hours of pre-service training, pass state and federal criminal background checks, have medical exams, and pass health and fire inspections of the home. — kinship care Yes. Maryland follows a 'kin-first' approach that gives relatives and kin priority for placement, and since December 2024 the state has separate kinship licensing standards (Social Services Administration policy SSA-CW #24-06). Relatives can become licensed (restricted) caregivers for children in their family and get extra support and benefits beyond the child's social worker. — Maryland Department of Human Services Maryland Legal Aid — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Massachusetts Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Massachusetts
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Massachusetts — when youth age out Youth age out of DCF care at 18, when they become legal adults, under Massachusetts General Laws chapter 119, section 23. DCF must offer continued services to young adults who were in its care or custody at 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Massachusetts offers extended foster care to age 22 (and to age 23 for a young adult finishing an associate's degree or higher), under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 119, § 23 and 110 CMR 23.00. To stay in care, the young adult signs a voluntary placement agreement and must be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in a program that helps them get work, employed at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition. — help after leaving care Young adults who age out can get Young Adult Support Payments from DCF while in extended care, and former foster youth keep MassHealth (Medicaid) coverage to age 26 under federal law. They can also get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, plus help with housing, jobs, and life skills through DCF's young adult services and the Chafee program. — becoming a foster parent Contact the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families to start — apply through mass.gov, attend an information session, and complete an application with background checks and a home safety review. Applicants must be at least 18, live in Massachusetts, and complete the 30-hour MAPP (Massachusetts Approach to Partnerships in Parenting) training plus a home study before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — DCF looks for relatives (kin) first when a child must leave home, and kin can be placed with a child right away and then become licensed as kinship foster parents under DCF Policy 23-01. Licensed kinship families get the same foster care payments and support as other foster families. — Massachusetts Department of Children and Families (DCF) MassLegalHelp — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Michigan Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Michigan
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Michigan — when youth age out Youth age out of Michigan foster care at 18, when they become legal adults. The Young Adult Voluntary Foster Care Act (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 400.645–400.663) lets them keep receiving care past 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Michigan's Young Adult Voluntary Foster Care (YAVFC) program extends foster care to age 21. To stay in, the youth must have been in MDHHS foster care on their 18th birthday, sign a voluntary agreement, and be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or job training, in a work program, employed at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things for medical reasons; youth who left after 18 can re-enter before 21. — help after leaving care Youth in YAVFC keep foster care payments, a caseworker, counseling, and health care coverage, plus independent living skills training. After leaving care, former foster youth can get Medicaid to age 26, Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year for college or training, and help with housing and jobs through MDHHS independent living services. — becoming a foster parent Start by contacting Michigan's Foster Care Navigators or MDHHS or a licensed child-placing agency, then attend an orientation and choose an agency. Applicants must be at least 18, pass fingerprint background checks, complete 20–25 hours of free GROW pre-service training, and pass a home evaluation before MDHHS issues a license. — kinship care Yes — relatives are a preferred placement in Michigan, and a relative can care for a child while getting licensed; under current MDHHS policy, relatives caring only for kin no longer have to become licensed unless they want to foster unrelated children. Licensed relative caregivers receive foster care payments, and MDHHS offers kinship support and navigation help. — Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) Michigan Legal Help — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Minnesota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Minnesota
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Minnesota — when youth age out Youth age out of Minnesota foster care at 18, when they become legal adults, under Minnesota Statutes chapter 260C. The agency must give written notice six months before a youth turns 18 that foster care can continue to age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — Minnesota offers extended foster care to age 21 under Minn. Stat. § 260C.451. A youth who was in foster care right before turning 18 can stay (or return) if they are finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in a work program, employed at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things for medical reasons; settings include traditional foster homes and supervised independent living like apartments or dorms. — help after leaving care Former foster youth keep Medical Assistance (Medicaid) to age 26 with no income or asset test under the former foster care youth basis (MA-FFY). They can also get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year, the Fostering Independence Grant covering college costs at Minnesota schools to age 27, and independent living services and housing help through their county or tribal agency. — becoming a foster parent Contact your county human services agency, a Tribal Nation, or a private child-placing agency to apply for a child foster care license. Applicants must be at least 21, pass DHS background studies for household members 13 and older, complete 6 hours of orientation training plus a home study and home safety check; licensing usually takes 90 to 120 days. — kinship care Yes — relatives and kin are preferred placements in Minnesota, and a relative can take a child on an emergency basis while working toward a license; relative applicants can even be licensed before finishing orientation training, as long as it is done within 30 days. Licensed kinship caregivers receive foster care payments, and the state supports kinship families through Northstar Care for Children benefits. — Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF) LawHelpMN — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

h: Foster care & youth aging out in Mississippi
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Mississippi — when youth age out Youth generally age out of Mississippi foster care at 18, when they become legal adults; youth court jurisdiction can continue to age 20 and the agency may serve youth to 21. Mississippi Code § 43-15-13 defines children in department custody as persons under 21, and the agency has confirmed it has no Title IV-E extended foster care program. — staying in care longer No — Mississippi does not offer Title IV-E extended foster care past 18, as confirmed by the MDCPS deputy commissioner. Code R. 6-1-D-IX. — help after leaving care Youth who leave MDCPS custody at 18 to 21 can get Independent Living services until 21, including life-skills training, help with housing and income, and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) for college or job training. Former foster youth also keep Medicaid coverage to age 26 under federal law, and MDCPS offers aftercare services and transitional living support. — becoming a foster parent Apply online through the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services (MDCPS) foster care page or call its foster parent information line to start. Applicants must be Mississippi residents at least 21 years old, financially self-supporting, pass criminal background checks, and complete pre-service training (Mississippi PATH, about 15.5 hours) and a home study before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — relatives can become licensed resource parents in Mississippi, and the rules allow a faster training track for relatives. Kinship caregivers who become licensed receive foster care payments and the same training and support as other foster parents. — Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services (MDCPS) Mississippi Center for Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

h: Foster care & youth aging out in Missouri
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Missouri — when youth age out Youth age out of Missouri foster care at 18, when they become legal adults. Under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 211.041, the juvenile court can keep jurisdiction over a youth until age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — Missouri lets youth stay in or re-enter foster care until 21 under Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 211.036 and 211.041.
