Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint criminal and child abuse/neglect checks, and complete the free 30-hour MO C.A.R.E. pre-service training and a home study before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — Missouri prefers placing children with relatives, and relative caregivers follow a shorter 9-hour STARS for Relative Placement training track instead of the full 30-hour course. Relatives who become licensed receive foster care payments and support, and the Children's Division helps kinship families with services and resources. — Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division Legal Services of Missouri — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Montana Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Montana
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Montana — when youth age out Youth age out of Montana foster care at 18, when they become legal adults. Under Montana Admin. Rules 37.51.102, a youth older than 18 may remain in foster care only if they are still in secondary school. — staying in care longer Montana has no broad extended foster care program to age 21 — the only way to stay in a foster placement past 18 is to still be in secondary school. Instead, youth who age out get help through the Montana Chafee Foster Care Independence Program, which serves youth ages 14 to 21 with transitional living plans, life-skills training, mentors, and room-and-board help. — help after leaving care The Chafee Foster Care Independence Program offers youth who aged out before 21 life-skills training, help getting a GED or job, mentors, and stipends for school, work, and setting up an apartment. Former foster youth can also get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year through Reach Higher Montana, Medicaid coverage to age 26, and Foster Youth to Independence housing vouchers in Missoula, Billings, and Butte. — becoming a foster parent Contact your local Child and Family Services Division (CFSD) office to request an inquiry packet and application. Applicants must be at least 18, pass criminal, motor vehicle, and child protective services background checks, complete 18 hours of free pre-service training, and pass a home study and fire-safety check before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — Montana issues a kinship foster home license for relatives, tribal members, godparents, stepparents, or others with a significant prior tie to a specific child. Kinship foster parents complete the same training and background checks and receive foster care payments. — Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division (DPHHS/CFSD) Montana Legal Services Association — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Nebraska Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Nebraska
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Nebraska — when youth age out Youth age out of Nebraska foster care at 19, the age of majority in Nebraska, under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-905. DHHS services and legal custody do not extend past the age of majority except for youth in the Bridge to Independence Program. — staying in care longer Yes — Nebraska's Bridge to Independence (B2i) program extends support to age 21 under the Young Adult Bridge to Independence Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 43-4501–43-4514). To join, a young adult must have been adjudicated neglected, be in out-of-home placement at 19 (or discharged to independent living), be a Nebraska resident, sign a voluntary services and support agreement, and be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in a work program, employed at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things for medical reasons. — help after leaving care Bridge to Independence participants get a monthly stipend for housing and living costs, Medicaid coverage, and a dedicated independence coordinator for case management. After leaving care, former foster youth can get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) for college or training, Medicaid to age 26, and help with housing, jobs, and education through DHHS independent living services. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) or a contracted foster care agency — start at the DHHS foster care page. Applicants must be the age of majority, pass national criminal history and central registry background checks, provide three character references and health reports, and complete at least 21 hours of DHHS-approved pre-service training plus a home study before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — relatives and kin can foster in Nebraska, and DHHS can waive licensing standards that are not related to child safety for a relative home working toward licensure. Relative foster parents get training and support from DHHS and the Nebraska Foster and Adoptive Parent Association, and licensed kinship homes receive foster care payments. — Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Children and Family Services Legal Aid of Nebraska — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Nevada Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Nevada
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Nevada — when youth age out Youth age out of Nevada foster care at 18, when they become legal adults. Under Nev. Rev. Stat. § 432B.594, a court that has jurisdiction over a child at 18 must keep jurisdiction if the youth asks, until age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — Nevada's Extended Young Adult Support Services Program provides extended support to young adults ages 18 to 21 under Nev. Rev. Stat. §§ 432B.591–432B.595. A young adult who was in foster care can ask the court to keep jurisdiction and sign a voluntary agreement for placement and care, with a written transition plan, and can re-enter the program before 21 if they left earlier. — help after leaving care Young adults in the program get monthly financial support, continued health coverage, and independent living services to help with school, work, and housing. Youth who leave care after 16 can also get Chafee independent living services and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) until age 26, and former foster youth keep Medicaid to age 26. — becoming a foster parent Contact the child welfare agency for your county — DCFS for rural Nevada, Clark County Family Services, or Washoe County Human Services — to start licensing. Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint background checks, complete the required pre-service training (about 27 hours in rural Nevada, 24 hours in Clark County), and pass a home study and safety inspection, a process that takes about three to six months. — kinship care Yes — Nevada strongly prefers kinship (relative) care, and relatives or fictive kin with a bond to the child can care for them; kinship caregivers can be licensed or unlicensed, but DCFS strongly encourages licensing. Licensed kinship caregivers receive the full foster care rate plus respite care, training, and support groups, while unlicensed relatives receive much lower reimbursements. — Nevada Division of Child and Family Services (DCFS), Department of Health and Human Services Nevada Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: New Hampshire Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in New Hampshire
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in New Hampshire — when youth age out Youth age out of New Hampshire foster care at 18, when they become legal adults. Under N.H. Rev. Stat. § 170-E:53, DCYF must offer extended foster care to youth who were in its custody at 18. — staying in care longer Yes — New Hampshire's HOPE (Housing and Opportunities to Personally Excel) program extends foster care to age 21 under N.H. Rev. Stat. § 170-E:53. A young adult who was in DCYF custody at 18 can voluntarily stay in or return to foster care — even if they first said no — by signing a voluntary participation agreement and finishing school, being enrolled in college or job training, being in a work program, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things for medical reasons. — help after leaving care HOPE participants keep a paid foster placement (including supervised independent living), case management, and financial help. After leaving care, young adults ages 18 to 23 (to 26 if in college or career training) can get Aftercare Services with limited financial help, Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) for college or training, housing vouchers, and LifeSet coaching, and former foster youth keep Medicaid to age 26. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the New Hampshire Division for Children, Youth and Families (DCYF) — submit a foster/adoptive parent application to your local DCYF district office. Applicants must be New Hampshire residents at least 21 years old, pass fingerprint and criminal records checks, complete at least 21 hours of DCYF pre-licensing training, and pass fire and health inspections and a home study before being licensed. — kinship care Yes — DCYF prefers relatives for placement and searches for parents and relatives throughout a case, and relatives can become licensed kinship caregivers with their own dedicated training course. Kinship caregivers get support from DCYF, and licensed kinship homes receive foster care payments. — New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, Division for Children, Youth and Families (DCYF) New Hampshire Legal Assistance — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: New Jersey Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in New Jersey
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in New Jersey — when youth age out Youth age out of New Jersey foster care at 18, the age of majority, under N.J. Stat. § 9:17B-3. Under N.J. Stat. § 30:4C-2.3, DCF must provide services to young adults ages 18 to 21 who were receiving DCF services at 16 or older. — staying in care longer Yes — New Jersey extends services to age 21 under N.J. Stat. § 30:4C-2.3 and DCF policy CP&P-III-A-1-500. A young adult who received DCF services at 16 or older can stay in care or ask to reopen their case before 21 if they have not refused services and CP&P finds continued services are in their best interest, such as finishing school, job training, or working toward goals in their transitional plan. — help after leaving care Young adults in extended care keep case management, board payments, and help with school, work, and housing through DCF's Office of Adolescent Services. After leaving care, former foster youth can get Chafee program services and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) for college or training, Medicaid coverage to age 26, and housing help through DCF's adolescent housing programs. — becoming a foster parent Start by creating a profile in DCF's online foster care portal (Binti) or calling the NJ Foster line, and a local Resource Family Recruiter will schedule you for an orientation (Group Engagement). Applicants must be at least 18 and New Jersey residents, pass criminal history and child abuse record checks, and complete nine weekly three-hour pre-service training sessions, a home evaluation, and a life-safety inspection; licensing usually takes about five months. — kinship care Yes — New Jersey supports kinship care in several ways: relatives can become licensed resource parents, and families caring for a relative's child can get help through DCF's Kinship Care program and Kinship Legal Guardianship (KLG), which provides a monthly subsidy to relatives who become a child's legal guardian. Kinship caregivers can also get support services and board payments when licensed. — New Jersey Department of Children and Families (DCF), Division of Child Protection and Permanency (CP&P) Legal Services of New Jersey — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: New Mexico Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in New Mexico
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in New Mexico — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18 under the New Mexico Children's Code, when CYFD custody generally ends. CYFD's Fostering Connections program then offers voluntary extended support. — staying in care longer Yes — New Mexico offers extended foster care to age 21 through Fostering Connections, created by 2019 legislation and fully in place by 2023. A youth who was in care at 18 can stay in or re-enter care to 21 by signing a Voluntary Services and Support Agreement and meeting one activity condition, such as finishing school, being in college or job training, working, or having a medical condition that prevents those activities. — help after leaving care Fostering Connections provides Medicaid, help paying for college, housing support (including Transitional Living for Young Adults, Transitions Supportive Housing, and Foster Youth Independence housing help), job help, and food access for youth ages 18 to 26. Youth who were in foster care at 18 can also keep Medicaid to age 26 and may qualify for federal Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Contact CYFD to express interest and start the process; CYFD will connect you with a representative or regional navigator. Applicants complete eligibility checks, a SAFE home study, background checks, and pre-service training, and are licensed through CYFD, with the license renewed every two years. — kinship care Yes — relatives and fictive kin can foster, and kinship placements are about half of New Mexico placements. Kinship caregivers can become licensed resource foster parents, and the Kinship Guardianship Program links grandparents and other relatives raising children to navigators, training, support groups, and free legal help. — New Mexico Children, Youth & Families Department (CYFD) New Mexico Legal Aid — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: New York Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in New York
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in New York — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, when placement generally cannot continue without the youth's consent, under Family Court Act sections 1055(e) and 756-a(f). No placement may continue past age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — youth may remain in foster care to age 21 if they consent, under Family Court Act sections 1055(e) and 1091. Youth who leave care after 18 can also ask to re-enter before age 21 (within 24 months of discharge), if they have no reasonable alternative to foster care and agree to enroll in school or vocational training, unless that is unnecessary for their situation. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. The Chafee Foster Care Program for Successful Transition to Adulthood offers life-skills, education, employment, and housing help, generally from age 14 to 21 (and to 23 for youth who aged out at 18-20), and the Education and Training Voucher program offers up to $5,000 a year for college or vocational training, with eligibility to age 26 if first awarded before 21. — becoming a foster parent Apply through your local department of social services or an authorized voluntary foster care agency, starting with OCFS's foster care inquiry process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks and a home study, and complete required training before certification. — kinship care Yes — relatives and certain non-relatives can be approved as kinship foster parents, and New York gives first consideration to placing a child with relatives. Kinship caregivers can also receive help through the Kinship Navigator program and, in some cases, the Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program (KinGAP). — New York State Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS) The Legal Aid Society — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: North Carolina Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in North Carolina
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in North Carolina — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18 under N.C.G.S. 131D-10.2B, which also authorizes continued foster care services to age 21. A youth who opts out at 18 may later opt back in before turning 21. — staying in care longer Yes — North Carolina's Foster Care 18 to 21 program lets a youth who was in foster care on their 18th birthday stay in or return to care until 21. The youth must sign a voluntary placement agreement with a county department and meet one condition: finishing high school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a medical condition or disability. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. The program also provides casework, a transition living plan, placement support, and help with education and employment, and former foster youth may qualify for federal Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) and Chafee independent-living services. — becoming a foster parent Contact your county department of social services or a licensed private foster care agency, watch the mandatory orientation video, and complete the licensing process. Applicants must be at least 21, complete 30 hours of training, pass background checks, and complete a mutual home assessment for licensing, renewed every two years. — kinship care Yes — kinship foster care is the preferred placement when a child must be removed, and kin can be relatives by birth or a person with a family-like relationship. Kinship caregivers do not have to be licensed to care for a child, but becoming licensed (with a reduced 15-hour NTDC training option for relatives) qualifies them for monthly financial help and, in some cases, the Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program (KinGAP). — North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Social Services Legal Aid of North Carolina — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: North Dakota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in North Dakota
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in North Dakota — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, when the child-in-need-of-protection court order terminates under N.D. Cent. Code 27-20.3-26 and the youth is discharged from custody. Youth who want to keep receiving help can move into the 18+ Continued Care program. — staying in care longer Yes — North Dakota's 18+ Continued Care program is available to eligible youth up to age 21 under N.D. Cent. Code 27-20-30.1. The youth must have aged out while under a court order to a North Dakota public agency, Tribal social services, or the Division of Juvenile Services, sign the 18+ Continued Foster Care Agreement, and meet an education, employment, employment-preparation, or medical-condition condition; youth can return within six months of discharge. — help after leaving care Youth who were in North Dakota foster care and on Medicaid when they turned 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26 regardless of income. The Chafee Program offers independent-living services, flex funds, and room-and-board funds to youth up to age 23, and Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year (lifetime maximum $25,000) for college or vocational training, available to apply for up to age 26. — becoming a foster parent Contact the North Dakota Children and Family Services licensing unit or a local Human Service Zone to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint-based criminal background and child abuse/neglect checks, provide references, complete a home study and required training (about 30 hours), and complete fire-prevention training. — kinship care Yes — relatives and other adults with a close relationship to the child can care for them as kinship caregivers, and no foster license is required for relative/kinship care, though a background check and home safety check are done. Kinship caregivers can get support through the Kinship-ND program, and children placed with relatives within the fifth degree may qualify for TANF Kinship Care funding. — North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Children and Family Services Legal Services of North Dakota — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Ohio Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Ohio
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Ohio — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, when custody of the public children services agency generally ends, under Ohio Rev. Code 2151.81. Eligible youth can then choose the voluntary Bridges program instead of leaving support behind. — staying in care longer Yes — Ohio's Bridges program, created by 2016 House Bill 50, supports young adults from 18 to 21 who emancipated from a PCSA, a Title IV-E juvenile court, or the Department of Youth Services. To qualify, the young adult must be finishing secondary school, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a physical or mental health condition. — help after leaving care Youth who age out of foster care in Ohio can keep Medicaid until age 26. Bridges provides help with stable housing, education, employment, and community resources, and former foster youth can apply for Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, as well as independent-living services through their county agency. — becoming a foster parent Start at FosterAndAdopt.ohio.gov or contact your county public children services agency or a private child-placing agency to choose an agency and begin certification. Applicants complete an application, background checks with fingerprinting, references, a home study, and 24 to 36 hours of pre-placement training. — kinship care Yes — a relative's home is the first choice for a child who needs temporary care in Ohio. Kinship caregivers can receive Kinship Support Program payments for up to six months while they work toward foster-care certification, and licensed kinship caregivers can receive foster care payments and help from the Ohio Kinship and Adoption Navigator (OhioKAN). — Ohio Department of Children & Youth Ohio Legal Help — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Oklahoma Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Oklahoma
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Oklahoma — when youth age out Youth age out of foster care at 18, when OKDHS custody generally ends. Oklahoma's Successful Adulthood services were already available to youth in care from age 14, and a new extended foster care law now carries support to 21. — staying in care longer Yes — Senate Bill 1806, signed in 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, created extended foster care to age 21 in Oklahoma. Eligible young adults who were in OKDHS custody at 18, or who reached permanency through guardianship or adoption at age 16 or older and no longer have caregiver support, can voluntarily continue services to 21 by finishing secondary school, being in college or career-tech, being in an employment-readiness program, working at least 80 hours a month, or having a documented medical condition that prevents those activities; services can include Medicaid, a monthly stipend, and continued caseworker support. — help after leaving care The Oklahoma Successful Adulthood Program (OKSA) helps youth in and from foster care with independent-living skills, education, employment, and housing as they move toward adulthood. Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26, and former foster youth up to age 26 may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Contact Oklahoma Human Services' Foster Care and Adoption Support Center or visit okfosters.org to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, financially stable without relying on foster care payments, pass background checks for household members age 13 and older, and complete required training and a home assessment. — kinship care Yes — Oklahoma has a Kinship Foster Care Program under 10A O.S. 1-9-106, and OKDHS must try to place a removed child with a person who has a kinship relationship with the child, including relatives by blood, marriage, or adoption and people with a close emotional tie or bond. Kinship foster parents complete training (at least 12 hours, within 120 days of placement where possible) and background checks, and can receive foster care payments once finally approved. — Oklahoma Human Services (OKDHS) Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Oregon Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Oregon
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Oregon — when youth age out Youth generally age out at 18, when the court may dismiss their case, but a ward's commitment to ODHS can continue until the court dismisses it or the youth turns 21, under ORS 419B.337(6). In practice, most youth who emancipate leave care at 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Oregon offers extended foster care to age 21. Under ORS 419B.337 and ODHS rule OAR 413-030-0220, a young adult can stay in substitute care to 21 if staying in care is in their best interest and they are working toward high school graduation or a GED, employed, in a training program, in approved volunteer work, in a special-education program, or an unaccompanied refugee minor; Oregon law does not allow re-entry once a youth has left care. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. ODHS transition services (the Independent Living Program) help youth age 14 and older, and former foster youth under 24, with life skills, education, employment, housing help including an independent-living housing subsidy, and flexible funds, and former foster youth may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Contact ODHS Child Welfare through its partner Every Child Oregon, which recruits and supports resource families, to start the certification process. Applicants must generally be at least 21, pass child-abuse and criminal background checks, have space and financial resources to support their household, and complete orientation and Foundations/RAFT training. — kinship care Yes — placing a child with relatives is the preferred option in Oregon, and relatives can become certified resource parents for a child in their family. Relatives are notified by ODHS when a child enters care, and kinship caregivers can get help through ODHS Relative and Kinship Connections and local Child Welfare offices. — Oregon Department of Human Services (ODHS), Child Welfare Legal Aid Services of Oregon — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Pennsylvania Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Pennsylvania
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Pennsylvania — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, when dependency jurisdiction generally ends, but under Act 91 (42 Pa.C.S. 6302) a youth adjudicated dependent before 18 can ask the court to retain jurisdiction to age 21. Youth whose jurisdiction ended within 90 days before turning 18, or on or after 18, may also seek resumption of jurisdiction. — staying in care longer Yes — Pennsylvania offers extended foster care to age 21 under Act 91. A youth under 21 who aged out within 90 days of turning 18 or after 18 can remain in or re-enter care by meeting one activity condition: completing secondary school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to promote or remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a medical or behavioral health condition. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. Pennsylvania's Chafee Independent Living Program serves youth in care ages 14 to 21 and offers aftercare services to age 23, including life-skills training, education and employment help, housing location and room-and-board help; the Chafee Education and Training Grant offers up to $5,000 a year for college or career school, and the Fostering Independence Tuition Waiver (FosterED) can waive tuition at Pennsylvania schools for eligible former foster youth. — becoming a foster parent Contact your county children and youth agency or a licensed private foster care agency to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass criminal, child-abuse, and FBI background checks for everyone in the home age 14 and older, pass a medical appraisal and home evaluation, and complete agency training and a home study. — kinship care Yes — Pennsylvania law requires the county agency to give first consideration to placing a child with relatives or kin, including a godparent or someone with an existing meaningful relationship. Relatives can serve as kinship foster parents, and kinship guardianship subsidies and adoption subsidies can be extended to age 21 for eligible youth under Act 80. — Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth and Families Pennsylvania Legal Aid Network — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Rhode Island Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Rhode Island
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Rhode Island — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, when Family Court jurisdiction generally ends under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-6, unless the youth elects the Voluntary Extension of Care program. DCYF must present a transition plan covering housing, health insurance, education or employment, mentors, and support services six months before a youth turns 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Rhode Island's Voluntary Extension of Care (VEC) program lets a youth who was in DCYF legal custody at 18 voluntarily stay under DCYF care and Family Court supervision to age 21, under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-6. The youth must sign a voluntary placement agreement and meet one condition: finishing high school or a GED, being in secondary or postsecondary/vocational education, being in job training or a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition; youth who leave VEC can ask to be reinstated before 21. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care on their 18th birthday can keep Medicaid to age 21 under DCYF's aftercare rules, and youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26 under federal former-foster-youth coverage. DCYF and its partner Foster Forward provide aftercare services, housing and employment help, and postsecondary education assistance to youth ages 18 to 21, and former foster youth may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Apply through DCYF's Resource Families program, using its online BINTI applicant portal, or through a licensed community partner agency. Applicants must generally be at least 21 (kinship caregivers ages 18 to 20 may be considered), pass background checks, be in good enough health and financially able to care for a child, pass fire and safety (and lead, where required) inspections, and complete 30 hours of pre-service training and a home study. — kinship care Yes — when DCYF gets temporary custody of a child, it must investigate placing the child with a fit and willing relative, under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-27. Relatives can be certified as kinship resource parents, with some licensing rules eased for relatives, and kinship caregivers ages 18 to 20 may be considered where other applicants must be 21. — Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth & Families (DCYF) Rhode Island Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: South Carolina Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in South Carolina
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in South Carolina — when youth age out Youth age out at 18, the age of majority, when DSS custody generally ends. South Carolina's extended foster care law, S.C. Code 63-7-2710 and following (Article 8, added in 2022), lets eligible youth stay under DSS placement and care to age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — South Carolina extends foster care to age 21 under S.C. Code 63-7-2710 to 63-7-2770 and DSS Policy 546. A youth who was in DSS legal custody on their 18th birthday can sign a Voluntary Placement Agreement to stay in or return to care before 21, and must meet one condition: finishing secondary school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to promote or remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a physical, intellectual, emotional, or psychiatric condition. — help after leaving care Youth who were in foster care on their 18th birthday can keep Medicaid to age 26. DSS's Chafee program provides casework, help finishing high school, education and employment help, housing and financial-management help, and aftercare services to former foster youth up to age 26, and Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) help pay for college or vocational school. — becoming a foster parent Choose a licensing partner (a private child-placing agency, or DSS in some circumstances) through DSS's foster care pages and complete the licensing process. Applicants complete an application, required pre-service training, criminal and central-registry background checks and fingerprinting for household members 18 and older, a home study, references, medical reports, and fire, health, sanitation, and lead inspections. — kinship care Yes — DSS must try to identify a relative or fictive kin for placement when a child is removed, under S.C. Code 63-7-2320, and preference is given to a relative or person known to the child with a caring relationship. Kin can become licensed kinship foster parents, which brings the full foster care board rate, Medicaid for the child, and child-care vouchers; kinship care coordinators in each region help caregivers through licensing and local resources. — South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS) South Carolina Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: South Dakota Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in South Dakota
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in South Dakota — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18, the age of majority in South Dakota. The juvenile court's jurisdiction over an abused or neglected child can extend until age 21, under S.D. Codified Laws sections 26-7A-1(6), 26-7A-102, and 26-8A-29. — staying in care longer Yes, but only narrowly: a child welfare agency, including DSS, may continue foster care to age 21 if the youth was in foster care immediately before turning 18, has not yet finished 12th grade or is in a continuing course of remedial treatment, and consents in writing, under S.D. Codified Laws section 26-6-6.1. Youth ages 16 through 20 can also take part in an Independent Living Preparation Program (ILPP) for supervision and training in self-sufficiency, and the law does not allow re-entry once a youth has left. — help after leaving care Youth who age out can get help through DSS transition services, including the Independent Living Preparation Program and the Foster Care Transition Program for youth ages 14 to 21, which cover life skills and education support. The federal Education and Training Voucher (ETV) program helps pay for college or job training, and youth who were in foster care and on Medicaid at 18 can keep Medicaid coverage as former foster youth until age 26. — becoming a foster parent Contact the South Dakota Department of Social Services, Division of Child Protection Services, to start the process through its Stronger Families Together program. Foster parents must be at least 21, pass background and abuse/neglect screening, have a safe home and enough income to support their own family, and complete foster parent education and training. — kinship care Yes — relatives are considered before any other placement whenever possible, under South Dakota's relative-preference law, S.D. Codified Laws section 26-7A-19. Relatives can become licensed kinship foster parents and receive the same monthly foster care support as other foster families. — South Dakota Department of Social Services, Division of Child Protection Services East River Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Tennessee Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Tennessee
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Tennessee — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. Tennessee law, Tenn. Code Ann. section 37-2-417, then allows voluntary extended foster care services for young adults ages 18 to 21 who were in DCS custody on their 18th birthday. — staying in care longer Yes — Tennessee offers Extension of Foster Care Services to age 21 for youth who were in DCS custody at 18 and voluntarily sign a placement agreement. To stay in care the youth must be finishing high school or its equivalent, enrolled in postsecondary or vocational education, in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition; youth who first declined can re-enter before age 21. — help after leaving care DCS provides Independent Living services and its Bright Futures program, and the federal Chafee program serves Tennessee youth up to age 23. Youth can get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, and Tennessee's TennCare Independent Foster Care Adolescents category continues Medicaid for youth who were in foster care at 18, up to age 21. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Tennessee Department of Children's Services foster care program, which also works with licensed private agencies. Applicants must be at least 21, pass state and federal criminal background checks, complete a home study, and finish the free TN KEY pre-service training. — kinship care Yes — under Tennessee's Kinship Foster Care Program, Tenn. Code Ann. section 37-2-414, DCS must try for at least 30 days after removal to place a child with a relative. Approved kinship foster parents, generally relatives within the first, second, or third degree who are 21 or older, can receive the full foster care rate and other foster parent benefits, and DCS also runs a separate Relative Caregiver Program with support services for relatives caring for children outside foster care. — Tennessee Department of Children's Services Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Texas Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Texas
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Texas — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. Texas Family Code sections 263.6015, 263.602, and 263.6021 govern extended foster care and trial independence after 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Texas offers Extended Foster Care to age 21, and to age 22 to finish high school, for youth who sign a voluntary foster care agreement. To stay in care the youth must be in school or vocational training, working at least 80 hours a month, in a program to remove barriers to employment, or unable to do those things because of a disability; youth who leave can return to extended care, and a Supervised Independent Living option lets them live on their own while still in care. — help after leaving care DFPS Transitional Living Services, including the Preparation for Adult Living (PAL) program, serve youth ages 14 to 23 with life-skills training, a Transitional Living Allowance, and Aftercare Room and Board help. Youth who were in foster care at 18 keep Former Foster Care Children's Medicaid until age 26, can get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year until age 23, and can use the state College Tuition and Fee Waiver at Texas public colleges if they enroll before age 27. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services or a licensed child-placing agency that works with DFPS. Applicants must be at least 21, financially stable, pass criminal history and abuse/neglect background checks for household members age 14 and older, complete a home study and free training, and hold CPR and first aid certification. — kinship care Yes — kinship caregivers are the preferred placement in Texas, and relatives or close family friends can care for a child in DFPS conservatorship. Kinship caregivers can get a monthly Relative and Other Designated Caregiver (RODC) payment and one-time placement help, and they can become verified kinship foster homes under separate kinship standards for extra financial support; relatives who take permanent care may qualify for Permanency Care Assistance. — Texas Department of Family and Protective Services Lone Star Legal Aid — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Utah Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Utah
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Utah — when youth age out A youth ages out of DCFS custody at 18. The juvenile court's jurisdiction over a minor's case can continue until the youth is 21, unless ended earlier by court order, under Utah Code section 78A-6-120. — staying in care longer Utah does not run a standard Title IV-E extended foster care program that keeps youth in a foster placement to age 21. Instead, DCFS provides Transition to Adult Living (TAL) services, including a supervised TAL placement for youth age 16 and older and aftercare services for youth who age out or are adopted from foster care at 16 or older, up to age 23, under Utah Admin. Code R512-305; youth work with a Child and Family Team on a TAL plan covering housing, education, and employment. — help after leaving care Through TAL and the federal Chafee program, Utah youth can get aftercare support, life-skills training, and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) for college or job training up to age 23. Youth who reached 18 in DCFS or tribal custody can get Medicaid as independent foster care adolescents until age 21 under Utah Code section 26B-3-201, and kinship caregivers can get help through a Specified Relative Grant from the Division of Workforce Services. — becoming a foster parent Apply through the Utah Division of Child and Family Services or Utah Foster Care, which provides the training for licensed resource families. Applicants must be 21 or older, be single or a legally married couple, pass background checks for everyone 18 and older in the home, complete agency-approved pre-service training and CPR/first aid, and pass a home study. — kinship care Yes — kinship care is the preferred placement when a child cannot safely stay home, and preference goes first to a noncustodial parent, then to relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles, siblings, and first cousins, then to a family friend willing to become a licensed foster parent for that child. Kinship caregivers can get support through the Children's Service Society Grandfamilies program and a Specified Relative Grant, and kinship applicants as young as 18 can seek a kinship-specific license under Utah Admin. Code R501-12-16. — Utah Division of Child and Family Services, Utah Department of Health and Human Services Utah Legal Services — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Vermont Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Vermont
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Vermont — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. Vermont law, 33 V.S.A. section 4904, then provides transitional foster care services for youth ages 18 to 22 who turned 18 in DCF custody or spent at least five years in DCF custody between ages 10 and 18. — staying in care longer Yes — Vermont provides foster care services to age 22, longer than most states, for youth who elect to continue after 18 or who left custody after age 16 and ask for support before age 22. To stay in the program the youth must be employed, in a program to promote employment or remove barriers to it, or in an educational or vocational program, unless excused for a disability or other good cause, and must sign a voluntary services agreement. — help after leaving care DCF's Youth Development Program provides transition and aftercare case management, housing assistance, transportation, and help getting and keeping health care coverage and employment, and the federal Chafee program serves Vermont youth up to age 23. Youth can get the Vermont Chafee Education and Training Scholarship of up to $5,000 a year through the Vermont Student Assistance Corporation (VSAC), and Vermont law also provides grants for former DCF youth accepted for degree study at Vermont public colleges. — becoming a foster parent Contact the resource coordinator at your local DCF Family Services district office to apply for a foster care license. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks including fingerprints for household members age 16 and older, pass home visits and a home safety review, and complete Orientation and Foundations for Foster Care training; licenses are valid for up to three years. — kinship care Yes — about 44 percent of children in DCF custody are placed with someone they already know, such as a relative, family friend, or other trusted adult. Relatives and kin can become licensed kinship foster parents through the same process as other foster parents and receive a monthly stipend, and the court can also transfer temporary custody to a noncustodial parent or relative under 33 V.S.A. section 5308. — Vermont Department for Children and Families, Family Services Division Vermont Legal Aid — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Virginia
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Virginia — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. Virginia's Fostering Futures program, Va. Code sections 63.2-917 through 63.2-920, then offers voluntary continued services and support to youth ages 18 to 21 who were in foster care when they turned 18. — staying in care longer Yes — the Fostering Futures program lets youth stay in foster care to age 21 if they turned 18 in foster care on or after July 1, 2016, or left a Department of Juvenile Justice commitment between 18 and 21 after being in foster care. To qualify the youth must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in postsecondary or vocational education, in a program to promote employment or remove barriers to it, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things for a documented medical reason, and must sign a Voluntary Continuing Services and Support Agreement; youth may exit and re-enter as often as needed before 21. — help after leaving care Fostering Futures participants get housing and placement support, case management, and medical care under the state Medicaid plan, plus independent living services. The John H. Chafee Foster Care Program serves Virginia youth in care from age 14 and those who left care after 14, up to age 23, and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) help youth ages 16 to 26 pay for postsecondary education. — becoming a foster parent Start through Foster Virginia and the Faster Families Highway by creating an account, which connects you with your local department of social services for a six-step readiness process. Applicants complete training, background checks, and a mutual family assessment before approval; you do not need to be married, own a home, or already have children. — kinship care Yes — Virginia prioritizes kinship care, and relatives or close family friends can become approved kinship foster (resource) parents when a child enters foster care. Other kinship options include a Parental Child Safety Placement of up to 90 days, a court-ordered custody transfer, and KinGAP, a kinship guardianship assistance program that pays monthly support to a relative who becomes the child's permanent legal guardian. — Virginia Department of Social Services Legal Aid Justice Center — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Washington Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Washington
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Washington — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. Washington law, RCW 13.34.267 and 74.13.031, lets a dependent youth who turns 18 in care continue in Extended Foster Care to age 21. — staying in care longer Yes — Extended Foster Care runs to age 21 for youth who were dependent and in foster care at 18 and who sign a voluntary placement agreement. To stay eligible the youth must be in a secondary education program, enrolled in or intending to enroll in postsecondary or vocational education, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition; youth can enter, leave, and re-enter as often as they wish before 21, and can live in a foster home or in supervised independent living. — help after leaving care Youth who leave foster care at or after 18 keep Apple Health (Medicaid) until age 26, and DCYF provides Independent Living Services to youth up to age 23. Washington also runs a Postextended Foster Care program for young adults ages 21 through 25 who were dependent at 18 or took part in Extended Foster Care, with supportive services, a financial subsidy, and housing navigation, and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) help pay for college or job training. — becoming a foster parent Apply through DCYF's Licensing Division or a licensed Child Placing Agency, starting with DCYF's foster parent inquiry form. Applicants must be over 21, complete pre-service training including Caregiver Core Training, first aid and CPR, and mandatory reporter training, pass background checks and fingerprinting for household members age 16 and older, and complete a home study; licensing takes about 120 days. — kinship care Yes — relatives and family friends can care for a child in foster care, and to receive monthly foster care payments they must get a kinship (child-specific) license through DCYF or a private or tribal Child Placing Agency. The kinship license requires a home safety inspection, background checks and fingerprinting, and a home study, and is valid for three years. — Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families Northwest Justice Project — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: West Virginia Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in West Virginia
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in West Virginia — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18. West Virginia law defines a 'transitioning adult' as a youth age 18 to 21 who was in department custody at 18 and enters a contract to continue an education, training, or treatment program, under W. Va. Code sections 49-1-202 and 49-4-110. — staying in care longer Yes — transitioning adults ages 18 to 21 who were in department custody at 18 can stay in or return to foster care by contracting with the department to continue an education, training, or treatment program. To stay eligible the youth must be finishing secondary education, enrolled in postsecondary or vocational education, in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition; transitional living placements are available from age 17 up to age 23 for youth who meet the criteria. — help after leaving care West Virginia's MODIFY program supports youth ages 18 to 23 who aged out of care, were adopted at 16 or older, or entered guardianship at 16 or older, with counseling, college preparation, financial help, and independent living services. Youth can also get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year for school, a foster care tuition waiver for postsecondary education, an independent living subsidy, and continued Medicaid coverage as former foster youth until age 26. — becoming a foster parent Start by completing the Foster Parent Inquiry Form with the Bureau for Social Services or contacting Mission West Virginia, which connects families with the private agencies that certify foster homes. Applicants must be 21 to 65 unless a waiver is granted, attend a pre-service orientation, complete training and a home study with background and protective-services checks on all adults in the home, and then receive approval. — kinship care Yes — West Virginia focuses heavily on kinship care, and relatives are the first placement choice when a child cannot stay home. The Bureau for Social Services certifies relative providers directly, and kinship caregivers can get kinship care payments and support; Legal Aid of West Virginia also runs a Kinship Care Services program for relative caregivers. — West Virginia Department of Human Services, Bureau for Social Services Legal Aid of West Virginia — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Wisconsin Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Wisconsin
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Wisconsin — when youth age out A youth ages out of out-of-home care at 18, when the placement order normally ends. Wisconsin law, Wis. Stat. section 48.366, allows a narrow extension past 18 only for a full-time secondary school student with an individualized education program (IEP) in effect. — staying in care longer Only narrowly — a youth who is a full-time student at a secondary school or its vocational or technical equivalent, with an IEP in effect, can stay in out-of-home care under an extended court order or a voluntary transition-to-independent-living agreement until they get a high school or equivalency diploma or turn 21, whichever comes first. Youth who do not meet both the full-time student and IEP conditions do not qualify for extended care, though they can re-enter before 21 if they later meet the conditions. — help after leaving care Wisconsin provides Independent Living services and Chafee-funded transition support, and the federal Chafee program serves Wisconsin youth up to age 23. Youth who age out can get Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, and youth who were in foster care and on Medicaid at 18 can keep Medicaid coverage as former foster youth until age 26. — becoming a foster parent Contact the county where you live, your tribe, or a private Child Placing Agency — counties, tribes, and child-placing agencies license foster parents in Wisconsin under Wis. Admin. Code chapter DCF 56. The agency will explain the application, background checks, home study, and pre-placement training, and the Wisconsin Family Connections Center offers free resources and support to foster, kinship, guardianship, and adoptive families. — kinship care Yes — Wisconsin tries first to place a child with a relative or like-kin caregiver, and a child's foster parent may be a relative, like-kin, or nonrelative. Relative caregivers can get kinship care payments under Wis. Stat. section 48.57 and Wis. Admin. Code chapter DCF 58, and a relative caring for a child under a court order or voluntary transition agreement generally must also apply for a foster home license. — Wisconsin Department of Children and Families Legal Action of Wisconsin — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan

p: Wyoming Legal Resources — The Legal Buffet
h: Foster care & youth aging out in Wyoming
t: foster care aging out extended foster care youth transition kinship — Foster care & youth aging out in Wyoming — when youth age out A youth ages out of foster care at 18, when orders under the Child Protection Act normally end. Under Wyo. Stat. section 14-3-431, the court must hold a review hearing at least six months before the youth turns 18 to decide whether care or transitional services should continue, and for how long, before age 21. — staying in care longer Yes, by court order — the court can order care or transitional services to continue past 18, up to age 21, after that pre-18 review hearing. The statute does not spell out activity requirements for staying in care, and Wyoming law does not allow re-entry once a youth has left care. — help after leaving care Wyoming's Chafee-funded Independent Living Program helps youth aging out with life-skills classes, education and job training help, and housing and employment support, and Education and Training Vouchers (ETV) help pay for college or vocational training. Youth who were in DFS or tribal foster care and on federally funded Medicaid at 18 can apply for the Former Foster Youth Medicaid program, which can cover them until age 26. — becoming a foster parent Contact a Foster Care Coordinator at your local Wyoming Department of Family Services office to learn about becoming a foster care provider. Applicants must be at least 21, single or a couple, in good physical and emotional health, financially stable, and pass criminal history and child abuse/neglect checks; foster parents complete an 18-hour orientation before caring for children and 18 hours of training each year. — kinship care Yes — Wyoming prioritizes placing children with relatives or family members before other options, after background checks and assessments of the relative's home. Relatives can become certified foster parents, and the state offers a Guardianship Assistance Program with financial help for relative caregivers who take permanent custody of a child from foster care. — Wyoming Department of Family Services Legal Aid of Wyoming — Medicaid to 26 education training voucher Chafee independent living housing transition plan
